Bangladesh tribunal orders 3 journalists held until trial in 2024 uprising case
DHAKA, Bangladesh (AP) — A special tribunal in Bangladesh’s capital on Monday asked authorities to keep three journalists jailed until their trial in a case involving a mass uprising that ousted former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina from office in 2024, lawyers said.
During the student-led uprising, hundreds of people were killed, and Hasina was later sentenced to death on charges of crimes against humanity. She fled to India two years ago and was tried in absentia.
The tribunal asked that Mozammel Babu, editor-in-chief of private Ekattor Television, its principal correspondent Farzana Rupa and Shyamal Dutta, editor of daily Bhorer Kagoj and former general secretary of the National Press Club in Dhaka, remain jailed.
After they appeared before the tribunal on Monday, the judge fixed Oct. 25 for the next court proceedings and asked the investigators to submit their findings against the journalists.
Global human rights groups have criticized the jailing of the journalists and the denial of bail, asking the government to drop the charges against them and stop criminalizing news reporting.
Prosecutors allege the three journalists incited the suppression of student demonstrators during the uprising. They say that the journalists asked Hasina provocative questions at a press conference on July 14, 2024, that led her to make disparaging remarks about the demonstrators before launching a bloody crackdown on the protesters leading to hundreds of deaths.
The three journalists have been in custody for years following Hasina’s ouster as they face various charges including murder involving the uprising in July-August 2024. They were arrested during an interim government headed by Nobel Peace Prize laureate Muhammad Yunus who handed over power in February to a new government.
The families of the journalists complained that they were held illegally.
“Launching a crimes-against-humanity case against journalists Shyamal Dutta, Mozammel Babu, and Farzana Rupa for simply asking questions at a press conference is outrageous and deeply troubling,” Kunal Majumder, CPJ’s Asia-Pacific Program Coordinator, said in a statement earlier this month.
He added that “editorial decisions may be partisan or ethically questionable, but they cannot be criminalized. Criminalizing editorial judgment sets a dangerous precedent and undermines Bangladesh’s reputation as a democracy. Authorities must immediately release the three journalists and drop the charges.”
Hasina has been in India since Aug. 5, 2024, but recently she said she would return to the country in December. The Yunus-led government and incumbent administration of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman requested India to extradite Hasina, but India refused.

Hungarian air force Gripen jet crashes, pilot ejects safely, prime minister says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
10:23:01 UTC
19:23:01 KST

Hungarian air force Gripen jet crashes, pilot ejects safely, prime minister says
BUDAPEST, Hungary (AP) — A Hungarian military pilot ejected safely when his fighter jet crashed on Monday, Prime Minister Péter Magyar said.
The Swedish-made JAS 39 Gripen came down near the city of Szolnok in central Hungary “for reasons that are still unknown,” Magyar wrote in a post on Facebook. An investigation into the incident is underway and Minister of Defense Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi was on his way to the scene, he added.
Ruszin-Szendi said the pilot was “alive and has not sustained any injuries.”
“It appears the pilot did everything he could to ensure the crashed aircraft landed on military property,” Ruszin-Szendi said in a video on Facebook, adding he was traveling to the crash site with the chief of staff of the Hungarian defense forces.
Mihály Győrfi, the mayor of Szolnok, told local media that the pilot “was probably training as usual” at the helicopter base just outside the city, and confirmed that there were no known injuries resulting from the crash.
Hungary has 18 JAS 39 Gripen fighters, 14 of which were acquired through a lease-purchase program launched in 2001 and four others that were ordered in 2024 and joined the fleet this year.

Indonesia intensifies aerial firefighting as forest fires scorch multiple provinces

Indonesia intensifies aerial firefighting as forest fires scorch multiple provinces
JAKARTA, Indonesia (AP) — Indonesia on Monday intensified ground and aerial firefighting operations as huge blazes in central and western parts of the country scorched thousands of hectares of forests and peatland, created a choking haze that blanketed cities and crossed borders.
Indonesian authorities have been battling fires driven by an intensifying El Nino pattern and a prolonged dry season, generating dense smoke that crossed into Malaysia and Brunei, according to Indonesia’s National Disaster Management Agency, or BNPB.
The BNPB said Monday that fires remain active in several regions, while large-scale suppression efforts continue in fire-prone provinces including West, Central and South Kalimantan on Borneo island and in Riau, South Sumatra and Jambi on Sumatra island. The fires are part of a broader surge in wildfire activity across Indonesia this year.
After visiting areas devastated by forest and peatland fires in Central Kalimantan on Saturday, Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto flew to fire-affected Riau province on Sumatra island, where more than 11,500 hectares (28,400 acres) have burned, to encourage authorities to get the haze cloud under control.
Prabowo vowed the government would continue supporting firefighting operations, including through the deployment of additional water-bombing helicopters and oxygen supplies for firefighters. He urged authorities to “thoroughly document and report the work being carried out by firefighting teams” directly to him.
The Transportation Ministry said it has authorized the use of 35 foreign-registered aircraft to support wildfire response operations, including water-bombing missions and aerial patrols. The ministry said the aircraft can be rapidly redeployed to disaster-hit areas as conditions change, while complying with Indonesian aviation safety regulations.
The Environment Ministry satellite data on Monday showed South Sumatra recorded the highest number of hot spots nationwide with 1,429, followed by West Kalimantan with 1,226 and Central Kalimantan with 811. East Kalimantan logged 576 hot spots, ahead of Riau with 503, while West Papua and Jambi recorded 468 and 458 hot spots, respectively.
Forestry Ministry data indicated that nearly 94,000 hectares (232,000 acres) burned in July alone.
Drought, strong winds and dry vegetation have complicated efforts to contain the fires, BNPB said in a statement on Monday. Some hot spots remained inaccessible to more than 10,700 ground firefighters who were deployed as of Sunday, prompting local officials to request additional water-bombing support and firefighting vehicles.
Cloud-seeding resumed over Kalimantan on Monday, with 30 helicopters for water-bombing and aerial patrol missions, and another 22 helicopters covering Sumatra.
Fires are a regular problem during dry season in Indonesia, a vast archipelago nation of more than 17,000 islands, and often strain relations with neighbors. Plantation owners and traditional farmers often start fires to clear land for farming. It triggers hazardous haze that reduces visibility, disrupts land and air transportation and threatens public health, sometimes affecting neighboring countries in Southeast Asia.
Meanwhile, Malaysia has suffered severe smoke from the fires, with its eastern state of Sarawak among the hardest hit, prompting the closure of nearly 600 schools and affecting about 200,000 students, the Sarawak government said.
___
Associated Press writer Eileen Ng in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, contributed to this report.

Haredi protesters plan demonstration on Highway 4 following arrest of draft dodger
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
10:22:47 UTC
19:22:47 KST

Dozens of haredi (ultra-Orthodox) protesters from the Jerusalem Faction (Peleg Yerushalmi) plan to block Highway 4 near Bnei Brak on Monday afternoon to protest the arrest of a haredi draft dodger, according to Israeli media.
The protest is expected to begin at 5:00 p.m.
Protests by the haredi community against the military draft and the arrest of draft dodgers have spurred numerous demonstrations throughout the year, resulting in the shutdown of multiple public transportation routes and key highways.
A-G calls for renewed arrests
Earlier this week, Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara called for renewed arrests and stricter economic sanctions against military draft evaders. She warned that weak enforcement against ultra-Orthodox men is undermining the draft process, ultimately leaving potential recruits out of the army and leading to unequal enforcement compared to the rest of the population.
The Attorney-General’s Office released these findings in a summary of an August 3 meeting chaired by Baharav-Miara that reviewed the enforcement of draft obligations for the 2025 draft year.
Military officials said the gap is closely tied to who is actually arrested.
Criminal proceedings typically begin when enforcement authorities detain a draft evader or when the evader voluntarily reports to a military facility. Fewer arrests result in fewer prosecutions.
Baharav-Miara concluded that the current level of criminal enforcement does not satisfy the requirements of the state. According to the summary, military officials warned that this gap harms effective draft enforcement, leaving recruitment potential unrealized and resulting in unequal enforcement against different sectors of the population.
Despite these issues, the review noted that Haredi enlistment has increased significantly over the past year.

Iran weapons smuggling to Hezbollah sparks Israeli debate over IDF strategy, Netanyahu's motives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
10:22:04 UTC
19:22:04 KST

Controversy is growing about the extent to which Iran is smuggling weapons to Hezbollah through Syria, with defense sources, probably connected to Defense Minister Israel Katz, leaking that the issue is heating up, while the IDF has said that there is no major change taking place.
A spokesman for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that a report by Channel 12 based on the anonymous defense sources did not come from them, but advocated that it correctly sized up the increasingly problematic situation.
Following Ahmad al-Sharaa taking power in Syria in December 2024, he cracked down on smuggling weapons through his territory to Hezbollah, given that he is Sunni and had been fighting Hezbollah for around a decade.
While al-Sharaa's relations with Israel have been cold to date, his cracking down on Iranian smuggling to Hezbollah has been a significant fringe benefit for Israel in keeping the Lebanese terror group from rearming.
This latest leak comes as there is a lively public debate about whether Israel will need to withdraw from part of its buffer zone in Syria and whether the IDF will need to carry out fewer military actions in Syria - all of this following a controversial Israeli attack on a Syrian airport in recent days.
Critics say Netanyahu creating unnecessary tensions with Syria, Turkey
Critics of Netanyahu say that he, and possibly then the defense sources leaking the latest report, are trying to unnecessarily create tension and fear related to Syria and Turkey for electoral purposes.
Netanyahu, Katz, and some IDF sources have said that the recent attack was necessary to prevent Turkey from encroaching on IDF freedom of military action in Syria.
Adding in the idea that smuggling from Iran to Hezbollah through Syria is a returning and growing problem would support the narrative that Israel must continue to act aggressively in Syria and that the recent attack, which led to a public fight with the US which wants Jerusalem to make more concessions to al-Sharaa as part of efforts to bring him deeper into the Western sphere of influence, was necessary and not political.
The fact that the IDF and the anonymous defense sources seem to disagree on that issue leaves a hazy picture of how large a problem increased weapons smuggling is.
No sources debate that Syria cannot hermetically seal off Iranian smuggling to Hezbollah, but IDF sources say that there has not been any spike in that smuggling recently compared to nearly the last two years under al-Sharaa.

Pakistan to hold talks in Tehran as US threatens Iran with ‘economic D-Day’

Pakistan to hold talks in Tehran as US threatens Iran with ‘economic D-Day’
- Pakistan’s army chief visited Tehran to mediate, as the US prepared its largest financial sanctions against Iran and its trade partners.
- Iran threatened to stop all oil exports from the Gulf if economic sanctions continue and warned ships not to pass the Strait of Hormuz without permission.
- The US aims to cripple Iran’s economy, as Iran warns an economic war may provoke military retaliation.
AI generated
DUBAI – Pakistan’s army chief flew to Tehran on a mediating mission on Aug 24 as the United States prepared to roll out “the greatest financial offensive ever” targeting Iran’s trade partners.
Iran dismissed the US threat, vowing to shut down all oil exports from the Gulf “if the economic war continues” and issued a new warning to shipping not to pass through the Strait of Hormuz without its permission.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has promised to reveal severe measures on Iran, which has endured near-continuous economic sanctions since the Islamic Revolution of 1979, when he gives a news conference on Aug 24.
“At dawn begins an economic D-Day – the single greatest financial offensive ever marshalled against an adversary,” Bessent wrote in an opinion piece published in the Financial Times on Aug 23.
Pakistan’s army chief Asim Munir, who has built a personal rapport with US President Donald Trump, arrived in Iran for talks, Iranian media said.
Pakistan said the visit was part of its efforts “to promote regional peace and stability”, and a Pakistani source said Munir was expected to meet people close to Iran’s supreme leader.
Tehran has said Oman’s foreign minister will visit on Aug 25 to discuss the Strait of Hormuz.
The US and Iran have not conducted strikes against each other’s militaries for weeks, but their last official face-to-face talks to end the six-month-old conflict took place in June, and strikes on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz have continued.
A projectile struck a tanker west of the Saudi port city of Yanbu in the Red Sea on Aug 24, causing a fire on the main deck, shipping monitors from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said. They did not say who launched the projectile.
Iran’s Houthi allies said in July they would block Saudi oil exports diverted to the Red Sea to avoid Hormuz.
Thousands of people have died, most of them in Iran and Lebanon, since the US and Israel began strikes on Feb 28, degrading much of Iran’s conventional military capacity and inflicting economic pain while killing Iran’s then-supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
But Iran has preserved enough missile and drone capability to attack its Gulf neighbours and threaten oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, bringing shipping in the key waterway to a near standstill and pressuring world fuel prices.
The exact state of Iran’s nuclear programme, which the Americans and Israelis aim to wipe out, remains unknown.
Oil prices slipped more than US$1 a barrel on Aug 24 as investors took profits ahead of the expected US announcement.
Without detailing specific measures, Bessent signalled the US would target “fearful nations” that practise “appeasement” by engaging with Iran’s economy and financial system.
“They would do well to consider the consequences of sustaining it,” he wrote in the Financial Times.
Iran has been bracing itself for the sanctions for days, issuing a series of strongly worded statements hinting at a major military response.
Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, suggested economic retaliation on Aug 23.
“If the economic war continues, not a single drop of oil will be exported, neither through the Strait of Hormuz nor from anywhere in the Persian Gulf,” Rezaei wrote in a social media post. “Iran will regard any country’s participation in or support for America’s economic war against the Iranian people as an act of war.”
Sanctions won’t work, says China
Bessent had urged China to cooperate with the US, noting China historically has received half of its oil imports from the Gulf region.
China’s foreign ministry said on Aug 24 that sanctions and pressure tactics do not help resolve issues, and that Beijing will do what is necessary to protect Chinese interests.
Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi dismissed the latest moves from Washington, which has said the measures will bring down the Iranian government, saying the US has been promising Iran’s end for 48 years, “each time under a new name”.
“Iran has remained steadfast and powerful, and only the names of the failed projects have changed,” he said on X.
Iran’s economy was already under pressure from international sanctions before the US and Israeli attacks destroyed parts of its infrastructure.
Though Tehran remains outwardly defiant, Iranian officials who spoke to Reuters have expressed concern that further economic punishment could increase hardships, reignite unrest and further erode Iran’s legitimacy.
Iran entered the war with high inflation, a weakening currency, energy shortages, sanctions and deep structural weaknesses, and must now contend with damaged infrastructure, disrupted trade, lost production and the cost of rebuilding. REUTERS

Taiwan environment ministry targets fraudulent grout pen ads
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
10:17:29 UTC
19:17:29 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of Environment said Monday it has never certified or issued permits for grout pens, according to a ministry press release.
The ministry said advertisements on Facebook and YouTube were promoting mold-resistant and waterproof grout pens for bathroom and kitchen tiles while falsely claiming that the products had received ministry certification. It urged consumers not to be deceived by the ads.
A grout pen resembles a felt-tip marker and is used to cover discolored grout between tiles. The ministry said unscrupulous businesses had attempted to deceive consumers by falsely claiming official certification.
The ministry has notified Facebook and Google Taiwan to remove the ads, restrict access to them, or stop displaying them within 24 hours under Article 32 of the Fraud Crime Hazard Prevention Act. It has also asked the Ministry of Digital Affairs to contact Meta and Google’s US headquarters to remove the fraudulent content.
The ministry said consumers should look for the Green Mark when selecting environmentally friendly products. They can verify certified products through the ministry’s Net-Zero Green Living Information Platform.
Suspected fraudulent advertisements can be reported through the ministry’s environmental hotline or the Ministry of Digital Affairs’ online fraud-reporting platform.
The Green Mark is Taiwan’s most authoritative label for environmentally friendly consumption and is based on the principles of recyclability, low pollution, and resource conservation. More than 26,000 certificates have been issued.
The ministry encouraged consumers to look for the label when purchasing cleaning products, building materials, and daily necessities.

Historic Yunlin police bureau to become county history museum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
10:17:07 UTC
19:17:07 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — A historic former police headquarters in Yunlin County will be restored and transformed into the Yunlin County History Museum, with a ceremony Monday marking the start of the project.
The Yunlin County Government is investing NT$46.5 million (US$1.46 million) in the restoration and adaptive reuse project, which is scheduled for completion in February 2028, per CNA.
The future museum will feature permanent and special exhibitions, historical documents, and digital archives. It will preserve Yunlin’s historical memory while providing resources for research, education, and cultural exchange.
Yunlin County Magistrate Chang Li-shan (張麗善) presided over the ceremony. Chang said Yunlin County was officially established on Oct. 25, 1950, and the existing front building was completed in December of the same year.
The building was subsequently used by the Yunlin County Police Bureau and the Douliu Precinct, witnessing the development of local government and policing in the county.
It was registered as a historic building in 2019. After police operations were gradually relocated to newer facilities, the building became available for a new cultural role.
Chang said the restoration would follow the principles of preserving the original appearance and minimizing intervention while balancing historical preservation, structural safety, and the requirements of future use.
The museum will document Yunlin’s administrative development, local history, and cultural assets while incorporating material from the Yunlin County Gazetteer.
Architect Chen Po-hong (陳柏宏), who is supervising the restoration, said the project would preserve the front building’s postwar government-office characteristics, including its brick and timber construction.
Restoration work will preserve or repair architectural details including the entrance porte-cochere, pebble-finished exterior walls, wooden doors and windows, and window sills.
Structural repairs will include work on the roof tiles, doors, windows, and exterior walls. Water and electrical systems will also be upgraded, along with fire-safety and accessibility facilities.

Rotterdam council sacks building officials over corrupt payments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
10:15:01 UTC
19:15:01 KST

Rotterdam council sacks building officials over corrupt payments
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Two civil servants have been dismissed in Rotterdam for corruption after an investigation found they accepted gifts from contractors working on city building projects.
The sackings were confirmed after prosecutors told the council executive that a fraud investigation had revealed “substantially more serious” allegations than were initially suspected.
The prosecution said a total of 11 people and six companies were implicated in the fraud inquiry. The NRC newspaper quoted sources who said the companies submitted inflated estimates with the help of the civil servants.
One of the officials, a project manager, used a company he set up to support promising young footballers as a slush fund to channel payments from a building firm working on cultural renovations.
After he took early retirement, the prosecution service began investigating allegations that he and a colleague had accepted bribes and forged documents, in breach of the law and the city’s code of ethics.
A third colleague was dismissed at the end of 2023 in connection with the criminal investigation.
Houses and business premises in The Hague, Echt, Capelle aan den IJssel and Nieuwekerk were searched in the course of the inquiry. They include the home of one of the civil servants, who both worked in the City Development department.
Boijmans van Beuningen
One of the projects was the removal of asbestos from the Boijmans van Beuningen museum. An earlier investigation by NRC found that the council had paid at least €3 million too much for the project.
The company that won the contract. Brabant-based A van Liempd, employed four people at the time, only one of whom was qualified to supervise asbestos removal.
The company based its estimate on the assumption that 5.7km of air vents would need to be stripped, but less than half the installation was found to contain asbestos. It also promised to use an innovative technique to contain carcinogenic materials, but carried out most of the work with standard methods, NRC reported.
A lawyer for the company would not comment because of the ongoing investigation.

Talk of Ukrainian victory like ‘Groundhog Day’ – ex-US official (VIDEO)
Repeated claims that Ukraine is about to turn the tide against Russia and achieve a military victory are like being trapped in a time loop, a former White House official has told RT.
The latest wave of media reports predicting a breakthrough in Kiev’s military campaign came on the heels of an escalation in Ukrainian long-range drone strikes on Russian oil refineries, retail warehouses, and cargo ships. Ukrainian officials claimed the attacks would pressure Moscow into accepting Kiev’s terms for a peace settlement.
Russia instead intensified its own strikes, virtually paralyzing crucial Ukrainian trade through Black Sea ports and inflicting other damage. On Sunday, President Vladimir Putin said Kiev was the one that “opened Pandora’s box.”
“I feel like the old American movie ‘Groundhog Day’,” conservative media host Steve Gill, who served in the office of the US Trade Representative under Presidents George H. W. Bush and Bill Clinton, told RT.
“How many times do we have to hear, ‘oh, it’s the spring offensive, the fall offensive, the summer offensive, the winter offensive that is going to win things for Ukraine? And it is the same cycle of promise and despair, promise and failure that, again, has done nothing but cost the lives of both Russian and Ukrainian men and increasingly women,” he added.
Gill also suggested that Ukrainians who want to end the hostilities are in no position to do so because the country does not determine its own foreign policy.
“The ones who are making the decisions in Western Europe – and some in the United States, some who have the ear of President [Donald] Trump – are feeding misinformation and disinformation both through media and through the policymakers that is continuing the violence, continuing the death, and continuing this folly of Ukraine thinking that they’re somehow winning on the battlefield when nothing could be further from the truth,” he explained.

Children’s Digital Rights Need More Than a False Promise of Safety
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
10:12:01 UTC
19:12:01 KST

By Lisa Dittmer, Amnesty International’s Children’s Digital Rights Researcher, and Paloma Candia and Ahmed Dhman both Amnesty International’s Digital Rights Champions, a global network of child and youth human rights defenders.
This article was first published in TechPolicy.Press
Children’s online safety has become a leading political issue as concerns about Big Tech harms have moved from academic debates to bestseller lists and mainstream news. French President Emmanuel Macron hailed France’s teen social media ban as “leading the way in Europe in protecting our children and our teenagers.” France’s top court later blocked the law, citing privacy and freedom of expression concerns. United Nations (UN) Secretary-General Guterres has called for an artificial intelligence (AI) Child Safety Pledge. Yet amid the flurry of high-level pledges and the rush to protect “our children,” the voices of one demographic are noticeably absent: children themselves.
A brief prerecorded video aside, not a single child got to speak when a new state coalition for the protection of children launched its work at the UN AI Dialogue in July. Kenya, one of the state parties to the coalition, is currently debating a new AI bill that lacks any child-specific protections or consultation mechanism. The absence of children and young people in policymaking spaces and the failure to recognize their demands and needs are clearly linked. Globally, a mixture of Big Tech state capture, political shortsightedness and a rise in digital authoritarian practices is hollowing out children’s rights just as the world proclaims to finally making children safe online.
Mitigating harm rather than fulfilling rights
Children and young people are frequently treated as passive subjects who need to be saved through regulation rather than as participants in shaping the rules that affect them. The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child recognizes children’s right to be heard, but their participation all too often remains tokenistic at best. Inviting comments from a select number of children within predefined confines and without means to materially shape processes and outcomes isn’t meaningful participation.
It is this paternalistic attitude that increasingly reduces children’s digital rights issues to a question of mitigating harm, rather than the fulfillment of their rights and the creation of a positive digital future. While social media harms need urgent addressing, teen social media bans exemplify the resulting performative politics, which seek to appease an adult voter base rather than address the root causes of tech harms.
Child and youth campaigners have long called for solutions that address the manipulative design choices and the privacy violations common to children’s experiences across social media, games and AI chatbots. Youth-led organizations such as ctrl+alt+reclaim, Design it for Us and Flippgen have been vocal advocates for more nuanced solutions that reflect children’s and young people’s lived experiences.
And still, these calls for systemic change all too often go unheard as political leaders embrace supposed quick wins for “our protection.” Risks such as cyberbullying, grooming, online violence, and problematic social media use need to be tackled, but attempting to lock children out who also rely on these platforms for community, information and activism dismisses a whole set of rights for a false promise of safety. Evidence from Australia shows clear flaws in this thinking: children continue to access the harmful platforms they were meant to be locked out of while those who evade the ban or are never excluded remain exposed to the very harms the policy seeks to tackle. Meanwhile, core challenges to children and young people’s digital rights remain unaddressed.
The normalization of online surveillance in children’s lives
Children and young people are growing up in a world where their personal data is constantly collected, tracked and shared, from the moment online platforms and advertisers pick up on a pregnancy to their first exploration of the digital world through videos and games, and on to schools and universities, which increasingly monitor learners through safeguarding tools, biometric attendance registration and AI-enabled performance analysis and behavior management. In this way, children are trained to grow accustomed to surveillance by a largely invisible network of government and private actors, in most cases without free and informed consent.
Many of the same governments currently debating teenage restrictions on social media enthusiastically embrace the AI hype in education, inviting collaborations with major AI firms to bring chatbots into schools despite serious concerns about the lack of child rights safeguards related to online privacy, manipulative design, discriminatory and otherwise harmful outputs, as well as a lack of research evidence of educational benefits and risks.
Children’s data remains poorly protected and is now at risk of being eroded further by the age assurance tools necessary to enforce teen bans. The global drive is one towards stricter age checks, presenting new risks of additional data trails, cybersecurity incidents and online surveillance by both corporate and state actors. France just sidestepped the question of enforcement of its new teen ban law to avoid a clash with European regulation, but so-called Digital Identity Wallets will soon pervade online experiences across the EU, despite concerns from privacy experts.
Governments including Turkey, Vietnam and the United Arab Emirates are seizing the child online safety moment to propose measures that will further add to existing privacy and free expression concerns affecting child and adult internet users alike.
Casting governments as a force for good amidst increasing digital repression
The current debate also ignores the many ways in which governments actively abuse technology to monitor and silence children and young people. The recent wave of influential Gen Z protests across diverse contexts, including, among others, Bangladesh, India, Nepal, Kenya, Madagascar and Peru, has highlighted the power of digitally connected and social media-savvy youths.
On the flip side, governments are increasingly turning young activists’ social media footprints and data trails into tools of censorship and repression. When students took to the streets of Delhi to demand the resignation of the education minister, the Indian government responded by first shutting down mobile data service in central parts of the city, then came for the Bluetooth-based app that young people had turned to amidst the shutdown. In Kenya, Amnesty International documented how authorities weaponized online harassment and surveillance to quell nationwide youth-led protests in 2024 and 2025. Big data analysis tools are already taking state surveillance capacities to new levels, facilitating crackdowns on migrants and protesters alike.
All of these are critical challenges to the digital rights of children and young people, which the current narrow fixation on social media bans overlooks. Politics that attempt to shut out the youth instead of working with them will fail, as Australian teens and Indian students are powerfully proving.
Nothing about us without us
Children and young people finally need to be meaningfully included in all their diversity as critical experts of their own experiences if their rights and safety are to be more than a step toward increased internet control and willful disenfranchisement.
Instead of tokenistic one-off engagements, governments need to create opportunities for children to feed into digital policy processes in safe and meaningful ways, showing accountability for how their input is reflected in policy, just as tech companies need to co-design products with children if they are to be used by children.
Regulators should look to build towards a positive digital future, investing in digital literacy and creating policies that preserve and reward the benefits of the digital world, rather than simply mitigating harms. That means effectively safeguarding children’s and adults’ privacy, regulating online services by mandating meaningful user choice and agency and banning manipulative design, reigning in Big Tech power and setting effective limits on state surveillance powers.
“Nobody should have to choose between their safety and their voice,” Kenyan high school student Mark Igathe recently wrote in his winning entry to Amnesty Kenya’s annual digital rights essay competition. Policymakers would do well to make more space for those voices and to listen.

For Republicans, Dallas convention is both rally and rescue mission

For Republicans, Dallas convention is both rally and rescue mission
Aug 24 - President Donald Trump's Republican Party is increasingly viewing its first-of-a-kind midterm convention in Dallas next month as crucial to regaining momentum at a time when opinion polls show voter frustration over the economy and the Iran war, according to party officials, donors and convention planners.
When Republicans announced the convention earlier this year, some strategists dismissed it as a distraction as campaigns entered the final stretch. They questioned the need for a national gathering with no official party business.
Now, after months of negative headlines tied to the war and rising living costs, party officials see the September 9-10 gathering as their best opportunity to rally voters behind Trump's agenda as Democrats mount a serious challenge to Republican control of both houses of Congress in the November 3 election. Some Republicans, however, remain skeptical it can meaningfully shift voter sentiment.
The party officials said the event offers a platform to refocus voters on Trump's tax cuts, immigration policies and other achievements. Organizers plan to spotlight Americans they say have benefited from those policies while portraying the Democratic Party as increasingly dominated by socialist ideas and activists, according to a source familiar with the planning.
The party plans to put Trump at the center of the convention, a tactic some strategists warn could backfire by drawing attention to a president with a low approval rating who has repeatedly urged Americans to endure the economic costs of the Iran war.
Republican National Committee spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre said the convention would rally voters behind Trump's agenda, including efforts to lower drug prices, cut taxes and secure the southern border with Mexico.
"President Trump turns out voters like no other candidate, and this convention will provide the momentum needed to expand our majorities in November," Baldassarre said in a statement.
CANDIDATES FACE TRUMP CONVENTION DILEMMA
It remains unclear which congressional candidates will speak during the two-day event. Advisers to three campaigns in competitive districts told Reuters they had yet to be informed whether their candidates would be offered speaking slots.
Reuters contacted representatives for Republican candidates in 37 competitive U.S. House races and eight closely contested U.S. Senate races to ask whether they planned to attend the convention and deliver a speech.
Of the 45, only one campaign offered a substantive response: Republican Representative Tom Barrett, seeking reelection in a tight race in Michigan, who plans to skip the convention and remain on the campaign trail.
"He's in a tough reelection campaign and his voters are in his district," said Jason Cabel Roe, a strategist working for the Barrett campaign.
Still, most of the dozen party insiders interviewed by Reuters, including convention planners and Republican National Committee members, described the convention as the party's best chance to energize Republican voters, whose enthusiasm trails that of Democrats, according to polls.
"There is no better salesman for the country than Donald Trump. I don't think it's going to hurt at all," said Rob Steele, a Republican National Committeeman from Michigan.
Ray Washburne, a Republican donor co-chairing the convention with his wife, told Reuters he expected about 30,000 attendees, a figure that would exceed the seating capacity of the American Airlines Center in Dallas by some 8,000 people. He said organizers raised $42 million and will fully fund the event.
The timing, just at the start of the school year, could pose challenges for some attendees. One state party chair told Reuters he had returned many of his delegation's allotted seats after members said they could not make the schedule work.
While declining to provide a complete speaker list, Washburne said most of Trump's cabinet secretaries would attend, along with "pretty much everyone running in a hot race." Vice President JD Vance will speak on September 9, followed by Trump on September 10.
Dave Wilson, a South Carolina-based Republican strategist, said he was skeptical a rally-style convention would move the needle unless it was used to unveil a major response to voters' top concern: the cost of living.
"I don't know that we're going to see a convention in Dallas change what happens in Cheyenne, Wyoming, or Charleston, South Carolina," Wilson said, invoking places far from the convention to illustrate his point. "I don't think the average Republican voter even knows there's a convention going on."
CANDIDATES SEEK DONORS AND SPOTLIGHT
Though it falls outside the traditional four-year presidential election cycle, the convention is expected to serve a familiar purpose as a fundraising and networking hub for candidates and donors. The RNC has already launched a website selling official convention hats, T-shirts and mugs.
Washburne said the event would give candidates significant media exposure to promote their campaigns. U.S. Senate candidate Ken Paxton of Texas, whose campaign has been dogged by scandal, was someone who could benefit from the attention generated by a convention in his home state, Washburne added.
With Trump's approval rating at 33%, some Republicans questioned the wisdom of the event. One strategist working on a competitive race, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said it made little sense to tie candidates more closely to Trump when many are trying to focus on local issues and win over independent voters.
Oscar Brock, an RNC member from Tennessee, said many candidates would feel obliged to attend the Dallas gathering to court donors and raise their profiles through media appearances, even as some remain wary of embracing Trump. REUTERS

Netherlands won't participate in next year's Eurovision due to Israel
The Netherlands will not participate in next year's Eurovision Song Contest, its broadcaster said Monday, saying the event can "no longer be considered neutral" given divisions over the Israel's genocidal war on Gaza.
"It is undeniable that international conflicts are increasingly affecting the Contest, undermining its neutral character. The Eurovision Song Contest has therefore become a platform for division," said Taco Zimmerman, Director-General of AVROTROS in a statement from the broadcaster.
The contest has recently been hit by a wave of boycotts over Israel's participation.
Earlier this month, organisers announced they were excluding any country involved in an armed conflict from hosting the competition.
"However, the recently announced changes... do not provide sufficient confidence that the independent and neutral character of the Eurovision Song Contest has been restored," said the AVROTROS statement.
Israel came close to winning the competition in both 2025 and 2026, ultimately finishing second on each occasion.
Next year's event, the world's biggest live televised music event, will take place on 15 May in Bulgaria's Black Sea city of Burgas.
It will be the first time that the Balkan nation hosts the contest, coming after Bulgarian singer Darina Yotova, known as Dara, won this year's contest in the Austrian capital Vienna with the catchy floor-filler "Bangaranga".
Since its launch in 1955, Eurovision has become the ultimate pop platform, catapulting Swedish icons ABBA to worldwide fame, as well as boosting the likes of Celine Dion, Cliff Richard and Olivia Newton-John.
The 2026 competition was watched by 131 million viewers, down 35 million on the year before after five countries boycotted it over Israel's participation.
The Netherlands, Iceland, Spain, Ireland and Slovenia all pulled out of the contest, with the latter three refusing to broadcast the show at all due to Israel's inclusion.
The Dutch took part in the very first Eurovision Song Contest back in 1956, and have won on five occasions.
The most recent winner was Duncan Laurence whose song Arcade won the contest in 2019, going on to top charts globally.
It became the first Eurovision entry to reach one billion streams on Spotify, according to the Eurovision website.
The withdrawal is "painful as we would have very much liked to be part of the Contest again next year," said Zimmerman.
"As a public broadcaster, we remain committed to our values. They guide us in everything we do, even when that means stepping away from an event that is very close to our hearts," he added.

Overall, global steel production amounted to 149.2 mln metric tons in July 2026, down 0.3% from a year earlier, according to the association’s report.
The World Steel Association is one of the world’s largest industry associations. Its member companies account for around 85% of global steel production.

====================================================================================================

Psychology researchers uncover an unexpected benefit of dance training
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
10:00:39 UTC
19:00:39 KST

Individuals who practice dance may be better at regulating their physical actions when they encounter positive emotional situations. A recent experiment found that dancers were faster at stopping an ongoing movement when shown happy faces, an advantage not seen in people without dance experience. The research was published in the Psychology of Sport & Exercise.
The ability to stop a physical action you have already started is known as response inhibition. This is a core executive function of the brain that people use every day. For example, you use response inhibition when you suddenly stop yourself from stepping into a crosswalk because a car runs a red light.
Psychologists generally divide this ability into two categories. Proactive inhibition involves anticipating that you might need to stop based on your surroundings. Reactive inhibition, which is the focus of this research, involves abruptly canceling a physical movement in reaction to an unexpected external signal.
In daily life, people often have to inhibit their responses while dealing with emotionally charged situations. Emotional information can easily capture human attention. Sometimes this emotional distraction helps the brain process information faster, and other times it disrupts our physical focus.
Dance offers a unique way to study how the brain handles movement and emotion at the same time. Unlike running or weightlifting, dance requires precise musical coordination and active emotional expression. Dancers must constantly adjust their physical movements while conveying feelings and responding to the emotions of their audience or partners.
Researchers wanted to know if this combination of physical and emotional training gives dancers an edge in controlling their actions. Stuti Mehta and Rashmi Gupta of the Indian Institute of Technology Bombay designed a study to test whether emotional distractions affect dancers differently than non-dancers.
The researchers recruited 83 young adults for the experiment. This group included 45 dancers and 38 people with no dance experience. The dancers had at least six months of formal training and currently practiced for at least six hours a week.
To ensure that general fitness was not the cause of any observed differences, the researchers only included participants who reported low to moderate levels of regular physical activity. The two groups were matched in terms of their overall physical exercise habits.
Participants completed two computer-based tests designed to measure reactive response inhibition. In the first test, participants watched a screen and pressed a specific keyboard key when they saw the letter X or O. They were instructed to respond as quickly as possible.
Occasionally, a green circle appeared over the letter immediately after it was shown. This green circle was a signal to stop and withhold the key press. The computer constantly adjusted the timing of this circle in 50-millisecond increments to keep the task challenging, measuring exactly how fast the participant could hit their mental brakes.
The second test followed the exact same rules, but it used emotional distractions instead of a simple green circle. When it was time to stop the key press, a photograph of a face from a standardized psychological database appeared over the letter. These faces displayed happy, angry, or neutral expressions.
The emotional faces were entirely irrelevant to the core task of identifying the letters. The researchers used them specifically to see if background emotional information would unconsciously alter the participants’ ability to stop their physical actions.
After finishing the computer tasks, participants filled out several questionnaires. These surveys measured their current moods, their typical levels of stress and depression, and their general sensitivity to rewards and punishments in life.
On the first test featuring the green circle, the dancers and non-dancers performed identically. The researchers observed no statistically significant differences in their ability to stop their responses. Without emotional information present, dance training provided no measurable advantage for physical response inhibition.
Different patterns emerged during the second test featuring the human faces. Dancers were much better at stopping their actions when the stop signal was a happy face. They made fewer errors when viewing happy expressions compared to when they saw angry or neutral expressions.
The participants without dance experience performed the exact same way across all face types. The happy faces did not give them any advantage or disadvantage in stopping their physical responses. The emotional content of the faces simply did not alter their physical control.
The questionnaire results aligned with the performance data. Dancers reported lower levels of stress and depression than the non-dancers. They also reported experiencing positive emotions more often and showed a more regulated sensitivity to rewards.
Within the dancer group, the researchers found that more years of dance experience correlated with better mental health. The longer a participant had been engaged in formal dance training, the lower their reported levels of depression and stress tended to be.
The study authors suggest that dance training might make people more sensitive to positive emotions. Dance is often associated with expressing joy and experiencing a sense of meaningful contentment. This repeated engagement with positive feelings might train the brain to process happy stimuli more efficiently.
According to psychological models of attention, positive emotions tend to broaden our mental focus. Negative emotions, on the other hand, tend to narrow our focus onto specific threats. Because dancers are highly attuned to positive expression, a happy face might require fewer mental resources for them to process, leaving more brain power available to successfully stop their physical movement.
Prior brain imaging research supports this idea. Studies have shown that dance training increases activity in areas of the brain like the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and the amygdala. These regions are highly involved in managing emotion regulation and executive functions, which might explain the dancers’ rapid processing of the happy faces.
The study compared two different groups of people at a single point in time. This type of research cannot prove that dance training actually caused the improved response control. It is entirely possible that people who are naturally better at processing positive emotions are simply more likely to pursue dance.
The participants were also mostly young adults, which limits how these findings apply to children or older adults. The dancers practiced a variety of different dance styles. This variety makes it difficult to know if specific types of dance, like ballet or hip-hop, provide different cognitive benefits.
Future research could track individuals over time, testing their cognitive control before and after they enroll in a dance program. Researchers could also use brain imaging technology to see exactly which neural pathways activate when dancers process happy expressions during these tasks.
The study, “Happy faces, faster stops: The cognitive benefits of dance in emotional contexts,” was authored by Stuti Mehta and Rashmi Gupta.

ICE “is putting these [gloves] in the hands of an agency that has dropped its hiring standards, its training, its background requirements in its hiring spree”, Sarah Mehta, deputy director of government affairs in the equality division of the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), said.
“We’re already seeing the consequences of that in lawless and violent enforcement actions in our streets,” she told the Guardian.
“What’s really terrifying is use of them on the streets, potentially to terrify people, to create a chilling effect. But what’s also scary is what [their] uses will be where we can’t see them. We don’t know how they’re going to be used in places like Fort Bliss,”she added, referring to the largest migrant detention facility in the US, where allegations of abuse are legion. The government denies claims of any inhumane conditions.
Mehta further said of the gloves: “There are no circumstances where we think their use is appropriate.”
The device carries the brand name G.L.O.V.E., which stands for Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter, and is manufactured by Compliant Technologies, a company owned by military veterans and based in Lexington, Kentucky. The glove is known as a conductive distraction and de-escalation deviceand can only be sold to certain verified entities, such as law enforcement, corrections, security, military, and emergency medical services (EMS) personnel, and requires training. It works by delivering an electric shock when the user pushes a button on the glove and touches or grips bare skin.
In one demonstration video, a man gives a brief, light touch for approximately one second to the lower back of a prone volunteer, who jerks his body and cries out: “Ow, fuck”.
Compliant Technologies has posted multiple video demonstrations on its Instagram page. In one video from November 2025, a woman wearing the glove grips firmly on the exposed forearm of a volunteer man for about two seconds. The man buckles to the ground, shouting expletives and says “Let me go!”
“I’m going to comply any time,” the man says from the ground in a half-humorous tone to the team running the demonstration. Jeff Niklaus, founder and CEO of Compliant Technologies, can be seen laughing in the video as the man fell to the ground. “Say that louder,” he says.
The man, seemingly a prospective customer, says: “Yeah, we need that [product].”
Compliant Technologies did not respond to a series of questions and requests for comment from the Guardian.
A DHS spokesperson sent this statement in response to questions: “ICE is constantly assessing the needs of our officers in the field to ensure they have the tools and equipment necessary to safely arrest and remove criminal illegal aliens from our country.
“Every decision is made with careful consideration and appropriately reviewed to ensure that any technology ICE utilizes is consistent with all applicable law enforcement policies and standards.”
The minimum voltage for the CT-G5 model is 324 volts, and the maximum is 380 volts. A Taser, by contrast, can typically fire prongs from a distance to incapacitate someone with 1,200 to 1,500 volts.
The glove user manual instructs wearers to avoid using the product on elderly people, small children, pregnant women and disabled people.
The gloves have been deployed to a limited extent in law enforcement, healthcare, and even some educational environments across the country. An estimated 50 police departments across 20 states are using the technology, according to an NPR analysis.
In May 2025, the Omaha police department purchased 40 pairs of gloves to be used in public schools for just under $66,000, according to city documents. The department confirmed in a statement that 29 of its 34 school resource officers (SROs) – typically police providing security full time in schools – have trained in use of the gloves and work in public middle and high schools.
A representative from the Omaha police department shared with the Guardian the report from an incident where the G.L.O.V.E. was used. The report says a female SRO used the shock glove on a male middle school student based on his “highly aggressive and assaultive behavior”. The officer placed the glove on the student’s forearm twice, once for one second, and then again for two to three seconds, which, the report continued, caused the student to drop to the floor, face down.
According to the report, the SRO asked if the student needed medical assistance after being shocked, and he said no.
Last week, Omaha police acceded to a request from the school superintendent to discontinue the gloves in Omaha, Nebraska’s largest public school district, NBC reported.
In a very different example, Joshua Elswick, formerly detained at the Bullitt county jail in Shepherdsville, near Louisville, Kentucky, sued Lt Ryan Derrough alleging excessive force, after Derrough, a guard, used the gloves on Elswick during pre-trial detention.
Elswick, who has paranoid schizophrenia and other serious mental illnesses, according to the lawsuit, was arrested and booked into jail in September 2022 after a domestic dispute involving methamphetamine use. Derrough and another deputy attempted to remove Elswick’s handcuffs and leg shackles before formally taking him into custody, but Elswick was paranoid that the officers were going to kill him and he resisted, whereupon Derrough shocked Elswick with the gloves, according to the lawsuit. The incident can be seen in surveillance footage featured in a report on the case from Kentucky TV station WDRB.
The footage shows a tense scene, with the guard wearing bright yellow gloves and using them on Elswick, who is struggling against three guards, and yells out.
The Kentucky federal court dismissed Elswick’s lawsuit in June 2025, finding that Derrough’s use of force was warranted, a decision upheld by an appeals court in January.
A representative for APB Consulting Solutions, a dealer and training partner for Compliant Technologies’ product, told WDRB in 2022 that agencies undergo a lot of training and that used properly the gloves can prevent further injury – while it is recommended not to apply them for more than 15 seconds.
Sara Collins, a lawyer representing Elswick, declined to comment on the specific civil case, but told the Guardian: “With proper training and use, effective, less-lethal force options are much-needed resources in law enforcement. Shock gloves, however, are not a new tool.”
“I am troubled by the fact that the overwhelming majority of law enforcement agencies across the country do not use them,” she added, noting that relatively few departments out of 18,000 across the US have bought the gloves.
“Feasibility, practicality, training, risk of error, and intent are among my many concerns about their implementation by ICE,” Collins said.
Meanwhile, Johnathan Mansfield, who was arrested on a public intoxication charge in 2024, suffered a cardiac arrest two weeks after he was allegedly shocked 27 times with the gloves and 13 times by a Taser at Madison county detention center in Richmond, Kentucky, according to the lawsuit filed by Mansfield’s family against the authorities, claiming wrongful death.
The complaint alleges: “An internal investigation by the Madison County Detention Center found that ‘ ... Mr Manfield [sic] suffered a cardiac arrest following the series of Taser and G.L.O.V.E. exposures.’”
The internal investigation, as cited in the lawsuit, stated that “four distinct use of force incidents were recorded… resulting in a total of 13 taser exposures – comprising both probes and drive-stun applications – lasting between 23 to 28 seconds. Additionally, there were 27 exposures using the G.L.O.V.E.”
Two of the stun-glove exposures lasted longer than the recommended 15 seconds – one 45 seconds and another 99 seconds, the document alleges.
The suit, filed in a Madison county, Kentucky circuit court, is still pending.

ICE’s tactics look increasingly like torture | Judith Levine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
10:00:31 UTC
19:00:31 KST

On 11 August, the Associated Press reported that the Homeland Security Agency will spend up to $20m to equip its agents with gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks to the skin of a person deemed uncooperative. The “conductive distraction and de-escalation devices”– branded Glove, for Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter – will be supplied by their manufacturer, Compliant Technologies, through a no-bid contract.
News of the acquisition inspired the editorial cartoonist Ann Telnaes to publish a cartoon of an ICE agent wearing the glove, underneath which are a branding iron, an iron maiden, a rack, and other compliance technologies. AKA, instruments of torture.
Indeed, Amnesty International reports that portable, convenient electric shock devices made for law enforcement like the glove can be, and have been, used for torture. Once called weapons, they’re now marketed as “humane”. They are the former. A prisoner in Kentucky died of a heart attack after 27 successive shocks, directly following 13 Taser hits.
ICE tactics, already sadistic, are looking increasingly like torture. The Geneva conventions define torture as the infliction of severe pain or suffering, whether physical or mental, by an agent of the state acting in their official capacity, to obtain intelligence or confession or to intimidate, coerce, or punish a prisoner or detainee. More than 90% of detainees are held in privately-owned immigration detention facilities, but their employees are contractual agents of the federal government.
According to an investigation by the Guardian, at least 10 immigrant detainees have been subjected to force-feeding and involuntary medical procedures. The detainees are on hunger strikes in protest of the appalling conditions of their incarceration, including, ironically, inedible food and denial of necessary medical treatment. One of the victims, a Kurdish film-maker, described being held in solitary confinement, tackled, shackled, and force fed twice daily for eight months. HSA anticipates hunger strike management will cost $169,000 in fiscal 2026.
To force-feed a person, a tube is inserted into their mouth or nose and pushed down into their stomach. Then liquid food or medicine is poured into the tube through a funnel. The person gags, chokes, and often vomits; when they struggle – a natural response – they are usually restrained. “What they’re doing qualifies as torture,” a doctor told the Guardian, expressing a contention widely held by medical professionals, ethicists and human rights experts.
Some of the torture is outsourced. The administration is sending asylum seekers back to the countries from which they fled under threat of imprisonment, torture or execution – and where they face torture or death on return. The US has built a gulag of collaborating third countries where deportees may be locked up indefinitely or deported to the home countries they fled. Forced return, or refoulement, of refugees and asylees – which is also the result of Trump’s recent revocations of temporary protective status for many foreign nationals – is banned under the UN Convention Against Torture, which the US signed.
And then there is the malign neglect. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has released detainees into the cold without adequate money or clothing. At least two – a Haitian woman, Daphy Michael, and a blind Rohingya man, Nurul Amin Shah Alam, a refugee from Myanmar – have frozen to death. Medical examiners are calling both deaths homicides. (DHS says ICE and border patrol had “nothing to do” with the deaths.)
Children, too, are being deliberately abandoned. In a bid to force them to release confidential information about their clients, the administration is withholding payments from the organizations that provide legal representation to unaccompanied migrant children. About 25,000 kids, some of them unable to speak English – or speak at all – have been left to fend for themselves in court. Such representation is mandated under a section of the 2008 federal anti-trafficking law, which Project 2025’s Homeland Security chapter recommends repealing.
Speaking to MSNOW, Lindsay Toczylowski, an attorney at the Immigrant Defenders Law Center, said that since her agency’s payments were cut off on 31 July, colleagues “witnessed a seven-year-old child taking a final order to leave the United States this week, without a lawyer”, she said. Where will that child go? Who, if anyone, will look after him? What permanent damage will befall him?
The number of infants and toddlers in custody has dramatically increased under the Trump administration, according to the Marshall Project, to 25 children under the age of three on an average day. That is “probably the most harmful time of their lives” to experience such trauma, said the cofounder of the executive committee of the American Academy of Pediatrics’ Council on Immigrant Child and Family Health. “Our immigration system is breaking children.”
Is this torture? Maybe not technically. It is surely child abuse, which is illegal under US criminal law and international human rights law – and immoral under any religious or ethical code.
“The fact is, being in detention is a choice,” HSA deputy assistant secretary Lauren Bis said in response to distraught parents’ reports of children sickening nearly to death at the South Texas Family Residential Center in Dilley. “We encourage all parents to take control of their departure by using the CBP Home app and receiving a free flight home and $2,600.” FAQs on the app’s website suggest that this “option” is not exactly voluntary either. “Illegal aliens” are informed that should they decline to take the deal, “ICE will continue to prioritize your removal.”
Routine practices of current immigration detention such as prolonged solitary confinement, beatings, and sleep deprivation are widely defined as torture. An argument can also been made – and advocates have made it – that even those aspects of the mass deportation policy that do not conform with the legal definition of torture are designed to create so much misery that immigrants will leave on their own or not come in the first place. During Trump’s first term, the administration unapologetically justified its “zero tolerance” family separation at the border as a deterrent to would-be immigrant parents.
These tactics, even when carried out in diffuse and intermittent ways, fit the general definition of torture precisely: the infliction of pain and suffering by the state to compel a person to do something they fiercely do not want to do.
The deportation machine is in high gear. In July, the New York Times reported that ICE had arrested 10,000 people in five days, having doubled its daily quota to the 2,000. The abuses inside detention facilities are bound to increase too.
At the same time, NPR reported on Thursday, the already teetering system through which ICE detainees could report abuse without fear of recrimination “has collapsed”, and there’s nowhere else to turn, since virtually all other government oversight has been demolished.
Civil liberties and immigrant rights lawyers are flooding the federal courts with lawsuits and petitions for interdiction of these sadistic practices. But any charge of torture is unlikely to get far. The constitution’s eighth amendment prohibits cruel and unusual punishment, and harm by police or prison guards can be redressed through state civil rights laws. But torture is effectively condoned in the US; federal anti-torture statute applies only to acts committed outside US borders.
The slim avenues to legal recourse and the refusal of transparency or accountability by the perpetrators of de jure and de facto torture are driving detainees to desperate measures like hunger strikes. They are “risking their lives to protest inhumane conditions and legal rights violations”, reports NPR. Self-deportation or self-starvation. That is not a choice.
- 
  Judith Levine is a Brooklyn-based journalist and frequent contributor to the Guardian. Her Substack is Today in Fascism

Devastation, doubt and blame: Hurricane Helene looms over North Carolina’s US Senate race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
10:00:30 UTC
19:00:30 KST

Two years after North Carolina suffered the worst natural disaster in its history when Hurricane Helene struck the state’s western half, life in the hardest-hit areas appears back to normal. Downtowns are lively, blocked roads have been reopened and rivers are flowing below their banks.
But the telltale evidence of the disaster’s expensive impacts can still be seen – from “for rent” signs in storefronts whose businesses never came back to debris from the storm still lurking in some waterways. And in the race for North Carolina’s US Senate seat, it’s almost as if the hurricane never left.
With the Republican senator Thom Tillis retiring, Democrats see a rare opportunity in November’s midterms to win a seat in a state that has repeatedly rejected the party’s candidates in recent elections, but which could this year decide the balance of power in the Senate for the remainder of Donald Trump’s presidency.
Whether they like it or not, the two frontrunners to succeed Tillis are tied to North Carolina’s recovery from a catastrophe that killed at least 107 people and caused nearly $60bn in damage. Roy Cooper, the Democratic nominee, was governor when Helene arrived as a tropical storm over the state’s western half in September 2024, and his opponent, former Republican National Committee chair Michael Whatley, has accused him of mishandling the recovery in the months before he left office.
Cooper has his own counterattack against Whatley, courtesy of Trump. When the US president visited the state shortly after returning to office, he said Whatley would be “in charge of making sure everything goes well” with the recovery. That’s led to Whatley being known in the state’s press as the Hurricane Helene “recovery czar”, a title the Republican’s campaign said he was never given, but which Cooper has wielded to argue that his opponent is the one letting North Carolinians down.
“I don’t think it’s to anybody’s political benefit to be tapped as the person who was in charge of Helene recovery – Democrat, Republican, Green, Libertarian – doesn’t matter,” said Christopher Cooper, a political science professor at Western Carolina University. “People … in western North Carolina are fairly united that there wasn’t enough done and that Helene relief has been more of a failure than a victory. The question is who they blame for that.”
Blame game
The debate has national implications in a state that has been a heartbreaker for Democrats for nearly two decades. Though its candidates have come close, no Democrat has won a US Senate election in North Carolina, or carried it at the presidential level, since 2008. The GOP’s dominance of the state legislature has meanwhile allowed the party to rewrite its laws and draw congressional maps to its advantage, over the objections of the Democratic governor, Josh Stein.
This year, Democratic party leaders have put North Carolina among the small group of red states where they’re hoping to win US Senate seats, and recent polls have shown Cooper leading Whatley. Western North Carolina is generally a Republican area, with none of its congressional districts in Democratic hands and the party carrying few of its counties in presidential years.
In 2024, Trump seized on the devastation in the region to accuse Joe Biden’s administration of bungling the disaster response. Trump ended up winning North Carolina by 51%.
The state’s return to national political prominence in the midterms has reinvigorated questions over how the storm recovery was handled, as North Carolinians weigh which candidate would better champion the needs of the region in Washington.
“I’m a Cooper man. I’ve met him several times,” said Aaron Haynie, a Democrat who serves as mayor of Marshall. “I feel like his interest for North Carolina and its citizens is probably personal. I think his personal thoughts on that would be much greater than Whatley’s will.”
A riverside town of 961 residents, Marshall suffered terribly when Helene hit and the French Broad River climbed 27ft above flood level, nearly to the windows of the town’s second-story buildings. The flood water took with it the town hall and the post office, and inundated the historic courthouse, rendering it unusable.
Today, Marshall’s main street is distinctly artsy, with a thrift store, a retailer selling high-end bicycles, and another advertising arcade games and cassette tapes. But it’s not the same.
Across the street from Zuma Coffee, a longstanding cafe situated right in the center of the main drag, the courthouse that used to drive so much business remains shuttered. The county plans to vacate it for good, in favor of a new complex to be built on high ground elsewhere, with money from the state general assembly and the Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema).
With so many locals losing their homes or employers, the nine-to-five economy that once sustained Zuma Coffee has now been replaced by visitors who show up after work or on the weekend, Joel Friedman, its owner, said. Sales at the cafe have recovered, but his margins are smaller due to inflation, while his employees are struggling to afford higher healthcare premiums after Congress let temporary federal subsidies expire.
As for the Senate election, “I don’t have a lot of hope for it, to be honest with you,” Friedman said. “I think we have an administration right now that’s rogue, and is going to do what they want to do, and living in a state with a Democrat governor is not very helpful right now.”
Matthew Wechtel, a Republican commissioner in Madison county, of which Marshall is the seat, said he wasn’t aware of Whatley specifically helping his area, but that Cooper deserved no credit for helping the town bounce back. Though the then governor visited Marshall about two weeks after the hurricane, Wechtel accused him of being a “no-show”.
“I don’t think Governor Cooper did much at all for Madison county, or for western North Carolina, when it came to storm recovery,” said Wechtel. “I think most of the stuff that came down came from the general assembly … and Governor Cooper just got out of the way and let it happen.”
A town rocked by catastrophe
A mountainous two dozen miles south of Marshall is the town of Canton, where Helene added grievous insult to economic injury that had been accumulating for years. Tropical Storm Fred flooded the town in 2021, and two years later, 1,100 jobs disappeared when a paper mill that had operated for more than a century closed. Then Helene came through and put Canton underwater.
“Everything was flooded. We lost homes, businesses, things that we had rebuilt from ’21, gone again,” recalled Zeb Smathers, the town’s Democratic mayor.
The multiple catastrophes have made him familiar with dealing with Fema, the federal emergency agency he said was slow in responding to Tropical Storm Fred, but more swift when Helene hit. In the early part of his second term, Trump mulled doing away with Fema altogether, and appointed Whatley to the Fema Council Review Board, which evaluated the agency’s operations and earlier this year released a report proposing shifting disaster response into the hands of state and local governments.
Pointing to Whatley’s position on the Fema review board, DJ Griffin, a spokesperson for Whatley’s campaign, said: “If you look very, very, very, very closely, you’ll notice there’s no czar in that description. Not a czar of any sort.”
Griffin said that Whatley had collaborated with Republican members of the state’s federal delegation to bring North Carolina $10.75bn in hurricane relief. “But the job is not yet done and Michael [Whatley] will continue speaking with local leaders about what they need help with,” he added.
A spokesperson for Cooper’s campaign argued that those federal dollars covered only about 15% of the damage from the storm, while the governor signed two bills allocating more than $877m in state funds to hurricane relief before leaving office. “DC insider Michael Whatley has completely failed in his role as federal recovery czar,” the spokesperson said.
Smathers said Canton’s recovery was hampered by Kristi Noem, Trump’s first homeland security secretary, who required she personally approve all spending over $100,000 by agencies such as Fema. But the pace has improved under the new secretary, Markwayne Mullin.
As for Whatley, Smathers said he’s never heard from him. “He wasn’t named the recovery sidekick. He was named the recovery czar,” Smathers said. “His leadership and presence has been absent.”
Brandon Rogers, a Republican county commissioner, complimented Cooper’s response to the storm, remembering the then governor calling to ask if he needed anything shortly after Helene came through, and then arranging for water, food and insulin to be delivered on helicopters.
But for Rogers, a conservative who opposes abortion, the former governor won’t be getting his vote in November. “As far as Whatley’s concerned, I think he would do a great job,” he said.
Rogers recalled pointing out their disagreements when Cooper came to Canton. “I appreciate you bringing the check,” he remembered telling Cooper during the visit. “However, a lot of our other politics may not line up.”
The two ended up laughing about it, Rogers said. “That doesn’t mean we couldn’t work together.”
