E1 settlement: Why Netanyahu, Israel’s right might not mind global outrage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
08:45:10 UTC
17:45:10 KST

E1 settlement: Why Netanyahu, Israel’s right might not mind global outrage
The proposed illegal settlement threatens Palestinian statehood. But it could help Israel’s PM, other far-right leaders before elections.
The Israeli government last week invited bids for the building of more than 1,200 units, a key step towards the construction of the E1 settlement in the occupied West Bank just two months before Israel’s general election.
E1 (East 1) would link Ma’ale Adumim and other illegal Israeli settlements to occupied East Jerusalem, effectively severing the West Bank in two. Both supporters and critics agree that its construction would end the possibility of a Palestinian state.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Analysis: Israel’s government can’t disown West Bank settler violence
- list 2 of 4Palestinians, UK condemn Israel’s ‘destructive’ E1 settlement plan
- list 3 of 4Europe, Canada condemn Israeli plans for new West Bank settlement
- list 4 of 4Why Israeli tenders for illegal E1 West Bank settlement prompted outrage
The move has drawn international outrage, including from the United Nations.
But sections of Israel’s political class are using this global backlash to their own ends and could frame their support for E1 as a key pitch in their election campaigns.
How could they benefit Israel?
Many on Israel’s right, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, thrive on the international outrage their comments and plans draw, particularly criticism from European nations.
Since October 2023, Netanyahu has cast international criticism of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza as an “us vs them” moment for the country. He has frequently framed Israel as alone in a hostile world and that he is the only leader strong enough to stand up to the country’s critics.
After the United Kingdom’s Foreign Minister Ed Miliband described E1 as an “unacceptable and destructive act”, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar criticised the “patronising tone” of his statement.
With the election approaching, the way ministers respond to the E1 project could determine their political futures.
Far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich has been one of the key proponents of E1 and could benefit from an uptick in support from right-wing Israelis over the proposed illegal settlement. His Religious Zionist Party is currently unlikely to pass the electoral threshold to even run in this year’s election.
“It’s Smotrich, he’s hyping up everything under his watch ahead of the election,” Israeli analyst Nimrod Flaschenberg told Al Jazeera from Berlin, Germany.
The fact that the government’s call for tenders to construct E1 falls so close to Israel’s election is not a coincidence, Flaschenberg said. Neither is the dramatic increase in settler violence in the occupied West Bank, where Smotrich has administrative control.
“Both he and even Netanyahu are benefitting from the outrage. Little of this is accidental,” the analyst added.
How extensive has this outrage been?
Condemnation of the E1 settlement has been almost universal. On Friday, the foreign ministers of Egypt, Indonesia, Jordan, Pakistan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and the United Arab Emirates rejected the E1 settlement, calling for “immediate action to halt the E1 settlement plan”.
Earlier in the week, 15 European and North American leaders, including those from Israel’s traditional allies the United Kingdom, France and Germany, condemned the settlement.
In a joint letter, they said E1 would “undermine the prospect of the two-state solution by driving a wedge through the West Bank”. Some have pointed out that their failure to present any penalties if Israel goes ahead with the plan makes their criticism moot.
The United States has not criticised E1 itself, but did on Friday state its opposition to Israel’s annexation of the West Bank, which the illegal settlement could effectively result in.
“As the president has clearly stated, the US does not support Israel annexing the West Bank. A stable West Bank keeps Israel secure and is in line with this administration’s goal to achieve peace in the region,” read a statement from the US Department of State.
So, is this really the end of the two-state solution?
Announcing plans for construction in August 2025, Smotrich had boasted that the new settlement would bury the “idea of a Palestinian state”.
Given that thousands of Palestinian homes have been demolished by Israel since its occupation of the West Bank began in 1967, some hope the same could happen to the illegal Israeli settlements that replaced them, if the two-state solution becomes a reality.
“The idea that this is irreversible is just nonsense. Every time there’s a new illegal settlement, voices in the West say that this is the end of the two-state solution,” Flaschenberg said.
“It definitely makes it less likely, but why the end? Every illegal settlement that’s been built can be demolished … why do we have to accept their presence as fact?”
Political analyst Ori Goldberg noted that the tender for the E1 settlement project came at a time Israel faced further international criticism for bombing an airfield in Syria and described the issuing of the tender as “a deliberate provocation”.
Is it all smoke and mirrors?
Thousands of Palestinians, most of them Bedouin, have already suffered home demolitions, displacement and restrictions on basic services as Israel expands its road network before construction in the occupied West Bank.
In April 2026, 23 Palestinians, including 15 children, were displaced from the az-Za’im Bedouin community following demolitions by the Israeli army.
The UN warns that the planned expansion of Israeli illegal settlements and associated infrastructure threatens to fragment the occupied West Bank and could forcibly displace the 18 Palestinian communities that have lived within the territory Israel now claims for decades.

Alimony system set for overhaul under proposed judicial package
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
08:38:36 UTC
17:38:36 KST

Türkiye’s ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) is preparing legislation that would introduce time limits for alimony payments, allow courts to extend them in certain circumstances and separate divorce proceedings from disputes over issues such as property division.
The proposed changes are expected to be submitted to Parliament in October as part of the 13th Judicial Package, following a Constitutional Court ruling on June 4 that annulled an existing provision concerning indefinite alimony.
According to news network CNN Türk, the draft would base the duration of alimony primarily on the length of the marriage. Under the proposal, couples married for three years would be eligible for alimony for up to five years, while those married for five years could receive payments for seven years. For marriages lasting 10 years, alimony could continue for 12 years.
The period between the date of marriage and the filing of the divorce case would be used to calculate the duration. In general, alimony could be paid for half the length of the marriage, subject to the minimum periods set out in the draft.
Courts would be able to extend payments when the recipient is unable to work or is elderly. Older women would have to apply to a court within one year after the original alimony period expires if they seek additional support. Failure to apply within that period would reportedly prevent further claims.
The proposal could also change how alimony is paid. Although courts could initially order monthly payments, they could later decide that the remaining amount should be paid as a lump sum.
The changes would not immediately terminate alimony awarded in divorce cases that have already become final. Under the draft, people currently receiving alimony would continue to receive payments for another year.
The government is also considering procedural changes aimed at speeding up contentious divorce cases. Under the proposed system, courts would first rule solely on whether the marriage should be dissolved. Disputes over alimony, child custody and division of property, which can prolong divorce proceedings, would then be handled separately.
The draft also proposes reducing the statute of limitations for lawsuits arising from property division from the current 10 years to five years.
The planned overhaul seeks to establish a more predictable framework for alimony while reducing the length and complexity of divorce litigation.

IEA chief says COP31 in Antalya could make history with ‘35 by 35’ target
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
08:35:52 UTC
17:35:52 KST

Antalya could go down in history as the site of a landmark global energy decision if countries agree at the COP31 climate summit to raise electricity’s share of total global energy consumption to 35 percent by 2035, International Energy Agency (IEA) chief Fatih Birol has said.
The United Nations climate summit will be held in the southwestern province of Antalya from Nov. 9 to 20, bringing together thousands of delegates and world leaders from about 198 UN member states. The first COP summit to be hosted by Türkiye, it will be chaired by Australia, while the IEA will serve as a strategic partner.
Birol said the proposed target, dubbed “35 by 35,” could become known as the “Antalya Decision” if adopted, in a development comparable in significance to the 2015 Paris Agreement.
“COP summits are judged by the number of leaders attending and whether concrete decisions are taken that can shape the global economy,” Birol said. He added that there was already strong interest from world leaders in the Antalya summit and broad support for the electricity target.
The proposal comes as countries grapple with the dual challenges of climate change and energy security, with geopolitical tensions continuing to disrupt energy markets and raise concerns over supply.
Birol said that greater reliance on domestically produced electricity would reduce countries’ dependence on external energy supplies and strengthen energy security.
“That is why we are focusing on electricity,” he said, adding that Türkiye’s decision to designate one of the summit’s key days as “Energy Day” was particularly timely.
Birol said he had recently held talks with President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, COP31 President Murat Kurum and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. Türkiye and Australia had agreed to work closely with the IEA throughout preparations for the summit, he said.
He described COP31 as a historic opportunity for Türkiye, saying Antalya could play a guiding role in the emerging global energy landscape.
“Antalya will be a kind of compass for the new world energy map being drawn,” Birol said.
The issue is also expected to feature prominently during the U.N. General Assembly in New York in the third week of September, where Türkiye and its partners plan to advance discussions ahead of the summit.

Heavy rain causes partial collapse of Great East Gate in Tainan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
08:31:39 UTC
17:31:39 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Heavy rain caused part of Tainan’s historic Great East Gate to collapse early Monday.
A resident surnamed Chu (朱) living near the gate discovered that one of the structure’s side walls had collapsed at about 6 a.m. on Monday after heavy overnight rain, UDN reported. Soil and debris spilled onto Section 1 of Dongmen Road, and police from Dongning Police Station were sent to the scene to control traffic.
Tainan Deputy Mayor Yeh Tse-shan (葉澤山) said the restoration project included repairs to cracks in the roof slab of the old structure, but work on the entire slab had not yet been completed, per CNA.
Yeh said an inspection of the collapsed section suggested that bricks, soil, and other materials used in an earlier restoration may not have been sufficiently solid. The materials may have softened after absorbing rainwater, causing the side wall to give way, but the city has asked the Ministry of Culture’s Bureau of Cultural Heritage to determine the exact cause.
The Great East Gate, also known as Yingchun Gate, is one of four remaining gates of the former Taiwan Prefectural City Wall and the only one located along a major thoroughfare, according to UDN. It was one of 14 gates built during the Qing dynasty and is designated a national historic site, with its two-story gate tower considered the largest surviving structure of its kind in Taiwan.
The Tainan City Government’s Cultural Affairs Bureau launched a restoration project for the Great East Gate and Great South Gate late last year. The project has a budget of about NT$55.6 million (US$1.75 million), including NT$36.14 million in central government funding and NT$19.46 million from the city, and is slated for completion in January 2028.
The restoration work is intended to enhance structural safety, restore the site’s historic appearance, improve the surrounding environment, and extend the cultural heritage site’s lifespan, UDN reported. The project was originally scheduled to take about 750 days.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan will host its first sports recovery techniques competition this weekend, bringing together 95 competitors from Taiwan, Japan, Hong Kong, and Malaysia to compete in four categories of sports massage and recovery techniques.
The inaugural Taiwan Exercise Recovery Open and Master Forum, organized by the Taiwan Exercise Recovery Association, will take place Aug. 29-30 at National Taiwan Sport University in Taoyuan’s Guishan District, per UDN.
The competition will feature four categories: sport-specific massage, freestyle manual techniques, tool-assisted methods, and sports aromatherapy. Participants will compete individually in general and student divisions.
The event is designed to promote sports recovery, improve professional education and training, and provide a platform for practitioners to exchange techniques and experience with international counterparts, according to TERA.
Canadian sports massage and bodywork educator Matthew Chalons arrived in Taiwan Monday to attend a news conference ahead of the competition and promote the importance of sports recovery.
Chalons has more than 13 years of practical and teaching experience and has led international workshops. He is the founder of The Matcha Method, which combines Thai massage with movement and bodywork techniques.
Speaking to reporters, Chalons said the body experiences significant fatigue during training, making recovery an important part of preparing for the next physical challenge.
TERA Spokesperson Chiu Chi-fei (邱琪霏) said similar sports massage competitions have been held overseas for years, but Taiwan is hosting one for the first time. Chiu said the association hopes the competition can develop into a platform where professionals exchange techniques and experience while helping Taiwan’s sports recovery industry expand and align with international practices.
The event will also include a master forum and practical sessions. Chalons will lead a workshop on integrated sports recovery techniques on Aug. 29.
The association also announced Taiwan’s first group of qualified sports massage judges after they completed training and assessments. It said establishing a formal judging system is an important step toward standardizing sports massage and bodywork practices in Taiwan.
The event will conclude Aug. 30 with demonstrations by judges and guests, followed by awards for the top three competitors in each category.

Lebanon arrests food influencer 'Dr Food' over drug-laced treats

Georges Dib, known on TikTok as "Doctor Food" and followed by more than eight million accounts, was apprehended at his home in the far north governorate of Akkar, a hudicial source told AFP.
Dib, who also owns a confectionery business, would be taken to a detention centre in Mount Lebanon, where he would face a new trial on further drug trafficking charges, the source added.
Two years ago, the Lebanese judiciary issued a warrant for Dib, accusing him of "manufacturing narcotics, trafficking and smuggling them abroad", according to Lebanon's state-run National News Agency (NNA).
The NNA said at the time that authorities had seized confectionery and other food products at Beirut's Rafic Hariri International Airport that contained narcotics and were manufactured in factories owned by Dib.
The products were to be shipped to a Gulf country, the news agency reported.
Despite an arrest warrant and conviction against him, Dib continued to post videos on TikTok.
Last month, after news of his conviction was made public, he denied the accusations in one of his videos, urging followers not to listen to what was being said about him.
Dib rose to prominence on social media posting content about cooking and daily life with his ex-wife, known as Shorouk, a Canadian of Palestinian origin who has more than 15 million followers.
They separated after she accused him of abuse. On Saturday night, she held a "divorce party" at a seaside resort in Lebanon attended by thousands of her followers.
The "Doctor Food" case began in 2023, when 16 pieces of cannabis resin in the form of rectangular blocks, wrapped in nylon and placed inside chocolate boxes bearing the "Dr Food" trademark, along with chocolate bars carrying the same brand, were found inside the luggage of defendant Abdel Karim Al-Sammak as he prepared to travel to Turkey through Beirut's Rafik Hariri International Airport.
According to the indictment, the contents of which were leaked at the time, "the documented evidence and information proved that Dib, in his personal capacity and in his capacity as chairman of the board and general manager of Doctor Food World Wide SAL, exploited his fame and influence on social media to promote his wafer products carrying the Doctor Food trademark in Lebanon and abroad".
It added that “he contracted defendant Mohsen Diab, who owns a biscuit manufacturing factory, to produce wafer bars while simultaneously manufacturing bars of pure cannabis resin and packaging them inside the same wrappers and boxes.”

A political amnesty law takes effect in Thailand but excludes lese majeste
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
08:23:01 UTC
17:23:01 KST

A political amnesty law takes effect in Thailand but excludes lese majeste
BANGKOK (AP) — An amnesty for political offenses committed in Thailand over the past two decades took effect Monday, but the law excludes some of the more serious cases, including those involving lese majeste, or defaming the monarchy.
The amnesty was introduced to promote reconciliation after past political instability, violent protests and military coups and could cover about 6,000 people, according to estimates made in Parliament. But the exclusion of lese majeste offenses has drawn criticism that the amnesty will not truly resolve political divisions.
The Peaceful Society Promotion Act passed a final vote by lawmakers in July and was published in the Royal Gazette on Sunday. A committee chaired by the prime minister will determine who qualifies for the amnesty. The committee must hold its first meeting within 30 days, although it’s unclear how long the process will take.
The law covers a range of offenses related to political activities from Jan. 1, 2005 to July 15, 2025. It will not only grant release for current prisoners, but also close investigations and prosecutions, dismiss pending court cases, and clear criminal records of those eligible for the amnesty.
In addition to lese majeste, the amnesty will also exclude corruption and crimes resulting in death or serious injury.
The lese majeste law, also known as Article 112 of the Criminal Code, is controversial not only because it has been used to punish things as simple as liking a post on Facebook, but also because anyone — not just royals or the authorities — can lodge a complaint that most of the time leads to detention during lengthy legal proceedings.
A conviction of defaming the monarchy carries a prison term of up to 15 years, and critics say Article 112 has often been used to quash political dissent.
Student-led pro-democracy demonstrations starting in 2020 sought reforms of the lese majeste law, but the protesters became targets of the law.
Thai Lawyers for Human Rights, a law advocacy group, says more than 290 people, many of them student activists, have been charged with violating Article 112 since early 2020.
As of July, the group said at least 54 people remained imprisoned in connection with political cases. Only about 10 were expected to benefit from the new amnesty, since the others were accused of lese majeste.
Thailand’s machinery of state remains deeply conservative. Its political establishment is sensitive about any perceived threats to the status of the monarchy.
The country’s political conflicts revolved mostly around former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra, who was ousted by a military coup in 2006.
His populist policies won strong support among poorer voters, particularly in the rural north and northeast, but his popularity and sometimes high-handed style created deep fractures between his base and the country’s urban elites, royalists and the military. Violent protests and political upheaval repeatedly followed as parties aligned with Thaksin returned to power while he remained in self-imposed exile.

Return to normal relations with Russia impossible while war in Ukraine continues – Czech FM
Czech Foreign Minister Petr Macinka said this at a meeting of the heads of the Czech Republic’s diplomatic missions abroad, according to a Ukrinform correspondent.
“Russia has fundamentally damaged European security through its invasion of Ukraine. A return to normal relations [with Russia] is impossible as long as this aggression continues,” Macinka emphasized.
He noted that as long as the aggression continues, there is no point in abandoning the tools of economic pressure on Russia, and assured that the Czech Republic and its allies would continue to use these pressure tools against Russia wherever they are effective.
“Russia’s war in Ukraine is a fundamental European security problem, and the Czech Republic has a clear interest in ensuring that military aggression does not become a successful tool of international policy,” the minister said.
The diplomat also noted that war is not a PR campaign but a tragic reality, and therefore there is no need to compete in displays of support.
“The task of responsible policy is not to compete in gestures, but to create the conditions for a safe and lasting peace while protecting the security interests of the Czech Republic,” he emphasized.

First LCU 1700-class vessel joins the U.S. Navy fleet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
08:20:37 UTC
17:20:37 KST

- Austal USA delivered LCU 1710 to the U.S. Navy on August 14, 2026, the first vessel under the LCU 1700-class program.
- LCU 1710 is also Austal USA's first steel-hulled ship delivered to the Navy, following the company's history of building aluminum vessels.
Austal USA delivered LCU 1710 to the U.S. Navy on August 14, 2026, the first vessel completed under the Navy’s LCU 1700-class program and the first steel-hulled ship the shipbuilder has ever delivered to the service.
Austal USA, based in Mobile, Alabama, has built its Navy business primarily on aluminum vessels, including Independence-variant littoral combat ships and Expeditionary Fast Transport ships. LCU 1710 marks the company’s shift into steel-hull construction for the Navy, a different set of fabrication and welding processes than its aluminum work.
“The delivery of LCU 1710 represents a major achievement for Austal USA and our shipbuilding team,” said Gene Miller, President of Austal USA. “As our first Landing Craft Utility and first steel ship delivered to the U.S. Navy, this accomplishment reflects the dedication and expertise of our workforce and our industry partners. It also demonstrates Austal USA’s ability to skillfully design, build and deliver highly complex steel vessels while continuing to support the Navy’s evolving mission requirements.”
Before delivery, LCU 1710 went through acceptance trials that tested the ship’s major systems and equipment for operational performance, reliability, and compliance with Navy requirements. The U.S. Navy’s Board of Inspection and Survey, known as INSURV, oversaw the trials and validated the ship’s construction quality and mission readiness.
“The successful completion of these trials reflects exceptional planning, flawless execution, dedication, and the collaboration of our shipbuilding team and Navy counterparts,” said Mike Pruitt, Vice President of Surface Ship Programs at Austal USA. “Our entire organization played a principal role in achieving these milestones, paving the way for delivery to the U.S. Navy.”
During testing, LCU 1710 got underway without the assistance of tugs or pilots and demonstrated a limited crew operating capability, meaning the ship can run with a smaller onboard crew than older landing craft in the fleet require.
LCU 1710 is built to move equipment and personnel from ship to shore in support of expeditionary operations. Austal USA and the Navy have described the LCU 1700 class as offering greater capability, endurance, and survivability than the legacy LCU 1610-class vessels it is replacing. Those legacy landing craft have been in Navy service since the 1970s.
PAE Maritime, a program support contractor working on the LCU 1700-class effort, said in a LinkedIn post that LCU 1710’s expanded capabilities are meant to support efficient production of steel-hulled connectors going forward, giving the Navy and Marine Corps added industrial base and heavy-lift capacity for expeditionary and littoral operations.
Austal USA is building the LCU 1700 class alongside a broader portfolio of Navy and Coast Guard work. The company said it currently has multiple vessels under construction and continues to support submarine module production and auxiliary ship programs for both services.

‘Barrel bomb mufti’ Ahmad Hassoun handed life sentence in Syria trial
Judge Fakhr al-Din al-Aryan sentenced Hassoun to life in prison for crimes including incitement to hatred and violence.
Ahmad Badreddin Hassoun, a top Muslim religious official under ousted Syrian President Bashar al-Assad, has been sentenced to life in prison for crimes committed during the country’s nearly 14-year civil war.
The Fourth Criminal Court in Damascus issued the ruling on Monday, finding Hassoun guilty of a range of crimes, including inciting violence, justifying killings and the abuse of his office.

list of 4 items

Hassoun, who was Syria’s grand mufti between 2005 and 2021, was arrested at Damascus airport in March 2025, after he emerged from hiding a month earlier. His trial began on June 25.
The court handed Hassoun several prison sentences for various charges, including 20 years after being found guilty of inciting killings.
The judge also sentenced him to 10 years in prison after being found guilty of prolonging the killings.
The court ordered the Muslim leader to pay compensation to make restitution to a number of his victims.
Judge Fakhr al-Din al-Aryan said that Hassoun and the official religious institution he headed were used to provide religious cover for military and security operations during al-Assad’s rule.
His teachings also justified the use of barrel bombs that targeted civilian areas and caused widespread destruction, which constitutes a violation of the rules of international humanitarian law, the judge said.
The court found that Hassoun also urged Syrian military officers and soldiers in his religious lectures to confront the country’s opposition, and made public calls through Syrian media for civilians in eastern Aleppo to evacuate their homes.
He also called on the army to “annihilate and destroy” the areas from which shells were launched, threatening the people of Idlib with killing and displacement.
The court confirmed that Hassoun is barred from any general or special amnesty, given the gravity of the crimes he was found guilty of committing.
His money and properties will also be confiscated by the state for the benefit of the public treasury, the court said.
The verdict comes weeks after Bashar al-Assad, his brother Maher and five other security officials were sentenced to death in absentia for war crimes and crimes against humanity.
Authorities have also handed death sentences to Atif Najib and Wassim al-Assad, cousins of the former ruler who were tried in person.
Reporting from Damascus, Al Jazeera’s Heidi Pett said Hassoun is an “unusual” example of the transitional justice cases that Syria has held since al-Assad’s ouster in 2024.
“All of the other ones were senior members of the regime itself, many of them were members of the Assad family,” said Pett.
“We’ve seen death sentences handed down to Bashar al-Assad, the former president, two of his cousins as well. But Sheikh Ahmad Hassoun, he is the first Sunni to have been tried, and he does still enjoy some level of popular support here in Syria.”
His supporters, who have largely mobilised online, say his statements have been taken out of context, Pett reported.
Many of his critics, however, had called for a death sentence, she added.

Ukraine is seeking interceptor missiles from Japan, the war-torn nation’s prime minister has said.
“I would like to kindly ask one and only thing ... anti-ballistic missiles,” Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi told Kyodo News in an interview released on Monday.
Koretskyi “expressed hope that Japan will provide Kyiv with air defense systems.”
The Russia-Ukraine war has been ongoing since February 2022.
“It's the most important thing we need to protect our people, infrastructure ... through this (winter) heating season," Koretskyi said about the interceptor missiles.
“I very much hope (for) and count on your country," he told the Japanese news agency.
Ukraine is supplied with Patriot interceptor missiles by a coalition of Western nations, but its stockpile has been depleting.
Japan, a defense ally of the US, is one of the manufacturers of the Patriot surface-to-air missile interceptors under a US license, the report added.
However, Japanese arms exports, under the country’s three principles on the transfer of defense equipment and technology, “to countries in which conflicts are taking place is, (are) in principle, prohibited.”
In April, Tokyo revised limits on defense equipment exports.
The revised terms “on the transfer of defense equipment and technology require countries to sign agreements with Japan on protecting related classified information to be eligible for the transfer of lethal weapons,” it said.
“Even if an agreement for the transfer of defense equipment and technology is signed, the provision of interceptor missiles would need to be green-lighted by (Prime Minister Sanae) Takaichi,” according to Kyodo News.

Bhushan Ramkrishna Gavai, Former Chief Justice of India

Ukraine’s Mi-8 gets drone interceptor launchers to hunt Shaheds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
08:09:54 UTC
17:09:54 KST

- Ukraine has mounted interceptor drone launchers on a Mi-8 helicopter, with footage shown in Zelensky's Independence Day address, Militarnyi reported.
- The helicopter carries at least three launch rails per side for up to six interceptors, similar to a configuration already used on a converted An-28 aircraft.
Ukraine has mounted interceptor drone launchers on a Mi-8 helicopter, with footage of the system shown in President Volodymyr Zelensky’s Independence Day address, Militarnyi reported.
The footage shows an interceptor launching from beneath one of the helicopter’s hardpoints, using simple metal launch rails mounted under the airframe. The drone is likely controlled either from inside the Mi-8’s cabin or remotely through Starlink, according to the outlet.
The helicopter carries at least three launch rails on each side, room for six interceptors in total. Militarnyi also reported the aircraft is likely fitted with an optical system for spotting aerial targets visually. The outlet did not disclose the unit flying the helicopter, the interceptor’s manufacturer, or when the modification entered service.
Ukraine has already fielded a similar concept on a fixed-wing aircraft. The Defence Blog reported in April 2026 that Ukrainian pilot Tymur Fatkullin had converted an Antonov An-28 light turboprop into an airborne interceptor platform, arming it with wing-mounted P1-Sun and Merops AS-3 Surveyor interceptor drones. Fatkullin said at the time that the aircraft-launched interceptor method had already proven effective against Shaheds in combat, not just in testing.
“Aircraft-launched P1-Sun interceptor against hostile Shaheds. This method has already proven effective in real combat conditions. We have also tested several other interceptor drones during training flights. You could call it a cheap air-to-air missile. For us, it is also a step toward technology that will allow drones to operate in zero visibility,” Fatkullin said.
The An-28, a Soviet-era transport aircraft never designed for intercept work, also carries a six-barrel M134 Minigun alongside its interceptor pylons. As of May 2026, the converted aircraft had destroyed 213 enemy drones using a combination of its onboard weapons and interceptor drones, part of a mix of tactics rather than interceptors alone.
The new Mi-8 configuration follows the same underlying logic as the An-28 conversion: use an aircraft already in the air to carry interceptors aloft, giving crews altitude, loiter time, and the ability to vector toward a target using onboard sensors before release, rather than relying only on ground-launched interceptors or gun-armed helicopters.
Ukrainian Mi-8 crews have engaged Shahed-type drones since at least 2024, but earlier missions relied on door-mounted or nose-mounted machine guns rather than dedicated interceptor drones. Footage from those operations showed gunners firing 7.62 mm PKT machine guns, and in some cases U.S.-supplied M134 miniguns, sometimes with a second helicopter carrying an optical tracking system to guide the engagement.
Ground-launched interceptor drones have separately become a larger part of Ukraine’s air defense mix through 2026. Zelensky has said interceptors have downed dozens of Shaheds in single overnight Russian attacks, and Ukrainian groups such as Wild Hornets have scaled production of systems like STING in response.

What one group of Afghan women and their supporters make of international engagement with the Taliban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
08:01:09 UTC
17:01:09 KST

You’ve heard it before. Women and girls pay a heavy price during humanitarian crises. She Said is an ongoing collection of reporting in which women offer glimpses of their lives, speaking with The New Humanitarian from situations of conflict and displacement, and other global emergencies.
AMSTERDAM, The Netherlands
Five years after the Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan, Afghan women and their supporters gathered last week on Amsterdam’s Dam Square to protest the continued erosion of women’s rights.
Rows of empty school desks and chairs stood across the square, with notebooks and yellow pens laid out on them: a visual reminder of the many girls whose educations have been cut short.
Sahar Shirzad, a Dutch-Afghan human rights activist and organiser with the Azadi Collective, led the crowd in a chant: “Azadi Afghanistan!” She asked: “What do we demand?” The crowd answered: “Let her learn!”
Since the Taliban returned to power in August 2021, international sanctions, frozen assets, and aid cuts have been intended to pressure the government over its treatment of women and girls. Yet the measures have also deepened economic hardship, weakened public services, and made it harder for businesses to access finance. Taliban restrictions have also compounded the economic damage.
Afghanistan has strengthened ties with Russia, China, India, Iran, and Türkiye, despite lacking widespread formal recognition. But closer diplomatic relations have done little to resolve practical problems for Afghans seeking visas, education, banking access, or work abroad. The situation has renewed calls for pragmatic engagement alongside continued pressure on human rights, even as some criticise this approach as only likely to embolden the Taliban while bringing limited to no easing of restrictions.
Mozhda Poyan/TNH
Empty school desks and chairs, along with notebooks and pens, symbolised the many Afghan girls whose educations have been cut short.
Mozhda Poyan/TNH
Sahar Shirzad, a Dutch-Afghan human rights activist and organiser with the Azadi Collective.
The demonstration in Amsterdam came as the European Union has been holding talks with the Taliban about the return of Afghan nationals. The EU does not recognise the Taliban government and says the talks are technical. But for Afghan women, the distinction between practical contact and normalisation matters.
Those at the demonstration offered different answers. Some argued that refusing to talk achieves little and can make it harder to address problems affecting ordinary Afghans. Others said engagement risks weakening pressure on a regime that has restricted women’s education, work, and public life. Deportations have sharpened the debate, with several interviewees warning about the risks facing Afghans returned to the country.
Here is what they said:
Melika Azimi, 20, Dolle Mina member and demonstration organiser
Azimi, a member of the Dutch feminist organisation Dolle Mina, initially questioned whether organising a demonstration would make a difference. But after seeing young Afghan girls post emotional videos asking people to stand behind them, she changed her mind.
“I realised that it would make a difference, because we are breaking that atmosphere. We are shouting that we see them and that we are fighting for them,” said Azima, who is Afghan by heritage but has never lived in Afghanistan.
After seeing footage of Afghan women protesting their arrests in Herat, she said she was struck by their courage. The ensuing crackdown left at least one person dead and several injured: “They were killed, yet they kept going. I felt so inspired by them; I could not do otherwise.”
Azimi said she believes there should be communication with the Taliban, but worries that engagement could become a compromise that encourages further human rights abuses.
“I understand that every country acts in its own interests, but I wonder where the line lies between tactical communication and compromising our values,” she said. “I think there should certainly be more discussions about the Taliban regime. Let’s address the elephant in the room: Do we really have so little backbone? Do we no longer stand for basic human rights?”
Sadia Tayeb Sadat, 19, student living in Kabul
Sadat was in eighth grade when the Taliban returned to power and girls’ schools were closed. She said she had hoped to become a dentist: “My dreams were put on hold, and I felt that my future had been taken away from me.”
Interviewed via text and voice messages from Kabul, Sadat said international discussions about Afghanistan have increasingly focused on migration, deportation, security, humanitarian aid, and diplomatic engagement, while the situation of Afghan women has become less central.
“I think many Afghan women now feel forgotten. When the world’s attention faded, our struggles continued, but fewer people were listening,” she said.
“Practical engagement may sometimes be necessary to help ordinary Afghans, but if that engagement gradually turns into acceptance of the Taliban as a normal and legitimate government, the international pressure for women’s rights could become weaker,” Sadat added.
For her, engagement should come with clear principles, with women’s rights and girls’ education remaining part of every serious conversation about Afghanistan.
“You can speak to the Taliban without forgetting the people who live under their rule,” she said. “Engagement should not mean silence about women’s rights.”
Jalwa Rahimi, 22, Afghan woman living in the Netherlands
Rahimi spent 20 years in Afghanistan before moving to the Netherlands eight months ago. She came to the demonstration because she wants girls’ schools to reopen beyond the sixth grade.
“It is education that creates a country,” she said. “The right of a woman is to study. If she wants to work, she can work.”
Rahimi supports European cooperation with the Taliban, arguing that talking to them does not necessarily mean recognising them.
“By talking, you can solve difficulties,” she said. “They don’t have to recognise them, but they can talk about the problems of Afghans.”
She also opposes deportations and warned that if Europe and the United States continue sending Afghans back, other countries could follow.
“If Afghanistan is good, no one would want to come here,” she said. “If the world forgets Afghanistan, there will be nothing left.”
Hamasa, 42, former teacher and women’s rights activist
For Hamasa, who prefers this adopted activist name for security reasons, the consequences of the Taliban’s rule are not abstract.
She lived in Afghanistan until January 2025 and now lives in an asylum centre in the Netherlands. She turned her home into a classroom, teaching girls and women for free; she said she initially taught 63 students.
After the Taliban takeover, she joined protests demanding education for girls and the right for women to work. She said Taliban fighters beat and kicked protesters during a September 2021 demonstration, causing her to lose her unborn child. She later said she was arrested and tortured after the Taliban discovered a gathering she had organised, and that threats against her family prompted her to leave Afghanistan.
She is strongly opposed to deportations. Questioning why European governments would demand rights for women at home while accepting their denial in Afghanistan, she said: “I want to ask the European government how they want democracy for their people, that women go to school; they should have the same wish for Afghanistan.”
On deportations, she asked: “And the European countries that unfortunately deport Afghans from their countries, and when those Afghans come to Afghanistan they die, don’t they regret doing this?”
Laura Iqbal, 35, Party for the Animals representative and Dolle Mina co-founder
Iqbal, who is Dutch and whose father was born in Pakistan, is a prominent Dolle Mina activist and was a candidate for the Party for the Animals in Amsterdam. “There is no ‘pragmatic’ middle ground with a regime that erases half of the population from society. The Taliban are waging a systematic, institutional war against women. We call that: gender apartheid,” she said.
Iqbal was particularly critical of European cooperation over deportations, arguing that it risks legitimising the Taliban while undermining the women protesting against them.
“European governments claim to stand up for women’s rights, but make those principles subordinate to a cruel migration agenda. You cannot say you are protecting human rights while making deals with the oppressors.”
Iqbal said European governments should instead stop deportations and put greater pressure on the Taliban. She also argued that European governments should involve Afghan women and women’s rights defenders in decisions about Afghanistan.
Meena Maryam Ahmad, 16, Afghan girl living in France
Ahmad, who was not at the protest, left Afghanistan in 2023, citing the closure of girls’ schools, a lack of job opportunities, and uncertainty about the future. She had been in eighth grade when the Taliban returned to power.
Interviewed via text and voice messages from France, she recalled watching her brothers continue their education while she was unable to do so: “I often felt sad and hopeless when I saw my brothers going to school while I was unable to continue my education.”
She said global attention on the plight of Afghan women has decreased even though the situation for women and girls has not improved.
“Sometimes I feel that the world has become used to the suffering of Afghan women,” Ahmad added.
She had a direct message for Europe’s politicians and lawmakers: “I want to tell European policymakers that Afghan women are not just a political issue; we are people with dreams and futures. If they negotiate with the Taliban, they should not forget the rights and voices of Afghan women.”
Despite the hardships of the past five years, she said she has not lost hope.
“I truly believe that no one can destroy a girl’s dreams forever. We are not only victims; we are women who continue to stand despite all the pain. We still have dreams, and we will continue to fight for a better future.”
Petra Hoogerwerf, Dutch strategic adviser to charities and non-profits
Hoogerwerf, a Dutch supporter of Afghan women who was at the demonstration, drew a distinction between necessary practical contact with the Taliban and normalisation of the regime.
She said contact can sometimes be necessary to facilitate humanitarian aid and support the Afghan population, but worries when returns and deportations become a major driver of engagement.
“Afghan women must not pay the price for European migration policy,” she said. “Necessary practical contact can only take place if the rights and position of women and girls remain firmly on the table. Diplomatic contact may be necessary for humanitarian and practical matters; normalisation is something else.”
She also called for continued political and financial support for organisations working with Afghan women and girls, and urged policymakers to listen directly to Afghan women.
“Not only talk about them, but with them,” she said.

Kellogg to Ukrainian veterans: You are the reason Ukraine still stands, the world knows your flag, anthem
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
11:01:06 EEST
17:01:06 KST

Former US Special Representative for Ukraine Lieutenant General Keith Kellogg, on the eve of the 35th anniversary of Ukraine’s independence, acknowledged the contribution of Ukrainian veterans in the fight for freedom and assured that veteran experience will help build a more resilient and cohesive nation.
"To every veteran who is here today and across the country: you are the reason why Ukraine still stands. You are the reason why the world knows your flag. Knows your anthem. Knows your unbroken spirit. When one Ukrainian says "Glory to Ukraine", the world answers "To the heroes – glory!," he said at the "35 Years of Faith and Freedom" forum in Kyiv on Sunday, an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent reports.
Kellogg called for a commitment to "take care of those who took care of us," highlighting the importance of proper medical care, psychological support, fair recognition, and assistance for veterans.
"A nation that forgets its defenders and its heroes forgets itself," the general emphasized.
Kellogg stressed that on February 24, 2022, Russia launched a full-scale invasion "with the goal of erasing Ukraine from the map; the world expected Kyiv to fall in three days, but instead Ukrainians stood firm."
"And at the center of this resistance were the veterans – men and women who had already been defending their sovereignty since 2014. And millions of others answered the call. Your veterans are the living embodiment of Ukraine’s will to be free. Men who held the defense in Donbas, who liberated Kherson and Kharkiv, who turned the tide of the war when no one believed it anymore. Women who served in the infantry, as snipers, drone operators, medics, and commanders," Kellogg noted.
He noted that Ukrainian veterans fought not for glory or conquest, but so that Ukraine would remain Ukraine.
"So that your children could speak Ukrainian. So that they could celebrate their birthdays, their holidays, and choose their own future without dictatorship from Moscow. They put their lives, their health, their youth on the line," the general said.
He emphasized that the name of every fallen soldier is remembered, because "freedom is not an abstraction. It is bought with blood and bought with determination."
At the same time, Kellogg stressed that veterans play an important role in the reconstruction of Ukraine, and their experience will help build a more resilient and cohesive nation.
"But veterans do not only defend. They build. When this war eventually ends – as all wars end – millions of veterans will return to civilian life. They will lead the government, they will lead businesses, and they will lead their communities. Programs are already preparing them for post-war leadership. Because the same discipline and the same sacrifice that saved Ukraine will rebuild it stronger than ever before," Kellogg expressed confidence.
On the eve of the 35th anniversary of Ukraine’s Independence, the general noted that thirty-five years ago, Ukrainians chose freedom.
"Today you defend it. Tomorrow you will build upon it. Ukraine’s independence is not a gift. It is a promise kept by every man and every woman who stood up [to defend it – IF-U] when it mattered most," he stated.

Cofnas Suspended by Ghent University
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
08:00:22 UTC
17:00:22 KST

Cofnas Suspended by Ghent University
Nathan Cofnas has been suspended from his postdoctoral philosophy position at Ghent University.
In a July 21st post on his newsletter, Cofnas accused Jason Arday, professor of sociology of education at the University of Cambridge, of plagiarism and fraudulent scholarship, and accused the university of covering this up.
Am international media blitz followed, with hundreds of articles reporting on Cofnas’s accusations and investigating Arday’s work and his autobiographical claims. Eventually, on August 5th, Cambridge announced it had decided to investigate Arday. Arday resigned shortly thereafter. The worldwide pile-on continued. On August 14th, Arday was found dead, presumably by suicide.
This past Thursday, Cofnas stated on X.com that he had been suspended from Ghent University and is being investigated.
Many had objected to his being hired there in the first place.
Most of the text of the suspension letter can be found here. Among the main reasons for the suspension, according to the letter, are the following:
- Cofnas’s continued work on “race realism” and the “hereditarian revolution” at Ghent “are fundamentally inconsistent with the contractual scope of your employment and constitute a manifest violation of your professional obligations towards this University”. Apparently, when he applied for the position, Cofnas had described the research he’d be engaging in as being about “the future of liberalism” and “liberalism as a political doctrine emphasizing individual liberty and equality,” not about “race realism” and “hereditarianism”.
- Cofnas’s ideas conflict with the Ghent University Code of Ethics, which “prohibits spreading ideas of racial superiority or inciting racial segregation.”
- “The current situation poses a risk to the proper functioning of the university and to the psychosocial wellbeing of members of its community”
Meanwhile, a Trump administration official has called for Cofnas to be reinstated, and others are defending him as a “whistleblower.”
Since Arday’s tragic death, Cofnas has defended himself in assorted public writings and appearances (for example).
Cofnas’s current suspension is until August 28th.

Hong Kong airport embraces future of travel with Terminal 2
Revamped terminal under the three-runway system blends thoughtful design with technological enhancements to provide efficiency and comfort to travellers
When Hong Kong International Airport (HKIA) opened in 1998 to replace its predecessor, the iconic Kai Tak Airport, the world was amazed by its engineering and architectural marvels.
HKIA’s construction transformed the geography of northern Lantau Island, adding 1 per cent to the city’s total land mass by reclaiming land to connect two other islands, Chek Lap Kok and Lam Chau. The main terminal, designed by the renowned architect Norman Foster, revolutionised the passenger experience with its pillarless interior set under a wave-shaped vaulted ceiling. Now known as Terminal 1 (T1), the building has been an inspiration for many other aviation facilities that followed.
Over the last three decades, the airport has gone through numerous upgrades to maintain its position as a leading international aviation hub. But none have been as transformative as the three-runway system, which commenced operations in November 2024 on time and within budget, and is set to expand HKIA’s capacity by 50 per cent to an impressive 120 million passengers per year.
On the passenger-facing side, one of the most significant updates happened in May with the opening of the revamped Terminal 2 (T2), designed to serve those travelling to and from regional destinations. A total of 15 airlines have moved to the new facility.
In addition to offering 24-hour dining and retail outlets, T2 has structural features that are crucial to the passenger experience, which include five vehicle lanes set under an entrance canopy. There are also waterfall displays and a sweeping cantilever roof that creates a sense of space.
Those were among the myriad details considered by Tommy Leung King-yin, executive director of engineering and technical services for the Airport Authority Hong Kong. And HKIA’s own track record was the toughest act to follow.
“T1 has collected multiple top international awards, and after 30 years, it’s still one of the best terminals in the world,” he says.
Leung says making T2 better than T1 seemed like a “mission impossible” at some point, but after numerous design revisions, they came up with the result: a feather-shaped roof that rests like a canopy on inclined “tree columns” – slender, tapering structural elements, each with a floating base that barely touches the ground.
“We created a feather roof which allows natural light to come in, and lifted the column off the ground,” he says, adding that this enhances orientation and reduces dependence on artificial lighting while also creating a calm, open and uplifting atmosphere within the terminal.
The interior is only one part of a multifaceted experience at T2. Steven Yiu Siu-chung, executive director of airport operations for the Airport Authority Hong Kong, says that by optimising the layout and technology, it takes passengers less than 20 minutes to get from the entrance to the boarding gate.
Yiu notes that T2 features “100 per cent in-house design” self bag-drop machines, each equipped with 10 artificial intelligence cameras that scan baggage to complete the process in 45 seconds. They also have ergonomically designed, ultra-low platforms that make it easier for passengers to place their luggage onto the conveyor belt.
“In T2, the security gates leading to the airside area are right in the middle of the hall, and that’s for operational efficiency,” Yiu adds. “You can get out of the taxi and walk through to the restricted area in two and a half minutes if you only have carry-on baggage.”
This substantial time savings is made possible by innovations such as the facial recognition technology that has replaced physical checks of passports and boarding passes at every security gate.
Yiu also highlights the LED screens with ocean-themed displays that surround passengers as they descend the escalators, which add a relaxing vibe to the experience. “These big screens give a very young, energetic feeling,” he says.
Hong Kong architect and frequent traveller Jacqueline Chak, who once worked at Foster + Partners – the architecture firm behind HKIA’s original design – is impressed. “This T2 gives me the feeling that it has the DNA of the amazing T1 we all know, but it feels a lot younger,” she says.
Watch the full video to find out more about Terminal 2 by following Jacqueline Chak on a walk through the new facility with Tommy Leung and Steven Yiu.

Hamas remains the main obstacle to further improving the situation in the Gaza Strip, a senior official from the Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT) said on Sunday.
"The organization interferes with humanitarian operations, exploits civilian infrastructure, influences distribution mechanisms, and continues its repeated attempts to smuggle prohibited items under the guise of humanitarian aid," the official said.
Since the beginning of the ceasefire in the Gaza Strip in October 2025, the IDF has continued to facilitate the entry of humanitarian aid and goods into the Gaza Strip, in coordination with the UN and international organizations.
According to a COGAT analysis, the volume of aid entering the Gaza Strip significantly exceeds humanitarian needs as defined by UN agencies, international organizations, and assessments conducted throughout the war.

According to the data, more than two million tons of food have entered the Gaza Strip since the beginning of the ceasefire, including meat, poultry, eggs, dairy products, fruits, and vegetables.
The data also shows that around 600 trucks enter the Gaza Strip every day, with 70% to 80% carrying food, while food prices have dropped by about 72%.
Currently, 41 bakeries run by international organizations operate in the Gaza Strip, producing more than three million pita breads per day, in addition to dozens of local bakeries.
Sixty liters of water per person enter Gaza each day, COGAT data shows
The data also showed that, on average, more than 70,000 cubic meters of water are supplied to the Gaza Strip each day, equivalent to more than 60 liters per person per day.
Around 250 water trucks operate daily, serving approximately 2,800 distribution points throughout the Gaza Strip.
In addition, more than 74,000 tons of hygiene and sanitation supplies have entered the Gaza Strip, alongside garbage disposal equipment and water purification tablets.
As noted, four water pipelines are currently operational in the Gaza Strip, three of which supply water from Israel. They operate alongside desalination facilities and dozens of water wells throughout the Strip.
Advanced medical equipment transferred to Gaza Strip
More than 21,000 tons of medical equipment have entered the Gaza Strip since the beginning of the ceasefire. According to COGAT data, hospital bed occupancy has increased by more than 50%. In coordination with international organizations, advanced medical equipment has been transferred into the Strip, including X-ray machines, generators, and oxygen tanks.
In northern Gaza, eight permanent hospitals, four field hospitals, and four medical centers are operating regularly. In the southern Gaza Strip, two permanent hospitals and eight field hospitals are operating.

After 78 years: Altalena ship found intact on seafloor decades after being sunk by IDF
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
07:55:13 UTC
16:55:13 KST

The Altalena ship was located intact on the seafloor 78 years after being sunk following an altercation between the IDF and the Irgun in 1948, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and the Heritage Ministry announced on Monday.
The Heritage Ministry said the ship was found at a depth of 503 meters, some 20 kilometers off Israel's west coast.
The Altalena arrived in Israel with new immigrants, weapons to fight in the Independence War, and fighters from the Irgun, a paramilitary force that operated before the independence and was absorbed into the IDF.
Although it was technically dissolved after the declaration of independence in June 1948, the Irgun kept operating separately from the IDF until September of that year.
The Altalena Affair started after a disagreement between the then Prime Minister David Ben-Gurion and the then Irgun leader Menachem Begin, who were fighting over how to divide the weapons inside the ship.
The discussion ended with the IDF shelling the Altalena, which destroyed the ship and left it heavily damaged and abandoned. During the fighting, 19 people were killed: 16 Irgun fighters and three IDF soldiers.
The ship was then abandoned in Frishman Beach in Tel Aviv, while it was towed 15 miles out and sank in 1949, in an effort to clear the area.
Discovery of Altalena is 'defining moment,' Heritage Minister says
"Tonight we are closing a historical circle on one of the most painful and formative events in the history of Israeli society," Ben-Gvir said.
"We have been dealing with this issue secretly for many years, and today – the fruits of the intelligence and operational effort have borne exciting fruit for the sake of historical truth, the memory of the fallen, and unity with Israel."
"The discovery of the Altalena is a defining moment for our national memory," Heritage Minister Amichai Eliyahu stated. "We worked on this operation out of a deep-seated mission to reveal the historical truth and make the story of the ship's heroes accessible to future generations."

Amazon struggles to win Israeli shoppers while Chinese e-commerce giants dominate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
07:55:10 UTC
16:55:10 KST

While Amazon goes from strength to strength worldwide, the US giant has struggled to gain a foothold in Israel in terms of online retail sales. Shop Analytics data in June 2026 shows that the three Chinese platforms AliExpress, Temu and Shein accounted for about 75% of Israelis' online orders, while Amazon only had a 6% market share.
E-commerce expert and ECommunity CEO Nir Zigdon says, "It's interesting, because in other countries Amazon is a very significant player, and here it hasn't been able to create the same traction.
And it's not because it hasn't tried. In April 2019, Amazon reached out to Israeli sellers and invited them to join the Local Delivery program.
The idea was to allow suppliers to present products to Israelis through Amazon and deliver them from inventory already in the country within five business days. But there was a critical difference from the model that Americans are familiar with: Amazon did not set up its own logistics center here, and sellers were required to handle inventory and delivery themselves.
Zigdon points out that Marketplace works well when it gives a supplier something that is difficult for them to achieve on their own - a huge target clientele, exceptional logistics, and trust that justifies a higher price.
'The Israeli consumer is in a very small and crowded market'
But in a small market, when the same importer can sell on its own website, and the consumer can compare prices in seconds, any additional commission may become a disadvantage.
"The Israeli consumer is in a very small and crowded market," explains Zigdon.
"If the same importer sells a product for NIS 1,000, and then on Marketplace has to add to the price because of the commissions, a problem arises. Maybe the customer is exposed to the product on Marketplace, but in the end they go to buy directly from the seller."
Compared with Amazon's partial experience in Israel, in recent years, it is AliExpress's investment in a local presence that stands out. Parcel Home, a logistics arm that delivers packages from AliExpress, launched operations in Israel in 2024 and operated about 45 distribution points as of April 2026.
At the same time, AliExpress operates local warehouses that, in some cases, allow shipping times to be shortened to 7-10 days and has added the option to pre-select a preferred pickup point near your home.
"The thing that hinders e-commerce the most is presence in the field and advertising," says Zigdon. "This is perhaps one of the reasons why it doesn't work for Amazon in Israel like it does in other markets."
Local marketplace trial failed
In December 2023, the marketplace activities of Azrieli, Melisron, and Shufersal were closed within a week.
Azrieli had invested in Azrieli.com over the years and recorded losses of about NIS 300 million. Melisron's investment in Groo's activity reached about NIS 100 million. Industry sources told "Globes" at the time that to maintain a trading arena, large investments are needed in traffic, advertising, customer service, technology, and logistics, and in the local market it is difficult to reach a turnover that justifies all this.
A marketplace is not just a site with many products. It is a business of economies of scale. More buyers bring more sellers, more sellers bring more selection, and selection brings more buyers, and then you can charge the sellers commissions, logistics services, and advertising.
In the US, Amazon is deep into this cycle. In Israel, anyone starting from scratch must finance it.
The KSP chain provides an interesting example. In June, it was the leading Israeli site in the Shop Analytics index, with 18% of orders on the top 20 local sites.
According to Zigdon, "KSP is very successful even though it is a retailer that buys and sells. It has become a multi-brand, and that is something that Israelis love. It also does a lot of parallel imports to really break the prices. Maybe the Israeli market has no place for a general marketplace in the classic model."
This conclusion also ties in with Shop Analytics data. In May, the three leading Israeli sites were KSP, SuperPharm, and Shufersal - three players that started with specific retail operations and only later expanded their offerings to other categories.
