The Syrian side said it had the right to rebuild and develop its armed forces and determine its alliances and partnerships, rejecting any arrangement that would limit those sovereign rights.
Damascus also reiterated its position that the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights are Syrian territory but said discussion of their final status was premature.
Its immediate priorities were the withdrawal of Israeli forces to positions held before Dec. 8, 2024, and the restoration and full implementation of the 1974 disengagement agreement, the ministry source said.
The 1974 accord established a U.N.-patrolled buffer zone between Israeli and Syrian forces. Israeli troops entered the zone following the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s government in December 2024.

Under the law, security institutions are responsible for determining whether the PKK and affiliated groups have ended their de facto existence and surrendered all weapons and ammunition under their control. The finding must then be confirmed by a National Security Council decision published in the Official Gazette.
The board will monitor and assess implementation of the law.
Following the council’s decision, it may periodically review whether the organization has been fully dismantled, drawing on observation reports, and request further judicial, administrative or legislative measures.
It will also review decisions to defer investigations, prosecutions and sentence enforcement.
Once the legal conditions are met, the board may ask the relevant courts to lift restrictions on rights arising from such proceedings or convictions.

He warned that continued disruption could affect shipments of energy products, grain, coal and steel, while the use of alternative routes would increase transport costs.
He also said damaged vessels stranded offshore posed an environmental risk because of the fuel they carried and called on Ankara to engage both Moscow and Kiev.
Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan earlier this month called for a mechanism allowing Russia and Ukraine to declare a moratorium on attacks against commercial shipping.
He said Ankara had relayed a Ukrainian proposal to Moscow.
Russia subsequently rejected the idea of a partial Black Sea ceasefire, while saying it had received no "formal" proposal.

130,000 or 230,000? The migration figures One Nation is trying to explain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
05:40:45 UTC
14:40:45 KST

in brief
- One Nation MPs presented conflicting figures regarding their proposed annual net overseas migration targets.
- Party leader Pauline Hanson clarified that the official policy remains a strict cap of 130,000.
One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce has faced questions over his party's immigration target, claiming fellow MP David Farley misspoke when he revealed their figures were "not too different" from Labor's.
The MP for Farrer told ABC's Insiders program on Sunday that One Nation's stated figure of 130,000 net overseas migration annually into Australia did not include those who enter under a Pacific labour scheme, aged-care nurses, and other in-demand skilled workers.
He conceded that those groups would add roughly 100,000 people, bringing their total to 230,000 — 5,000 fewer than the current Labor budget projections.
Party leader Pauline Hanson intervened just hours later, writing on social media that One Nation's policy is to reduce net overseas migration (NOM) to 130,000.
Speaking to Channel Seven's Sunrise program on Monday, Joyce added that Farley simply made a mistake while explaining the numbers.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"Show me a political career where people haven't made a mistake, and I'll show you a person who's not told the truth," Joyce said.
"I'm not going to throw anybody under a bus. When people are new in parliament, they can sometimes get things incorrect, and that's what happens. God knows, I've done it enough."
The debate over Australia's migration figures has intensified in recent months, with a recent Redbridge/Accent Research poll, conducted for the Australian Financial Review, indicating that voters trust One Nation and its traditionally restrictive approach to handle migration better than Labor or the Liberal Party.
However, the disjointed nature of One Nation's ongoing public discourse on the topic has prompted claims that the party is "incoherent" and "not fit to govern" from federal minister Pat Conroy.
What is One Nation's immigration target?
Since its 1997 inception, cutting immigration has been seemingly a foundational pillar of One Nation policy. During her first speech to federal parliament, Hanson alleged Australia was in danger of being "swamped by Asians", that migrants never assimilated, and that multiculturalism should be abolished.
Its website currently states One Nation would "cut immigration by over 570,000 people" through "capping visas at 130,000 per year".
In a social media post on Sunday, Hanson wrote that NOM would be cut to 130,000 — a figure the party has previously clarified to SBS News. This number would be achieved by reducing international students, temporary graduate visas, and a "much more targeted" skilled migration program, Hanson said.
Those figures are different to the ones put forward by Farley, who said One Nation is focusing on "the NOM in its true form", as separate to labour programs "that drive our economy".
"The raw number is not too different [to current projections], but the reality is, where do we need them?" he asked.
"We don't need them in the great urban metroplex — we need them out to be productive, working in agriculture, engineering, mining."
Joyce further affirmed Hanson's view that One Nation's policy remained at 130,000 people annually for NOM.
SBS News has contacted One Nation for comment.
Where do Labor and the Coalition stand on immigration?
NOM hit 306,000 in the 2024-2025 period, down from a post-pandemic peak of 538,000.
Labor is yet to unveil its plan to restrict migration, but has previously set an official cap of 185,000 places on the permanent migration program. Treasury figures project that NOM will fall to 225,000 by the 2027-28 financial year.
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke was set to detail Labor's plan to ensure that forecast was met, but pulled out of a National Press Club address at the last minute over fears about the implications cuts would have for certain sectors.
"Our policy will be released when Tony Burke is in a position to do so," Conroy told ABC Radio National on Monday. "But we've been very focused on getting the right migration mix to grow the economy as well as the broader interests of Australia."
Opposition leader Angus Taylor has said the Coalition will cap NOM at or below the number of homes built in Australia the previous year. Current building rates suggest their figure would be under 180,000; however, the Coalition is yet to announce where they would restrict immigration to reach that figure.
Opposition immigration spokesperson Jonathon Duniam told ABC Radio National that the Coalition is being "fairly methodical" in assessing its figures but that he would not "put a date" on when it will reveal details.
Duniam attacked One Nation for being cavalier with its migration figures, saying it had not detailed the impact such reductions would have on industries like agriculture, which relies on working holiday visa holders for seasonal labour.
"It was the same leader of One Nation who said in an interview about a week ago as well that she did not care about the impact on business any change to the migration system would have," Duniam said.
What's in a NOM?
NOM is difficult for governments to control because it is a measurement of human behaviour rather than a fixed quota.
NOM is calculated by the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) based on the movement of people, subtracting overseas departures from overseas arrivals. To be included, a person must remain in the country for any 12 out of 16 months.
Citizens, permanent residents, temporary visa holders, and asylum seekers are included, as are backpackers and working holiday makers who stay for more than a year.
In 2024-2025, 568,000 people entered Australia, according to the ABS, down 14 per cent on the previous year.
Of that cohort, 88,000 were permanent visa holders, 53,000 were New Zealand citizens, and 64,000 were returning Australians. At the same time, 263,000 people left the country.
As Hanson stated, "short-term seasonal agricultural workers who do not meet the ABS residency test are not counted in net overseas migration".
However, using Farley's figures, many of the 100,000 additional workers he says would be able to enter the country — such as workers under the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme — would be included in NOM.
PALM workers can enter under a short-term placement of up to nine months or a long-term placement of one to four years.
The visa caps One Nation plans to set would place policy restrictions on NOM, but they can't control it entirely. Australians suddenly returning home en masse from abroad would, for example, elevate the figure regardless of visa caps.
Migration experts have long cautioned that linking migration to housing shortages is a flawed argument and that, in fact, migrant workers are essential to increase housing stock.
"If we don't have workers doing the jobs we need, if we don't get the right skill set into our country, then we all are worse off," Duniam said.
"One Nation has zero regard for that, as evidenced by the multiple positions they've had on migration policy all over the last few weeks."

====================================================================================================

AI tokens getting cheaper but businesses paying more than ever
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
05:36:43 UTC
14:36:43 KST

AI costs are rising for Australian businesses even as tokens get cheaper
In short:
Businesses are looking for ways to measure the return on the billions being spent on AI. Some say they are "years away" from judging bottom-line impacts.
In this story:
Australian businesses paying to use AI are weighing up what value they are getting from the disruptive technology.
"It's actually only really a relatively new thing that we have started to speak about," Anna Volkova, the head of people and culture at HR software company HiBob, told ABC News.
The platform has seen wins from using artificial intelligence, but it has been difficult to judge that against the mounting cost.
With AI capabilities changing so quickly, Ms Volkova said the business can "never catch up" with the need to redesign how it works to get the most out of it.
This has made it hard to work out precisely if the money is being spent effectively.
"We'll probably start to see impact to our bottom line in maybe two or three years, and I think most businesses are in that boat."
Jeremy Pell, whose firm Elastic helps companies to manage the cost of AI, agreed with that estimate.
"We're in a really interesting time at the moment," he said.
"Businesses are forced to pay this additional investment into AI, but they haven't yet reaped the 'bottom-line' benefits of the cost savings yet."
Last week, Assistant Minister for Technology and the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton described the value flowing out of Australia via AI as a "distant sucking sound".
In a speech at the ANU Crawford School of Public Policy, he said Australians were already spending $5-8 billion each year on artificial intelligence.
"With the overwhelming majority of those payments flowing offshore, in effect, we are creating a new import bill. An import bill for intelligence."
That is just the start, with the government estimating local spending on AI could "plausibly" reach $20 billion to $40 billion annually within a decade.
Tokens adding up to billions
Even a few years ago, AI was not a line item companies had in annual budgets.
Now, in the current reporting season for ASX-listed companies, you can measure it in billions.
The technology spend at Australia's biggest bank, the Commonwealth Bank, increased from $2.3 billion in the 2025 financial year to $2.4 billion in this most recent financial year. It lists savings too.
"Measured gross benefits from AI use cases, including reinvested capacity, were [around] $200 million in FY26," its results presentation noted.
"Gross benefits from AI use cases are expected to double in FY27, and to exceed investment."
On Wall Street, investors are asking whether the billions invested by US tech giants in AI will ever be justified by returns, creating concern about an AI-fuelled stock market bubble.
Stu Scotis, AI leader for consulting firm Deloitte, said the equation of how to spend an IT budget is getting tougher.
Clients are weighing up long-term information technology costs — like storage and refreshing laptops — with a new, runaway expense.
"What we used to plan for as a static activity is now somewhat variable," he said.
Mr Scotis said current conversations are around "tokens": units of data processed by AI, or essentially the amount of grunt used to compute tasks.
Complex requests use more tokens, simple ones fewer.
The cost of tokens has plummeted in recent years, with increased competition, more efficient chips and more supply.
An unprecedented amount of data centre construction has increased the computing power available in the world.
Adding in more energy-efficient microchips, increased competition and the technology improving how much it can compute per token, it is now cheaper than ever.
As the below chart from research institute Epoch shows, the cost of the most powerful models has fallen the fastest.
Epoch used the "Massive Multitask Language Understanding" benchmark to rank AI large language models.
The price for large language models GPT-4 Turbo level or better (the most powerful, shown by the blue line) fell from $US15 ($20.90) for one million tokens in November 2023, to 17.5 US cents (24.4 cents) per million in February last year.
Despite this trend, what companies are spending on AI is rising.
That is because firms are finding new tasks for AI to take on, leading to increasingly difficult computations, requiring more tokens per request.
AI not necessarily cheaper than workers
Mr Scotis put it another way: Human workers are paid in dollars, digital workers — or AI models — are paid in tokens.
"You want to get value for the digital workers and their output," he explained.
That means companies investing in AI need to examine the "value, outcome or growth" that comes from the tasks they complete, just as companies evaluate the work of human employees.
"You start to get pretty clear, measurable outcomes that mean your investment in AI dollars or AI tokens actually pay a return."
He said the human workers should not be too worried about being replaced.
"The cost of a digital worker doesn't necessarily mean it's cheaper than a human," he said.
"The complexity of the task, the length of time which a digital worker runs can, in some instances, be more expensive than a person."
Mr Scotis said firms needed to make a judgement "as to where you want to invest that type of work in your organisation, and does it make sense to do so".
It is a question being weighed in boardrooms right now.
How do companies pay for AI?
There are multiple ways that companies pay for artificial intelligence.
Some use "seats", paying per employee that accesses the technology.
This model is often used with platforms like Microsoft's Copilot, where AI abilities can be unlocked in existing programs, like writing documents in Word or juggling numbers in Excel spreadsheets.
The most common way to pay is by tokens.
The frequency with which employees are using AI models and the amount of tokens used in the queries is a new and increasing cost for businesses — which many of them will not have been paying for in even last financial year's report.
"That's the cost metric these businesses are grappling with," said Elastic's Jeremy Pell.
Different model, different prices
Another variable is that some of the cutting-edge or "frontier" AI models use more tokens.
That has led to companies using different models for different tasks, to avoid paying top dollar for tasks a more basic model can handle.
Some firms have also become more deliberate about the use of AI, sometimes capping the amount of tokens employees can use in a certain time frame.
"Businesses can no longer do AI for AI's sake,"
"It's a matter of making sure that you are driving the business forward and these initiatives are driven and tied to the business's return on investment … It's working out which bits are useful."
'Scattergun' AI approach
AI expert Jon Whittle has warned the "scattergun" approach business has taken to using AI means the cost calculations are becoming more difficult, even as the price of tokens falls.
"I don't think companies are being very strategic right now about their AI use cases," he told The Business.
"They're just trying to find any place where they can use it, and that's why they're having costs increase so much."
Professor Whittle, a former technical lead at NASA, director of CSIRO's AI capability and founder of Australia's National AI Centre, said a particular issue was that AI itself did a poor job at estimating the amount of tokens required.
Research has shown estimates can differ "by a factor of 30" running the same request on the same technology.
"I think that's the number one thing keeping [chief financial officers] up at night right now,"
"It turns out that even the AI itself is not very good at predicting the cost that a particular AI task will take."
Speed increases as AI crunches data faster
From her Sydney office, Anna Volkova says the major advantage her firm currently gets from AI is speed.
By connecting artificial intelligence to the software tools the company already uses, staff have been able to do more, at greater pace.
But the bill is mounting.
She said, eventually, the business would likely need to evaluate usage "by need", not "limiting responsible experimentation" but looking for uses that maximise what staff get out of using AI as a tool.
"I think the things that we're looking for in terms of really seeing the return for our people … is it making their work better, easier?" she asks.
"Is it helping our leaders make decisions faster?"
It turns out the questions business leaders are asking about AI are very human.

Reused Brick and Timber Shape Reiulf Ramstad Arkitekter's New Railway Station in Sweden
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
05:30:00 UTC
14:30:00 KST

Construction is advancing on Gothenburg Grand Central, a new station building and prominent western entrance designed by Reiulf Ramstad Arkitekter. The project is part of the West Link (Västlänken) commuter rail project at Gothenburg Central Station, consisting of 8 kilometers of railway, including three new stations: Centralen, Haga, and Korsvägen. The new route is projected to increase capacity during peak hours and reduce travel times for commuter and regional trains, connecting directly to the existing central station and the Nils Ericson Terminal. The new station is scheduled to open alongside Västlänken's Centralen underground station in December 2026, with office tenants moving in during 2027, and the rest of the tunnel planned to be ready for traffic by December 2030.
The new building, now entering a decisive stage on site, will act as the main entrance hall above the new underground commuter station Västlänken, becoming a public threshold between the historic central station, the emerging Centralstaden district, and the wider city. The design for Gothenburg Grand Central includes station functions, retail and service areas, and three upper office floors with space for around 700 workplaces across a total of 15,000 m². Retail includes shops, restaurants, and cafés, accessible from several entrances. The existing station and Nils Ericson Terminal will be accessible from inside the new building.
Reiulf Ramstad Arkitekter's design incorporates material reuse as part of the architectural expression. A reused brick facade with deep vertical reliefs and large arched openings is now visible, following the removal of much of the scaffolding. According to the architects, the brickwork was chosen to give the building a tactile dimension and reference Gothenburg's history of railway architecture and public infrastructure. The structure combines timber, steel, and concrete, with 9,100 m² of cross-laminated timber (CLT) already assembled in the completed frames. The station hall is an ample, daylit space with large glazed areas, where concrete arches, timber structures, and detailed surfaces are intended to contribute to a legible environment for travelers.
The building's material strategy is meant to reduce the construction's climate impact. Around 600,000 bricks were used in total, complemented by reused steel in place of virgin steel. The project's design also contributes to urban biodiversity and public value with a 200-meter roof promenade featuring 54 plant species supporting insects, birds, and local ecology. The project itself supports sustainable mobility for everyday life, particularly by connecting rail, tram, bus, and bicycle infrastructure within the same development.
Also in Europe, construction advances on the Grand Paris Express, a major transport project comprising 200 kilometers of new, fully automated metro lines, 68 new stations, four new orbital lines, and an existing line extension, connecting outer suburbs, major airports, and business hubs in the Greater Paris region directly by rail. In Italy, Park is reimagining the interiors of Milano Centrale, Mussolini's fascist-era rail monument, redesigning the station's ground floor and mezzanine levels to transform the historic city landmark into a contemporary urban platform. Earlier this year, UNS and Settanta7 were selected to design Turin Metro Line 2 as a 32-station network, with the project envisioning the new line as a new "urban river," guided by three design principles to facilitate this flow: branding, transit experience, and scales of identity.

China opens exhibition hall on language preservation, diversity

A visitor listens to dialects of various regions in Hunan at the Exhibition Hall of the Project for the Protection of Language Resources of China in Changsha, central China's Hunan Province, Aug. 24, 2026. A new exhibition hall dedicated to the preservation of China's diverse language resources opened on Monday in Changsha, capital of central China's Hunan Province, bringing a decade-long effort to document languages and dialects to the public through digital and interactive displays. (Xinhua/Xue Yuge)
CHANGSHA, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- A new exhibition hall dedicated to the preservation of China's diverse language resources opened on Monday in Changsha, capital of central China's Hunan Province, bringing a decade-long effort to document languages and dialects to the public through digital and interactive displays.
The Exhibition Hall of the Project for the Protection of Language Resources of China, located in the Hunan Museum, brings together recordings and other language materials collected from more than 1,800 field survey sites across China, covering Chinese dialects, ethnic minority languages and related cultural traditions.
More than 30 language-related cultural relics are also on display.
The exhibition features original sound recordings representing 10 major Chinese dialects and more than 100 ethnic minority languages, including Mongolian, Tibetan, Uygur and Zhuang, said Chen Xuliang, deputy Party secretary of the Hunan Museum.
Visitors can listen to regional dialects, folk songs and field recordings of some endangered languages, while interactive installations allow them to explore the development and diversity of languages across China, Chen added.
The exhibition draws on materials collected through a national language preservation project launched in 2015 to document and preserve the country's diverse languages and dialects. It is the world's largest project of its kind, according to experts.
An alliance was also launched on Monday, bringing together universities and research institutions to promote the use of language technologies in areas including education, scientific research and cultural preservation. ■

Opinion: What 9.39 seconds says about human ingenuity
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
13:21:18 CST
14:21:18 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- At the second World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing on Saturday, China's Tien Kung Ultra humanoid robot clocked 9.39 seconds at the finish line, shattering the 9.58-second men's 100-meter world record set by Jamaican sprinter Usain Bolt 17 years ago.
The comparison is irresistible, though the two feats are hardly equivalent: Bolt shows how fast the human body can run; the robot shows how far human ingenuity can go.
At the current stage of humanoid robot development, running remains a formidable challenge. The robot must generate force, absorb repeated impacts and maintain dynamic balance while coordinating multiple joints simultaneously. Speed tests every technical limit: the faster the machine moves, the less time it has to recover from a mistake.
That makes the pace of improvement remarkable. At last year's Games, Tien Kung Ultra took 21.5 seconds over the same distance. One year later, it had more than halved that time.
Progress on that scale rarely comes from a single breakthrough. Over the past year, engineers upgraded the robot's joints, refined its structure and reworked its control algorithms for high-speed running. They have also improved its navigation, allowing it to hold its course at speed without relying on track markings.
Breaking the human record, however, is never the ultimate goal of engineering. Every improvement reveals the next weakness. Even Saturday's 9.39-second run pointed to the next challenge: the robot had a slower start, although its higher top speed allowed it to pull ahead later in the race.
Competition helps accelerate that process. It provides clear targets, common benchmarks and visible results. Once one team raises the bar, everyone else has a new standard to meet -- and proof that a higher level of performance is attainable.
Ultimately, the goal of humanoid robot innovation is not simply to make robots move like humans, but to enable them to work alongside people and take on useful tasks in the real world.
A factory robot does not need to win a sprint, nor does a service robot need a medal. But every gain in speed, stability and precision on the competition floor can bring robots one step closer to becoming genuinely useful beyond it.
That is what gives 9.39 seconds significance beyond the stopwatch. The speed record captures how far the machine has come in a year; behind it are countless human decisions, experiments and refinements that made that progress possible. The next test will be how far those advances can go beyond the track. ■

Feature: Chicago concert bridges cultures through Chinese, American folk songs
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
13:21:13 CST
14:21:13 KST

CHICAGO, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- The familiar strains of "Shenandoah" brought tears to Marci Jarog's eyes during a downtown Chicago concert on Saturday. For a song she thought she knew by heart, something was different this time.
Performed in a newly arranged symphonic choral version featuring a Chinese community chorus, the American folk classic offered Jarog a fresh perspective on a melody deeply rooted in American musical tradition.
"I thought I had heard this song a million times already, and then today I heard it differently," Jarog told Xinhua after the performance. "I think that hearing an unexpected cultural representation of 'Shenandoah' was even more moving than anything I would have expected."
More than 500 musicians, singers, dancers and community artists took part in the concert titled "Bridges We Build, Memories We Keep" at Chicago Symphony Center, drawing an audience of more than 2,000. The event was organized by the Midwest Asian Health Association.
Among the highlights were the world premieres of newly arranged symphonic choral versions of the American folk song "Shenandoah" and the Chinese folk song "Jasmine Flower."
"Music has a unique power to connect us across cultures, generations, and memories," said Elizabeth Jia, artistic director of the concert.
"I wanted those traditions to listen to one another, speak to one another, and ultimately create something that none of them could create alone," she said.
The concert brought together Western classical repertoire, Chinese art songs and instrumental works, opera, choral music and dance, taking audiences on a journey across different musical traditions.
Internationally acclaimed violinist Liu Yang performed an excerpt from the Chinese violin concerto "The Butterfly Lovers." Chinese baritone Hu Sihao, a member of the Patrick G. and Shirley W. Ryan Opera Center at Lyric Opera of Chicago and a prizewinner of China's Golden Bell Awards, also took the stage alongside soprano Boya Wei and other featured artists.
"It was fantastic. It was very well put together, and everyone was very professional," Jackie Carreras, who attended the concert at the invitation of a friend, told Xinhua after the performance.
"It's just beautiful to learn about different cultures, such as the Chinese culture, so I really enjoyed it," she said.
For Shelly Carter, the concert left her wanting to learn more. "It was like the whole world was up there, that mixed a lot of culture," she said, adding that she hoped to learn more about Chinese music and culture in the future.
As two folk traditions met in newly created symphonic arrangements and artists from different cultural backgrounds shared the same stage, the concert became more than a performance -- it served as a musical bridge connecting cultures, generations and memories. ■

Hong Kong urged to adopt trait-based dog tiers, DNA checks after fatal attacks
Proposal calls for risk tiers, certified handlers, muzzles or possible confiscation of highest-risk dogs as authorities review fighting-dog rules
Hong Kong should introduce a tiered risk framework and carry out DNA testing and physical checks to identify dogs with aggressive traits, a veterinarian and a lawmaker have said after a woman and two pets were all fatally mauled within a week.
Preliminary inspections by authorities revealed the dog shared genetic traits with the pit bull terrier, a banned fighting breed in the city. Yet, the dog’s microchip indicated it was a mongrel.
Veterinarian Lai Cheong-sang said Hong Kong should replace the city’s breed-specific categorisation system with a trait-based, tiered system to classify dogs’ danger levels and assign corresponding control measures.
“If a dog is suspected of having the potential to cause danger after a risk assessment, it can be required to undergo mandatory training, be leashed or otherwise constrained, and receive regular assessments,” he said on a radio show.
He also called for a certification system for people who keep or train high-risk breeds.

Norway will drill in Arctic regardless of EU's position, says energy minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
05:13:24 UTC
14:13:24 KST

Norway will drill in Arctic regardless of EU's position, says energy minister
STAVANGER, Norway, Aug 24 - Norway will continue developing its oil and gas resources in the Barents Sea regardless of the European Union's support for a moratorium on Arctic hydrocarbon supplies, and no longer sees itself as Europe's "green battery", Energy Minister Terje Aasland told Reuters.
Following Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Norway has become Europe's largest supplier of natural gas, meeting around 30% of gas demand of both the European Union and Britain.
Last year, the country's gas production was near record levels, while oil output reached its highest level since 2009. Official forecasts, however, show production falling sharply after 2030 unless new resources are discovered and developed.
"In today's geopolitical and security environment, and given the resource situation, I believe continued activity in the Barents Sea serves both Norwegian and European interests," Aasland said in a Reuters interview ahead of ONS, Norway's biannual energy conference, which begins in Stavanger on Monday.
The European Union currently supports a ban on new drilling in the Arctic on environmental grounds but is considering revising its policy in response to concerns about energy security.
Anders Opedal, CEO of Equinor, Norway's biggest oil firm, said oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) from the Barents Sea can be shipped anywhere in the world if rejected by the EU.
"The only thing that will suffer from this is actually European security. We have the flexibility," Opedal told Reuters on Monday.
NORWAY AIMS TO MAINTAIN OUTPUT LEVELS
Aasland said Norway aims to maintain petroleum production and exports at roughly current levels until at least 2035, and Barents Sea production will be key.
"If Norway is to remain a long-term supplier of oil and gas to Europe..., then the Arctic must be part of that discussion," the energy minister said.
In talks with EU officials, Norway has argued that the parts of the Barents Sea opened to petroleum activity are also ice-free like in the North Sea, and so less prone to oil spills and other environmental impacts, and are helping to sustain jobs and settlement in the country's northern regions bordering Russia.
Aasland believes Norway's arguments are being heard in Brussels, but added that it was the country's sovereign right to develop the Barents Sea resources even if the EU continued to support a moratorium.
"We would develop these areas, and then it will be up to the EU whether they should have a moratorium on buying that gas or oil," Aasland said.
Arctic oil would be sold into global markets regardless, while gas could be exported worldwide as liquefied natural gas from Equinor's Melkoeya LNG plant near Hammerfest, he added.
International Energy Agency Executive Director Fatih Birol has also urged the EU to reconsider its opposition to new Arctic oil and gas developments, arguing that future supplies will be needed to support energy security.
Critics of such a move argue that new Arctic projects would take many years to come online and would do little to address Europe's near-term energy challenges.
GREEN BATTERY "A FLAWED IDEA"
In addition to oil and gas, Norway produces a surplus of renewable energy most years from an extensive network of reservoirs and waterways feeding hydroelectrical plants, which it has exported to Europe via cross-border power cables.
Norway has previously presented itself as "the green battery" of Europe, but the minister says this idea is now outdated as Norway alone can't balance the European power market.
"It was a flawed idea," Aasland said.
The idea helped drive the construction of new power interconnectors, including links to Britain and Germany, but has drawn some opposition in Norway as European electricity prices have escalated.
Deeper integration with Europe's power system left Norway more vulnerable to continental price swings.
Aasland said Norway will not build new interconnectors but remains committed to strong power sector cooperation with Europe.
He urged countries on the continent to strengthen their stable power supply, weakened by coal and nuclear plant closures and a lack of investment in new gas-fired generation.
Doing so will lower prices and build greater reciprocity when it comes to power flows between different countries.
"The future lies in having a very strong and integrated system," Aasland said. REUTERS

John Lee urges start-ups to seize opportunities through ‘golden gateway’ of Hong Kong

Hong Kong’s leader has called on scientists, leading enterprises and investment institutions from around the world to seize opportunities in the city, describing it as a “golden gateway” for overseas companies to enter the mainland Chinese market and mainland unicorn firms to expand globally.

World’s oldest person celebrates 117th birthday with family and friends in Britain
Unknown

2026-08-24

World’s oldest person celebrates 117th birthday with family and friends in Britain
- Ethel Caterham, the world’s oldest person and first British to reach 117, celebrated her birthday with family and friends in Surrey.
- She lived through major historical events, survived Covid-19 at age 110, and credits her longevity to avoiding arguments.
- Caterham became the oldest living person in April 2025 and received a birthday card from King Charles on her 116th birthday.
AI generated
The world’s oldest person, Englishwoman Ethel Caterham, celebrated her 117th birthday on Aug 21 with her family and friends.
Caterham, who lives in a care home in Surrey, about 40km away from the British capital London, also chalked up another milestone – she is the first British person to reach that age.
“I’ve had a lovely day celebrating with my family and friends, and I look forward to seeing what next year brings,” she told British national news agency PA Media.
The world’s oldest man, 113-year-old Joao Marinho Neto, was among the well-wishers. He held up a celebratory photo of Caterham from his home in Brazil, reported Guinness World Records.
Born on Aug 21, 1909, Caterham is the last living subject of King Edward VII and has lived through two world wars, the sinking of the Titanic and the Russian Revolution.
She also survived the Covid-19 pandemic, when she became the oldest person to contract the virus at the age of 110 in 2020.
The second youngest of eight children, Caterham moved to India at the age of 18 to work as a nanny for a British family.
She met British Army Major Norman Caterham at a dinner party in 1931, and they married two years later.
The couple spent some time in Hong Kong before settling down in Surrey with their two daughters.
Caterham’s husband died in 1976, and she also outlived her daughters.
She currently has three granddaughters and five great-grandchildren.
Caterham became the world’s oldest living person in April 2025 following the death of the Brazilian nun, Sister Inah Canabarro Lucas, at the age of 116.
At that time, she revealed her secret to living a long life. “Never arguing with anyone, I listen, and I do what I like,” she told the Associated Press in May 2025.
On her 116th birthday in 2025, Caterham received a special visit from Britain’s King Charles, who gave her a birthday card.
During the visit, Caterham recalled when Queen Elizabeth invested him as the Prince of Wales in 1969, when he was 21.
“All the girls were in love with you and wanted to marry you,” she told him, prompting a laugh from the British monarch.
Despite her latest milestone, Caterham is still not the oldest person ever.
That honour belongs to French woman Jeanne Calment, who was 122 years and 164 days old when she died in 1997, according to Guinness.

South Korean president’s approval rating hits record low as decline extends to 6th week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Faisal Mahmud
24 August 2026•Update: 24 August 2026
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung’s approval rating fell to its lowest level since he took office, extending its decline for a sixth consecutive week, according to a Realmeter poll released Monday.
The survey, conducted from Aug. 18-21 among 2,026 adults, showed Lee’s approval rating falling 2.8 percentage points from the previous week to 40.2%.
His disapproval rating rose by the same margin to 56.9%, the Korea Herald reported.
Realmeter attributed the decline to growing public distrust over the government’s housing policies, political clashes involving judicial and constitutional issues, and security concerns following the scaling back of South Korea-US joint military exercises.
The pollster also noted weakening support for Lee among conservative voters and people aged 70 and above.
A separate Realmeter survey of 1,009 adults conducted Aug. 20-21 showed support for the ruling Democratic Party of Korea falling 6 percentage points to 41.9%.
Support for the opposition People Power Party, meanwhile, climbed 4.5 points to 37.6%, narrowing the gap between the two parties.
Both surveys were conducted using wireless automated response systems. The presidential approval poll had a margin of error of plus or minus 2 percentage points at a 95% confidence level.

Netherlands unveils underground stabilization facility project to mark Ukraine’s Independence Day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
04:32:00 UTC
13:32:00 KST

Netherlands unveils underground stabilization facility project to mark Ukraine’s Independence Day
According to a Ukrinform correspondent in The Hague, Dutch and Norwegian volunteers are working to implement this project in Ukraine.
“This is a single facility that will serve as a stabilization center for the wounded while also housing several operating rooms. Emergency surgeries will be able to be performed there. The main goal is to increase the chances of survival for Ukraine’s defenders,” said Jaap Scholten, a Dutch volunteer and co-founder of the Protect Ukraine Foundation, in an exclusive comment to Ukrinform.
He also noted that the total cost of the project is 2.5 million euros, and 750,000 euros have already been raised.
“We can’t say exactly where it will be located, but yes, the site where it will be built has already been determined. However, we don’t want to help the Russians, so we’re not naming it. And it’s important to note that this isn’t a hospital where patients will stay for a long time. They’ll only be there for a certain period, after which they’ll be transported to a military or other specialized hospital. Usually, they try to stabilize the wounded already in the ambulance and then at a stabilization point. But this facility will allow us to take it one step further. For example, it will be possible to perform certain surgeries, which will significantly increase a soldier’s chances of survival, rather than having to wait another three, four, or five hours until they are transported to a military hospital. That is the idea,” he said.
According to Zita Yankovich, a member of the Protect Ukraine Foundation’s board responsible for medical issues, drones have radically changed the conditions for evacuating the wounded. Even evacuation vehicles can become targets, which is why transporting the wounded to hospitals takes significantly longer.
“We used to talk about the ‘golden hour,’ when a wounded person had to be rescued within the first hour. But now that’s often impossible, because it’s simply not possible to quickly remove a person from the battlefield. So this project involves building a medical complex about 6–8 meters underground. For security reasons, its exact location and technical details are not being disclosed. The plan is to equip the facility with six operating rooms where surgical procedures can be performed, as well as to provide blood transfusions, anesthesia, and other emergency care. Most importantly, doctors will be able to work there safely,” she emphasized.
According to her, Russia’s war in Ukraine—particularly the widespread use of drones—has led to a change in the nature of injuries. Medical personnel are increasingly dealing with severe trauma, amputations, and internal bleeding caused by shrapnel. At the same time, stabilization points near the front lines are often set up under extremely challenging conditions—in makeshift underground facilities where medical personnel work with minimal resources and constant risk.
“About 2 million euros are needed to build the medical complex itself; the remaining funds will go toward medical equipment, supplies, and transportation, including armored vehicles for the safe evacuation of the wounded. The project aims not only to strengthen Ukraine’s medical capabilities on the front lines but also to protect doctors and medical personnel working in close proximity to combat operations. “We want to save as many lives as possible among Ukrainians who are fighting for their freedom—and for our freedom as well,” she emphasized.
Also during the event, Khrystyna N. (call sign “Ice Queen”)—a Dutch-Bulgarian senior combat medic who has been working on the front lines for four years— and Nataliia Tsyplytska—a former Ukrainian combat medic and executive director of the organization “Vdachni”—shared their personal experiences working in the combat zone and evacuating the wounded. They also showed the audience photos and videos depicting the real-life conditions under which medics work and the process of evacuating the wounded.
As reported by Ukrinform, a Dutch volunteer received the Order of Merit, Third Class, for his support of Ukraine.

Iceland to vote on resuming EU accession talks amid fears over Trump

Iceland to vote on resuming EU accession talks amid fears over Trump
Kyiv • UNN
On August 29, Icelanders will vote on resuming EU accession talks amid concerns over Trump's policy toward Greenland. The key disputes concern sovereignty and control over fisheries.
Icelandic voters will decide on August 29 whether to resume negotiations on the country's accession to the European Union amid rising geopolitical tensions and concerns over U.S. President Donald Trump's policy toward Greenland. Associated Press reports, UNN writes.
Details
The referendum will be the first direct vote by Icelanders on resuming negotiations on EU membership. Iceland, with a population of about 400,000, is a NATO member, participates in the EU single market through the European Economic Area, and is part of the Schengen Area.
Iceland's Foreign Ministry is "optimistic" about joining the EU in 202818.03.26, 23:03 • 5547 views
One of the factors that accelerated the referendum was Trump's statements about Greenland. The American president has repeatedly spoken about the need for the United States to control the Danish autonomous territory, and in one speech he called Greenland Iceland several times.
We can no longer truly trust the United States. Trump was not joking about Greenland. There was a lot of fear in Iceland because if he takes Greenland by force, we will probably be next
Sovereignty and fishing remain the main issues
Supporters of EU membership believe that closer ties with Europe could strengthen Iceland's security and protect it from geopolitical instability. Among the possible economic benefits, they cite a more stable currency, lower interest rates, and inflation.
Opponents of accession emphasize the preservation of sovereignty. Iceland gained independence from Denmark in 1944, and control over its own laws and natural resources remains an important part of national policy.
Iceland's independence is the most valuable resource we have. The ability to create our own laws and decide how to do everything is extremely important
Fishing is a separate issue. Iceland has extensive fish resources in the North Atlantic, and concerns about losing control over them have remained one of the main arguments against joining the EU for many years. Icelandic opponents of membership fear that European trawlers will gain access to its waters under the EU's Common Fisheries Policy.
Minister of Foreign Affairs and Defense Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir said that Iceland would not agree to a deal that did not guarantee the country's full control over its own fisheries.
Iceland has already attempted to join the EU. Negotiations began after the country submitted its application in 2009 amid the global financial crisis, but they were suspended in 2013 and formally ended in 2015.
If Icelanders support resuming negotiations in the referendum, a years-long process with the European Commission will begin. It will assess the country's compliance with 35 groups of criteria, including in the areas of finance, fisheries, transport, agriculture, and rights and freedoms. The final agreement must be approved by all EU member states, after which the decision on accession will again be put to a vote in Iceland.

Another case of acute liver damage in counterfeit peptide user
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
04:25:20 UTC
13:25:20 KST

Doctors fear possible contaminated counterfeit peptide batch after seventh case of acute liver damage
In short:
There are fears a "contaminated batch" of counterfeit peptides is causing hospitalisations for acute liver toxicity.
The latest patient became seriously unwell after taking unapproved peptide labelled as retatrutide.
What's next?
Doctors are testing the counterfeit peptides linked to the liver failure cases, amid warnings that unapproved products can cause serious harm.
Another black market peptide user has suffered a severe liver injury, with doctors concerned a possible "contaminated batch" might be to blame.
The latest case means seven Victorian patients have now been hospitalised for acute liver toxicity, after using a counterfeit of the weight loss peptide retatrutide.
Liver transplant specialist Marie Sinclair, who has treated liver failure patients in Victoria, said another patient had recently become seriously unwell after taking an unapproved peptide labelled as retatrutide.
"We have seen a recent case again, fairly similar to previous cases, where after a second dose of unregulated retatrutide there was severe liver injury," Dr Sinclair said.
"It's uncertain as to why this has happened, but one possibility is that there could be a contaminated batch of [counterfeit] retatrutide that is in Victoria.
"It's one possible explanation … we don't have any testing results to support that, it's purely a hypothesis at this stage."
Dr Sinclair said she had commissioned testing of counterfeit peptides used by liver failure patients.
"This is something I think we are going to continue to see with peptides if the unregulated market continues," she said.
Dr Sinclair said the affected patients sustained liver injuries "within a few weeks" of taking the black market retatrutide.
"They may become yellow or jaundiced, which is very frightening for patients, and they can become very unwell," she said.
The Therapeutic Goods Administration's (TGA) chief medical advisor Robyn Langham told the ABC "the localised nature" of the liver issues in Victoria suggested "a batch problem".
"We are seeing reports of acute liver failure which might be related to some batch issues certainly from Victoria," Professor Langham said.
She said the cluster of liver harm cases did not appear to be happening elsewhere in Australia.
Professor Langham warned consumers black market retatrutide was a "counterfeit product" and taking it was a risk.
"The retatrutide that's being sold is not the retatrutide that's currently in clinical trials," she said.
Professor Langham said her comments were not the result of an investigation.
Peptides are small chains of amino acids which act as signalling agents in the body, telling it to carry out certain processes such as hormone release or tissue repair.
There are regulated peptide medications including insulin and GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic.
This year there has been a boom in social media promotion of counterfeit, unapproved peptides, which are not safe for human use.
Victoria's health department has been contacted for comment.
It previously warned products labelled "retatrutide" may contain contaminants that could have "toxic effects".
The ABC contacted all other state and territory health departments to ask if there had been any cases of liver toxicity associated with unapproved peptide use.
Canberra Health Services confirmed it had detected liver damage from products sold as retatrutide, but would not say how many "due to the low numbers involved".
US-based pharmaceutical company Eli Lilly is the sole owner of the patent for retatrutide and is currently running clinical trials.
"Lilly continues to warn the public about the potential dangers of fake medicines," Manny Simons, general manager of Lilly Australia, said.
"Any retatrutide available online is unapproved, unverified and simply not worth the risk."
Adolescents 'injecting' counterfeit peptides
Professor Langham said it was important to note there were no good batches or safe unapproved peptides — the risk of serious harm applied to all the products.
"There are hospital admissions happening across the country because of the use of unapproved peptides," she said.
"The risks are real, they are not theoretical."
Professor Langham said the TGA was particularly worried about young people using unapproved peptides being promoted on social media.
"What concerns us most is that adolescents, young children are buying these and injecting them into themselves, so goodness knows what is happening," she said.
"[The counterfeit products] have not been tested in clinical trials, they have not been tested in terms of their manufacturing, and they've not been tested for their safety and people are injecting these into their body."
The TGA said more than 94,500 unapproved peptide products had been destroyed this year, in collaboration with Australian Border Force.
Last week, the TGA and New South Wales Police seized more than $120,000 of "illicit peptide and anabolic steroid products" from premises allegedly linked to a social media influencers.
In April, authorities seized $2 million worth of steroids and peptides.

"The President has created the conditions to leverage every agency, every authority and action many assumed we would never summon. Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains the tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone," he said.
He also warned governments and other actors against assuming that Washington would be unwilling to impose costs on those challenging its Iran policy.
"The Islamic Republic has subsisted by dressing extortion as security guarantees. It has drawn strength from a calculus that regards Iranian retaliation as certain and American enforcement as negotiable. Under President Trump, that era is over. And those who fear the danger of defying Tehran ought not to discount the cost of testing Washington," he said.
Bessent did not provide details in the post on the specific economic measures or agencies that would be involved in the planned offensive.

Ebola responders were chased with machetes, while the outbreak in Congo has already spread across an area larger than France
Kyiv • UNN
In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ebola has infected more than 5,500 people and claimed 2,642 lives. Attacks, strikes, and refusal to isolate are complicating the response.
Rescuers who tried to bury an Ebola victim in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo were chased with machetes, while the outbreak had already spread across an area larger than France. Bloomberg reports this, citing data from the authorities of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the UN and humanitarian organizations, UNN writes.
Details
Just over 100 days after the outbreak was declared, more than 5,500 people have been infected and 2,642 have died. Julien Harneis, the UN’s senior Ebola coordinator, said the scale of the epidemic is growing faster than the response capacity.
The outbreak is spreading faster and more widely than the response to Ebola
According to him, the epidemic already covers an area larger than France.
Attacks complicate the fight against the epidemic
The violence has already forced some rescuers to leave the affected areas. Last week, the Uganda Red Cross Society evacuated staff from the Congo after an attack on an Ebola response team near the epicenter in Ituri province. One worker was seriously injured, one response vehicle was destroyed, and two others were damaged.
A burial team was also attacked in North Kivu, leaving several people injured and one person dead. In other areas, families obstructed the examination of bodies, took the deceased away from treatment centers and blocked the work of burial teams.
There are also problems with isolating infected people. Fourteen patients left treatment centers in Ituri, while the authorities separately recorded 14 cases of refusal to isolate in various health zones.
Workers are on strike
At the same time, some medical workers are on strike because of unpaid salaries. Five screening points were not operating in Haut-Uele, while workers from public organizations in North Kivu and Tshopo have not received payments for months.
Médecins Sans Frontières is calling for intensified case detection and infection control directly within communities. According to the organization, more than 60% of deaths since the beginning of the current outbreak have occurred outside healthcare facilities.
The authorities in Congo are also preparing to expand the use of the Ervebo vaccine. The first 16,520 doses arrived in Kinshasa as part of a shipment of more than 50,000 doses. At the same time, the vaccine is not approved against the Bundibugyo strain, which caused the current outbreak, so its potential effectiveness is still being assessed.

Gauff beats Pegula for 2nd Cincinnati Open title; France’s Fils beats American Tiafoe in men’s final
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
04:23:02 UTC
13:23:02 KST

Gauff beats Pegula for 2nd Cincinnati Open title; France’s Fils beats American Tiafoe in men’s final
MASON, Ohio (AP) — Coco Gauff defeated fellow American Jessica Pegula, 6-2, 6-4, to capture her second women’s Cincinnati Open title on Sunday, and Arthur Fils of France defeated American Frances Tiafoe 6-3, 1-6, 6-0, in the men’s final for his first Masters 1000 title.
In Saturday’s semifinals, Pegula beat defending champion Iga Swiatek and Gauff defeated Sara Bejlek to set up the first all-American women’s final at the Cincinnati Open in 56 years.
The last time two American women played in the Cincinnati final was in 1970, when Rosie Casals beat Nancy Richey.
Pegula’s best finish in Cincinnati came in 2024, when she lost to Aryna Sabalenka in the final.
Gauff, who won the 2023 title beating Karolina Muchova, stormed out to a 5-0 lead in the first set on Sunday before winning 6-2. Pegula battled back to within 5-4 in the second before Gauff closed out the win. Gauff won five of six break points.
“I think it was a long journey, but I’m happy,” Gauff said. “I think it’s night and day, the player I was last year to now. I don’t think that this is an indicator that I’m going to do well in New York. Just knowing the quality ones that I had this week, hopefully I can use that experience.”
Gauff had five wins in straight sets in Cincinnati.
“I thought she just played at a really high level and didn’t really have many dips,” Pegula said. “I didn’t really think I played bad. The more you construct the point (against her), the worse it is because she almost likes to run. It was tough today. A dangerous, confident Coco is going to New York.”
The head-to-head series between Gauff and Pegula is now tied at five apiece. Sunday was their second meeting in a final, with Gauff winning at Wuhan last year.
The Fils-Tiafoe match was the first time two Black players have met in an ATP Masters 1000 final.
Fils is the third Black man to win a Masters 1000 title, joining Ben Shelton, who won twice in Canada, and Jo-Wilfried Tsonga, who won in Paris in 2008 and Canada in 2014.
At 22 years old, Fils is the youngest French champion in Masters 1000 history. He became the second French player to win a Cincinnati final, joining Guy Forget in 1991.
“Very happy with that,” Fils said. “It’s been a tough last year. I didn’t play the French Open (due to a hip injury). I lost early in Washington. People think that I’m done. But here we are. I got the title.”
It was the second time Tiafoe has appeared in the Cincinnati Open final, losing to Jannik Sinner in 2024. He was looking to become the first American male to win in Cincinnati since Andy Roddick in 2006.
“I’m going to have two Cincinnati finals trophies at the crib,” Tiafoe said. “I wish they were both champion ones. Losing on Sunday sucks. I’ve had a tough summer. I was able to play five great matches and beat quality players.”
Fils overpowered Tiafoe early in the first set on Sunday, winning 12 of 13 points to take a 3-0 lead. Tiafoe was dominant in the second, rolling to a 3-0 lead.
Tiafoe used the time break before the third set to stretch and receive massage treatment on his upper left leg and lower back.
“My hip bothered me a little bit, but that’s neither here nor there,” Tiafoe said. “It’s not about how I feel. I’ll be alright in a week (for the US Open).”
Tiafoe saved three championship points in the final game before Fils closed out the victory.
The Frenchman had 11 aces and won 71% of his points on first serve. He improved to 10-0 in deciding sets this year and 8-0 against American opponents.
Fils also won his only previous meeting with Tiafoe in Miami last year, also in three sets.
“It feels very good to have a trophy next to me, especially Masters 1000,” Fils said. “Never won one before. You just have to stay positive and find a way to make it work. Being positive is going to help me in the next weeks in the US Open.”

Father of sailor aboard USS Abraham Lincoln taken into US immigration detention
WASHINGTON, Aug 23 - The immigrant father of a U.S. sailor on board the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier, which was deployed in the Middle East during the Iran war, was taken into federal immigration detention, the sailor said in a Facebook post.
U.S. Border Patrol arrested Luis Manuel Aviles Roa, originally from Nicaragua, after conducting a vehicle stop in Key West, Florida, a spokesperson of the Department of Homeland Security, of which Border Patrol is a part, separately said on Sunday.
"I've been deployed for over nine months, out at sea in the Middle East aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, fighting for a country that has given me everything," Joshua Aviles, the son of the detained immigrant, said on Facebook.
"I just got a call that my dad was taken by ICE," he said on Saturday, adding his father had his driver's license, social security card and work permit.
"We have done everything through immigration to get his green card approved, and we are just waiting. This is heartbreaking for me. I don't know how I can mentally continue working 12+ hour days knowing that my dad is somewhere, possibly being treated like a criminal," the Facebook post added.
The DHS said Luis Manuel Aviles Roa entered the U.S. illegally and would remain in Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention pending removal proceedings.
"Having a family member in the military is not a free pass to violate our nation's laws," the DHS said.
President Donald Trump says his immigration crackdown is aimed at improving domestic security. Rights groups say the crackdown has violated free speech and due process rights and created an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities, who have raised concerns about racial profiling.
The Lincoln, which left the Middle East on Saturday, did not make a port call in more than 200 days. That set a modern-day record for consecutive days at sea, according to Democratic lawmakers who called for answers after sailors' families raised concerns about worsening conditions on the Lincoln. Taiwan machine tool orders see improvement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
04:03:23 UTC
13:03:23 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s machine tool industry is seeing a recovery in orders as market conditions improve, with several manufacturers expecting stronger operations in the third quarter, CTEE reported Sunday.
Machine tools are used to shape metal and other materials into precision parts for a wide range of products. They play a key role in manufacturing, as many industrial machines and products rely on components made using these tools, according to Gugu Fund.
Order visibility at many companies has extended to at least two to three months, while some manufacturers have bookings stretching into 2027. Component-related manufacturers, including Hiwin Technologies Corp., Chieftek Precision Co., and Tbi Motion Technology Co., have reported better order visibility and stronger revenue growth than other companies in the sector.
All three companies are benefiting from continued orders from the semiconductor and automation industries and are targeting double-digit revenue growth this year. Their backlogs extend into at least the fourth quarter.
Tongtai Machine & Tool Co. has benefited from strong orders for printed circuit board drilling machines. PCBs are the boards on which electronic components are mounted and interconnected, while drilling creates the holes needed to connect different circuit layers and install components, according to Stockfeel and Business Weekly.
The company has also made progress in semiconductor applications, including chip-on-wafer-on-substrate (CoWoS) advanced packaging. This has increased its total order backlog from NT$2.8 billion (US$88 million) at the start of the year to NT$3.2 billion.
Meanwhile, manufacturers of large-scale equipment are also seeing longer order visibility. Honor Seiki Co. and Shieh Yih Machinery Industry Co. have delivery schedules of at least six months, with some orders extending beyond a year.
Honor Seiki said its order backlog stands at about NT$1.7 billion to NT$1.8 billion, with new bookings mainly coming from the aerospace and basic processing industries in China and India. The company expects operations to improve in the third quarter and for the full year.
Shieh Yih reported a loss in its core business in the second quarter, partly because some customers postponed shipments until the third quarter due to higher freight costs. It expects its core operations to return to profitability in the third quarter.
Taiwan Takisawa Technology Co. said its bookings extend through the end of the year. Its orders mainly come from manufacturers of AI server cooling plates and liquid-cooling systems, as well as Chinese producers of robot reducers and components for robotic hands.
Looking ahead, global supply chain shifts and emerging markets are reshaping Taiwan’s machine tool industry. Growth is expected to come from new markets and higher-value applications, according to the Industrial Economics & Knowledge Center.
Semiconductor equipment, aerospace, AI servers, drones, and humanoid robot components are emerging as potential growth areas. Manufacturers are also shifting toward integrated solutions that combine automation, AI, digital monitoring, and multiple machining processes.
Taiwanese machine tool makers including Anderson Industrial Corp., Awea Mechantronic Co., Goodway Machine Corp., Kao Fong Machinery Co., Tongtai, and Shieh Yih are diversifying their businesses to capture new growth opportunities.

Report urges Taiwan to lean more on city diplomacy to deepen Europe ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
04:03:17 UTC
13:03:17 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan should pursue more ‘paradiplomacy’ to deepen its ties with Europe, according to a Central European Institute of Asian Studies (CEIAS) report.
The Slovakia-based think tank defines paradiplomacy as “the international activities of sub-state actors that may operate alongside, complement, or at times even diverge from central government foreign policy.”
Taiwan currently has 33 partnerships in Europe, including in Poland, Germany, France, Latvia, Czech Republic, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Slovakia, Ukraine, Belgium, Denmark, Hungary, and Italy, CEIAS said. These local-level ties give Taiwan another way to connect internationally, especially since its formal diplomatic options are limited, it said.
Sister-city ties, in particular, allow Taiwan to collaborate with European cities on areas like innovation, green development, urban planning, and public health, CEIAS said. Regular exchanges and projects can also promote Taiwan as a more widely accepted, reliable partner, it added.
CEIAS said that for European partners, working with Taiwanese cities offers access to advanced industrial systems, opportunities to share knowledge, and avenues to attract investment. “These partnerships are, therefore, less about symbolic recognition than about practical cooperation in areas where Taiwanese expertise overlaps with local European policy and economic priorities,” the think tank said.
Additionally, as Europe works to reduce dependence on China and diversify its supply chains, local-level ties with Taiwan offer a flexible and inexpensive way to expand cooperation, CEIAS said.
The think tank said that Taiwan has not yet used paradiplomacy to its fullest potential in Europe due to practical constraints and political factors. Taiwanese cities have at least 34 partnerships in Japan, while in the US, there are more than 100, it said.
The Taiwanese diaspora in Europe “is smaller, more fragmented, and generally less connected to local political institutions,” the think tank said.
While Taiwan’s representative offices do help with outreach, efforts by overseas Taiwanese communities to influence local or regional governments are still limited, CEIAS said. However, Taiwanese businesses, industries, and research links are increasingly helping drive city-to-city and regional cooperation, making up for the limited influence of overseas diaspora lobbying, it said.
The think tank said that the Smart City Summit & Expo in Taipei and Kaohsiung is an effective tool to facilitate global cooperation. “The expo attracts the attention of municipal leaders beyond the formal partners of Taiwanese cities, often serving as the first point of exposure for foreign municipal leaders to Taiwan,” it said, adding that their participation often results in city-level projects or agreements.
CEAIS also suggested more Taiwanese cities join the Pact of Free Cities, which was established in 2019 to share best practices in city planning and local government management. So far, only Taipei and Taoyuan are members.
Overall, the think tank recommended that Taiwan strengthen existing partnerships and expand outreach in areas where national-level diplomacy is limited.

China team brings X-ray vision to life with a compact high-speed ghost video cam
Tabletop imaging camera can capture ‘see-through’ medical videos of beating hearts using a lower radiation dose than traditional methods
3-MIN READ3-MIN
2
 Listen
Chinese scientists have developed a new tabletop X-ray ghost imaging method that allows them to capture real-time “see-through” video of fast-moving objects.
The team’s system could be used to capture dynamic objects such as rotating aircraft engines or biological movements like a beating heart.
Importantly, this could all be accomplished with a lower radiation dose and simpler set-up than traditional X-ray methods.
“In contrast to other available X-ray imaging techniques for moving objects, our method can be implemented with a conventional tabletop X-ray source,” the team said in a paper published in the peer-reviewed journal Communications Physics on August 15.
“The set-up is simple, relatively inexpensive and easy to operate.”
The researchers from the Chinese Academy of Sciences and Shanghai Jiao Tong University said their method had “great potential” for medical imaging as well as non-destructive imaging of moving mechanical components.

Ephemeral Architecture Prototypes: The Future of Public Spaces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

Concéntrico returned to Logroño for its 12th edition in June 2026, transforming the city into a working site for architecture. Since its founding in 2015, the festival has built an identity on resisting a distant, controlled exhibition of design by constructing full-scale installations in the city's streets, plazas, and vacant lots. Concéntrico embeds installations directly into daily life, engaging residents and visitors as active, observant participants. This year's program brought together more than twenty projects by architects, designers, and researchers working across geographies and methods, each contributing to a citywide experiment in reimagining public space.
The festival organized its participants around three curatorial lines, each offering a unique framing on how architecture operates within the contemporary city. Identity and Fiction approaches the city as a site of narrative and memory, treating architecture as a way of recovering stories embedded in urban space. Projects in this category included Smiljan Radic's transposition of a traveling circus into collective architecture and OFREIA's research into memories and historical bathing practices in the fluvial landscape. Urban Ecologies addresses the relationships between architecture, climate, matter, and landscape in the contemporary city, ranging from NOOF Group's experimental pavilions capable of generating microclimates to Sahra Hersi's civic garden for cultivation and seed exchange. Ephemeral Agents considers temporary structures as tools to activate social dynamics and open opportunities for public space use, encompassing projects such as Gabriel Fontana's Multiform, the urban listening capsules developed by AAU Anastas, and a connection point between a pedestrian bridge and the riverside park below installed by Future Firm.

Syria, Israel hold US-mediated talks in Jordan to de-escalate tensions

Syria, Israel hold US-mediated talks in Jordan to de-escalate tensions
Syria’s foreign minister meets with an Israeli delegation led by the chief of the Mossad to de-escalate tensions after an Israeli strike near the Turkish border.
Syria’s Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani has met with Israeli intelligence officials in Jordan, according to Syrian state media, as the two sides work to de-escalate tensions following an Israeli attack on a Syrian airbase near the Turkish border.
Syria’s Sana news agency, citing a diplomatic source, said the talks were mediated by the United States and involved a “high-level Israeli delegation”.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Israel bombs Syria as US envoy says base attack aimed at ‘baiting’ Turkiye
- list 2 of 3Envoy says Israel did not give the US notice before strikes on Syrian base
- list 3 of 3Syria’s foreign minister says door open for diplomacy with Israel
The AFP news agency reported that al-Shaibani met the head of Israel’s Mossad intelligence agency, Roman Gofman.
According to Sana, the discussions “focused on establishing practical mechanisms to halt Israeli attacks, arrests and targeting operations” as well as “reviving negotiations for a lasting security agreement between the two sides”.
They also discussed efforts to ease tensions between Israel and Turkiye and to prevent their rivalry from spilling onto Syrian territory, Sana reported.
The US has sought to broker a security agreement between Israel and the government of Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa for more than a year. Israel has launched hundreds of strikes on Syria since the fall of longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad in December 2024 and sent troops into a United Nations-patrolled buffer zone that had long separated Israeli and Syrian forces in the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights.
It also bombed the Abu Duhur airbase in northwestern Idlib on Thursday, claiming the attack was to prevent Turkish troops from deploying at the base, a claim Syria and Turkiye have denied.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan have also traded barbs since the incident, with tensions high between the two leaders.
According to Sana, the Syrian side stressed during Sunday’s talks “that Syria is a sovereign state with the full right to rebuild and develop its national army and determine its alliances and partnerships in line with its national interests”. The Syrian side rejected “any arrangements or mechanisms that would restrict these sovereign rights,” it said.
Syria’s immediate priorities in the talks remained an Israeli withdrawal to positions held before al-Assad’s overthrow and the full restoration of a 1974 disengagement agreement, Sana reported.
The Syrian officials also reaffirmed Damascus’s sovereignty over the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights, it added.
Israel’s ‘red lines’
Israeli media reported that the talks were “positive” and said Israeli officials had adopted a number of red lines going into talks.
These include preventing Turkish military activity in Syria, keeping the Syrian side of the Golan Heights demilitarised, “ensuring the security” of Syria’s Druze community and preventing the Syrian army from acquiring certain strategic weapons systems.
They also conditioned any withdrawal from Syrian territories occupied by Israel on “diplomatic achievements”.
During previous rounds of US-mediated talks, Syria and Israel had agreed on a joint mechanism to share intelligence and defuse tensions. But the negotiations froze at the end of February, when the US and Israel launched their war on Iran, without a date set for resumption.
In an interview published ahead of the meeting, al-Shaibani told Reuters news agency that Damascus did not trust Israel, but that the door remained open for diplomacy. He said Syria had cut off contact entirely after the Israeli attack on Syria’s Abu al-Duhur airbase last week.
Al-Shaibani said the two sides had agreed on paper to “almost everything” around the beginning of the year, including arrangements for security zones in southern Syria and a buffer zone where only UN forces would be present.
Hassan Mneimneh, a political analyst and researcher at the Middle East Institute, told Al Jazeera that the current round of talks was unlikely to de-escalate tensions given Israel’s track record.
“It’s quite the opposite, meaning now that Syria has indicated its desire to have the situation de-escalate, Israel is likely to bring in more demands and have the Americans basically negotiate these new demands with Syria, against any kind of expansion of Turkish presence in the north and beyond the north,” he said.
Mneimneh added that Syria was “afraid that the country will become a battlefield” between Israel and Turkiye and was concerned about Israel’s territorial grab in the country, stretching “all the way to Hermon, to Jabal al-Sheikh in its totality almost, and all the way to three southern provinces”.
So, from the Syrian perspective, Mneimneh added, the talks with Israel seem to be aimed at avoiding “the disintegration of Syrian authority” as well as ensuring any conflict between Israel and Turkiye does not prevent Syria from “forming, establishing, consolidating polity after the fall of” al-Assad.
