The deal struck by then-treasurer Scott Morrison ensures WA gets a bigger slice of GST revenue every year than it would under the national formula, which is meant to give more money per person to states with the highest need and lowest financial means.
Earlier this month, the Productivity Commission published its interim report into the deal, calling it a "costly mistake" and recommending the government scrap it.
A number of premiers, including NSW's Chris Minns, are unhappy with the arrangement.
So - is the PM considering changing the way the pie is sliced?
"There will be no change to WA's GST arrangements while I'm prime minister," Albanese says.
"I think that WA deserves that, because WA contributes to the national economy and helps to drive that economy."
The PM is speaking in WA
Albanese is back in Western Australia today, joined by Defence Minister Richard Marles and WA Premier, Roger Cook.
They're at the Henderson shipyard, announcing details of what will be a big defence precinct where thousands of ADF staff will work on the AUKUS submarine project.
"We're absolutely thrilled to be here to mark this important milestone today," Albanese says.
"This has been through all of our processes, many meetings and many hours... this is a once in many generations investment."
Joyce says One Nation 'sticking' to 130k immigration number
Barnaby Joyce is back, this time on News24 (previously Sky), still holding the proverbial mop to clean up what David Farley said about immigration yesterday.
He says people should "ignore" the number of people coming in to the country on the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme, because they generally stay for under 12 months, which means they are not counted in the NOM.
"They come, and they go," he says.
"We've reviewed the numbers, we've got far too many, 130,000 Net Overseas Migration is our number and we're sticking to it."
He's pressed on how a significant reduction in migrant workers might mean for productivity, but deflects to talk about energy prices.
"Go back to coal-fire power, increase productivity as a nation, stop small businesses going out of business," he says.
Data centre renewable push 'not that different' from Qld smelter deal
Industry Minister Tim Ayres is in Perth today to announce a $120 million investment for a manufacturing pilot designed to speed up build times for apartments.
While we're on the topic of development, Ayres is asked about resistance from some states and territories to sign up to minimum standards for data centres which would require developers to power the sites with renewable energy.
"I want to be respectful of the National Cabinet process, which is meeting in a couple of days' time," Ayres says.
"But we have set out our objective here to legislate AI, data centre standards for Australia, and that means not having a race to the bottom on electricity and water."
Ayres says the deal would be "not all that different" from the one struck by Queensland premier David Crisafulli to secure the future of the Boyne aluminium smelter.
Queensland is one of the jurisdictions holding out on the data centre standards.
"They're not that different really, large scale industrial electricity users and data centres," he says.
"It is now thanks to the deal with the Crisafulli government going to be powered by wind and solar."
Taylor answers question about Exclusive Brethren
Last week, a parliamentary inquiry into the 2025 election heard from a director of the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church, formerly known as the Exclusive Brethren.
The Church has denied allegations it secretly paid people to disrupt Labor's re-election campaign last year in a coordinated effort involving far-right influencers.
Overwhelmingly, members of the church appeared to support the Liberals during the campaign, although at the time both the church and the party denied any official affiliation.
Taylor says he's seen the reporting but doesn't answer a question about his level of concern over the allegations.
Instead, he talks about volunteers from the Rapid Relief Team, run by the church, who are helping with the Pollie Pedal, a bike ride event which raises money for charity.
Taylor is taking part in the ride.
"We're being supported by the rapid relief team and they are an extraordinary group of people," he says.
"That is an extraordinary organisation, and I am sure there are many Labor members who have been supported by that organisation because of the great work that they do."
Energy for data centres should be up to the people who build it
Taylor says the states and territories should get to decide what energy sources power data centres built in their jurisdictions, not the federal government.
On Wednesday, Albanese is expected to push minimum standards through National Cabinet which would require data centres to provide their own renewable energy sources.
Queensland and the NT are resisting, in part because they don't agree that renewable power should be the only option.
"The problem with Chris Bowen and this Prime Minister is that they always have their favourites," he says.
"We are absolutely neutral to the fuel source... we need to make sure that we have the energy to support Australian households, Australian industry, and any new data centres.
"But we won't be picking the fuel source, that should be done by people who are actually paying for it and building it."
Taylor says Labor, One Nation 'all over the shop' on immigration
Opposition leader Angus Taylor is shining bright in orange high vis today, holding a press conference at a gas-fired generator in Swanbank, Queensland.
He claims the opposition has "laid out" how it will bring the "numbers down and standards up" on immigration, despite the fact we're yet to see their policy position on the subject and apparently won't see it before the year is out.
Taylor is relying on an earlier announcement from the Coalition that immigration would be tied to housing supply.
"We'll cap migration based on housing supply, we'll put Australian values at the centre of our immigration policy," he says.
"Our opponents are all over the shop on this."
Could AI be an election sleeper issue?
At the last federal election, Tim Wilson won back the seat of Goldstein by 175 votes. The LNP held Longman by 269 votes, and in Bradfield, 26 votes determined who went to Canberra.
Tiny margins.
We've all heard about the risk of deepfakes, misinformation campaigns and foreign interference meddling in elections and compromising democracy.
But what if the more seismic change at the next election isn't just the usual flood of misleading material on social media?
Patricia Karvelas digs in to how AI and chatbots might be the next frontier to sway voters.
New rules coming for data centres even if Qld doesn't like them
The government expects to settle new rules for how data centres use energy in Australia at Wednesday's national cabinet meeting, despite Queensland confirming it will remain opposed to the plan.

The Coalition's immigration policy
There are more questions than answers on immigration this week.
Liberal senator Jonno Duniam, who is leading the internal process for the Coalition's immigration policy, does not have an answer for when the public will get to see it.
"I'm not going to put a date on it," he says.
"We are in 2026, and the world in 2028, which is the first opportunity the Coalition will have at the election to form government if we win, so we need to make sure we are as relevant to that point in time as possible."
Don't expect the policy this year, he says, but maybe a "short time after that".
Conroy defends lobbying relationships
We're back talking about lobbyists at Parliament House.
Conroy insists the government has strict codes of conduct that guide its interactions with the lobbying industry, including the defence industry (his portfolio).
He says it would be unfair to exclude former defence ministers and Australian Defence Force officers who still want to contribute to policy debate.
"They obviously want to keep making a contribution to public policy, and that is their right," he says.
"I don't think people should be excluded from working in the Australian defence industry automatically, just because they happened to be a defence minister."
When will we see the government's immigration numbers?
Labor frontbencher Pat Conroy says the federal government is working to find the "right" answer for its migration policy rather than a fast answer.
Treasury has forecast a NOM of 225,000 in the financial year after this one, but Conroy won't say if that is in line with the government's own targets.
Last month Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke hastily withdrew from a planned speech at the National Press Club in which he was expected to unveil an immigration policy that included moving the families of skilled migrants into offshore processing.
We still don't have a new date for the speech, nor do we have an immigration policy, and Conroy says we won't be getting either until Burke is ready.
"I understand some in the community wanted answers to this yesterday, but it's a complex area, and it's important we get the answer right, rather than get the fast answer," he says.
"That's why Minister Burke is working through this in a serious, considered way, consulting with all his colleagues in the relevant areas."
Government to bail out SunRice
One Nation MP David Farley covered a lot of ground in his Insiders interview on Sunday, including an interaction he had with the PM after raising the issue of a struggling SunRice manufacturing plant in his electorate of Farrer.
And apparently the PM was very wiling to help.
This morning, Murray Watt confirms a bail out is being discussed for the factory, which is part of the supply chain for rice cakes.
"I can confirm that we have advised SunRice that we are prepared to co-invest with them in new investment in a rice processing plant," he says.
"SunRice has indicated that investment as well as their own would protect their jobs as well as potentially creating more."
The cost to taxpayers isn't clear yet, but we know the company has requested $15 million from the government, which it would then match.
The government says it's waiting on a formal written proposal from SunRice.
Watt defends lobbyist access
Watt is defending the government's rules around lobbyist access to parliament after a Four Corners investigation revealed dozens of former defence officials have jumped into lucrative lobbying roles or the defence sector.
Critics say there's a "revolving door" where former officials can use their connections to potentially influence the awarding of multi-million-dollar contracts.
It's prompted calls for tighter regulations and greater transparency.
But Watt says there are already strict lobbyist rules in place.
"[They] regulate, for example, the activities of former politicians, former staffers, [and] periods of time that they can't lobby and use information that they have been privy to," he says.
"And of course, any lobbyist needs to be on the lobbyist register, so there is a high degree of disclosure and transparency."
Expect more mass bird flu mortalities
Environment Minister Murray Watt is speaking with ABC News Breakfast about the first Australian detection of bird flu in a mammal.
Watt says the weekend discovery of the disease in a long-nose fur seal in South Australia is a "very serious development" but "not unexpected".
"We are likely to see more mass mortalities, which is obviously a terrible thing for all Australians who love our nature," he says.
"But we have been preparing this for some time … to make sure our populations are resilient, and we will continue to do everything we can."

Hongkong Post should focus on public service, not profit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
21:30:05 UTC
06:30:05 KST

Hongkong Post should focus on public service, not profit
The traditional self-funding operating model is no longer viable in an increasingly competitive e-commerce market
The crisis facing the city’s postal service has been a long time coming – snail mail has been slowing for postal services worldwide for decades, forcing changes to ensure survival.
That has included axing jobs and rethinking the purpose they serve in the 21st century. One of the most drastic moves came from Denmark where PostNord ended its letter delivery service at the end of 2025 to focus entirely on parcel delivery. The country is one of the world’s most digitalised nations, with 95 per cent of Danes fully integrated into its digital platforms. Ending its 400-year letter service was the correct move.
Obviously, that’s not the case with Hong Kong. We are nowhere near Denmark in terms of development and adoption of digital platforms. But if the government’s ambitious digitalisation plans bear fruit, Hongkong Post’s existential crisis will only deepen.
The government is pushing for more residents to use the iAM Smart one-stop digital services platform to access government services and others. Increasingly, there will be fewer letters to deliver. By the end of 2025, iAM Smart had already accumulated over 4 million users. Hongkong Post must brace itself to adapt to this irreversible trend, unless it wants the government’s digitalisation push to fail.

Tens of thousands ordered to evacuate as fire threatens US state of Nevada

Tens of thousands ordered to evacuate as fire threatens US state of Nevada
NEW YORK - Tens of thousands of people have been evacuated this weekend from the area of Reno, Nevada, and many others were under orders to leave on Aug 23 as a wildfire reached the outskirts of the state’s third-most-populous city.
About 42,000 residents have been displaced or are in active evacuations with an additional 45,000 in “be prepared to evacuate” status as the Hawk Fire threatened northern Reno, local officials said late Aug 23 morning.
Local TV footage showed flames approaching roads. In eyewitness video verified by Reuters, smoke from the hills billowed over nearby residential neighbourhoods.
Fire-tracking websites showed evacuation zones extending from the Sierra Nevada hills to the University of Nevada in north-west Reno.
The fire has burned 5,261ha so far, officials said at a press conference on Aug 23. The fire was human-caused and remains under investigation, they said.
Three civilians and three first responders have been injured, said Shane Akerson, a commander leading fire and rescue operations.
Officials first received reports of a fire off Hawk Meadow Trail at about 11.15am PDT on Aug 22 (2.15am on Aug 23, Singapore time), said Richard Edwards, chief of Truckee Meadows Fire Protection District. Firefighters on Aug 22 worked amid “extreme red flag conditions,” he said.
Red flag conditions are a combination of warm temperatures, very low humidity and strong winds that raise the risk of wildfires.
“We expect those same strong conditions to come back this afternoon,” Edwards said on Aug 23.
Nevada Governor Joe Lombardo declared a state of emergency late on Aug 22 in Washoe County, which includes Reno and parts of Lake Tahoe.
“This is an active and rapidly evolving situation, and I urge everyone in the affected areas to remain vigilant and follow the direction of local officials,” Lombardo said in a statement.
Lombardo authorized the deployment of two National Guard helicopters to help fight fires and 60 National Guard personnel to support operations with the Washoe County Sheriff’s Office, officials said.
The Reno-Tahoe International Airport remained outside the evacuation area, and commercial flights were operating normally on Aug 23. REUTERS

Meta and other social networks come under fire over accusations of harming children
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
00:29:00 EEST
06:29:00 KST

Meta and other social networks come under fire over accusations of harming children
Kyiv • UNN
29 U.S. states accuse social networks of harming children and demand up to $1.4 trillion. The companies deny wrongdoing.
U.S. states and thousands of young users are suing Meta, Google, TikTok and Snap, accusing the social media companies of creating platforms that foster addiction and harm children and teenagers. In the case against Meta, being heard in federal court in Oakland, 29 states are seeking penalties that could potentially reach $1.4 trillion, Bloomberg reports, writes UNN.
Details
The lawsuits allege that the companies deliberately created features that encourage young users to spend extended periods of time on the platforms compulsively. These include endless feeds, algorithmic recommendations and notifications that prompt users to constantly return to social media.
In March, a Los Angeles jury found Meta and Google negligent in the design and operation of their platforms and awarded a 20-year-old plaintiff $6 million. Overall, the companies face more than 3,000 similar lawsuits from children, teenagers and young people who report psychological and physical problems, and in some cases—deaths.
Companies deny the allegations
The plaintiffs cite the companies' internal documents. In particular, materials made public in 2021 by former Facebook employee Frances Haugen indicated that Meta knew about the negative impact of its platforms on young people. Documents from ByteDance, TikTok's parent company, also stated that teenagers, due to their underdeveloped ability to assess risks, are more likely to repeat dangerous stunts seen online.
Meta, Google, TikTok and Snap reject the allegations. The companies say they did not create their products to attract children, are implementing safety tools and are working to protect young users. Meta also argues that social media helps children stay connected with friends and family.
Separately, more than 1,300 U.S. school districts have filed lawsuits. They are seeking compensation for expenses related to problems that, in their view, are caused by social media, including additional psychologists, security and teacher training. In May, Meta, TikTok, Snap and Google agreed to pay $27 million to settle one such lawsuit.

Wife of Palestinian terrorist convicted in Israeli minister’s assassination gives birth to twins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
21:28:03 UTC
06:28:03 KST

Sanabel al-Ra’i, the wife of Palestinian prisoner Basel al-Asmar, who is serving a lengthy prison sentence for his role in the assassination of former tourism minister Rehavam Ze’evi, gave birth to twins Saturday in Qalqilya in the West Bank.
According to the family, al-Ra’i became pregnant through fertility treatment using sperm from her imprisoned husband that had been smuggled out of prison and frozen. Family members said the process took more than two years and involved several attempts at fertilization before the latest attempt succeeded, resulting in a twin pregnancy.
Palestinian photographer Mohammed Nazzal documented the birth. He said al-Ra’i, a former nurse, experienced a mixture of joy over the birth of her children and pain because their father remains in prison and could not be at her side.
After giving birth, al-Ra’i said she felt strong and had succeeded in “defeating the prison,” according to Nazzal.
A relationship that began through prison visits
Al-Ra’i’s relationship with al-Asmar began when she visited her brother, Shaher al-Ra’i, who had been imprisoned by Israel several times.
Her brother was placed in administrative detention — a measure Israel uses to hold suspects without filing criminal charges, generally on the basis of classified security evidence — in June 2015. His detention order was extended several times before he was released in 2017. He was arrested again this year and released in June.
During her prison visits, al-Ra’i met al-Asmar. The couple married in 2022 while he was still incarcerated. The marriage was conducted by proxy, with al-Asmar’s brother signing the marriage documents on his behalf.
Four years later, the couple’s twins have been born while al-Asmar remains behind bars.
Al-Asmar was arrested in 2002 and is serving a life sentence plus an additional 20 years for his involvement in the assassination of Ze’evi, a right-wing Israeli politician who was tourism minister at the time of his death.
Ze’evi was shot and killed at Jerusalem’s Hyatt Hotel on Oct. 17, 2001.
According to details released in al-Asmar’s case, he served as a secondary gunman in the assassination squad. His role was to provide security for the killing and shoot Ze’evi’s bodyguards if they attempted to intervene.
Ze’evi was killed by members of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, or PFLP, a Palestinian terrorist organization. The group said the assassination was retaliation for Israel’s killing of its leader, Abu Ali Mustafa, in an Israeli missile strike in the West Bank city of Ramallah earlier that year.
Sperm reportedly smuggled from Israeli prison
The al-Asmar case is the latest example of a phenomenon in which Palestinian prisoners serving lengthy sentences have, according to Palestinian reports, smuggled sperm out of Israeli prisons in an effort to have children while incarcerated.
Al-Asmar’s family said his sperm was smuggled out about two years ago and subsequently frozen.
An Israeli security official said the smuggling referred to in the reports occurred before the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack on southern Israel.
According to the official, Israel Prison Service policies have since changed, and the types of meetings that previously allowed Palestinian prisoners to transfer materials or have private visits with their spouses are no longer permitted.

A newly formed pro-government party has won a large majority in Kazakhstan's snap parliamentary election, three exit polls showed, in a result set to cement President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev's power over the major energy and minerals exporter.
The exit polls, published by Kazakh state media, showed the Adilet party winning between 70 percent and 72 percent of the vote, with turnout above 74 percent.
Four small opposition parties also won seats, according to the polls.
Adilet was formed earlier this year by the president's top aides and swiftly absorbed the previously long-ruling Amanat party.
Sunday's election was triggered by the adoption of a new constitution earlier this year, which streamlines parliament from two chambers into one.
A former Soviet diplomat and top United Nations official, Tokayev has led Central Asia's largest economy since 2019, maintaining warm relations with the West, Russia and China.
One chamber
Kazakhstan's Supreme Court said last month that the new constitution allowed Tokayev to run for a fresh seven-year term.
Tokayev took office as the chosen successor of Nazarbayev, Kazakhstan's founding president, who ruled from 1991 to 2019.
He broke with Nazarbayev after unrest in 2022 that Tokayev has described as a coup attempt by Nazarbayev allies.
Voting in the capital, Astana, Tokayev told journalists it was too early to say whether he would seek another term.
He also said he would announce his choice of vice president, an office created under the new constitution, within the next seven to 10 days, adding that the nominee would be a "well-known" person.

Their story began in 1999, when Sakolsky taught English at a school in central China's Henan Province under a teachers' exchange program between the two countries.
After watching a television news report featuring Yin's tireless work, he was deeply moved and raised 5,000 U.S. dollars to help Yin and her husband in their afforestation efforts against desertification.
At the time, the donation was a staggering amount that was enough for Yin to build a house, cover her children's upbringing costs, and even completely change the trajectory of her family's life.
The saplings bought and planted with that donation have since grown into a forest of more than 50,000 towering trees.
In May this year, Yin took to the internet in search of the American friend who had offered the donation decades ago, and their online reunion, a moment that moved many, soon followed.
On May 18, the two finally connected over a video call. Yin, who had been practicing over and over, greeted him in her slightly broken English: "You are brother!"
Upon arriving in Beijing, Sakolsky said he was eager to meet Yin in northern China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, reconnect with former colleagues and students, and see the forest with his own eyes. He also received mooncakes sent by Yin, a traditional Chinese symbol of reunion, and tomatoes grown in the desert.
Ahead of Sakolsky's arrival in Inner Mongolia on Sunday afternoon, Yin, no less excited, brought with her pepino melons freshly picked from her orchard.
"I went to pick some pepino melons for him, so he can taste the fruit from the desert the moment he steps off the plane," she said. "When I tell him I grew these in the desert, he won't believe it."
At the Ordos Ejin Horo Airport in Inner Mongolia, as soon as Yin spotted him coming down the escalator, she rushed to him. Overcome with emotion, the two hugged tightly, weeping with joy after more than two decades apart.
"This is a dream come true," said Sakolsky. "She made a promise 27 years ago and she kept her promise. I never thought I would see her again. It is a miracle, but it shows culture and people can still keep promises."
Invited by the China Education Association for International Exchange (CEAIE), his itinerary from Aug. 23 to Sept. 1 will also include China-U.S. teacher exchange events, a visit to Henan to meet with teachers and students at the school where he worked, a visit to the press briefing hall of the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and visits to historical and cultural landmarks.
The invitation is intended to further promote China-U.S. educational exchanges, convey the Chinese people's deep appreciation of friendship, and inspire more people to carry forward heartwarming stories of goodwill between the two peoples, a CEAIE official said.
Over the decades, China has set up special funds, offered preferential tax policies, and mobilized farmers and locals in afforestation campaigns. Today, beyond dedicated local farmers like Yin, China's afforestation campaign also attracts large numbers of environment-conscious volunteers, especially young urban dwellers and international students.
Official figures show that China has contributed about one-quarter of the world's increase in green vegetation and rehabilitated 152 million mu (about 10.13 million hectares) of sandified land between 2021 and 2025. ■

US-Canada trade talks fell apart over fine print, says envoy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
21:15:57 UTC
06:15:57 KST

US-Canada trade talks fell apart over fine print, says envoy
OTTAWA – US-Canada trade talks collapsed over a range of issues on which the written text of a potential deal was at odds with what the Canadian side believed it had agreed to, said Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s top US envoy.
Mark Wiseman, Canada’s Ambassador to the US, said in an interview on Aug 23 that there was no one issue that led talks to collapse late on Aug 21, a development that triggered new tariffs and a potentially escalating trade fight.
Wiseman likened the negotiations to a handshake deal to buy a house – only for the prospective buyer to learn appliances were not included, the furnace had no warranty, and neither the garage nor the yard was on the same property, and ultimately walk away.
“As we drilled down, what we discovered was that what our understanding of what had been agreed to was quite different from what was showing up in the documents,” he said.
“When that kind of happens once or twice, it’s kind of understandable, but when it happens consistently, and every interpretation is the most negative interpretation”, then it “got to a point” where they walked away.
Wiseman’s comments come as the countries grapple with the sudden, jarring collapse of trade talks on Aug 21.
The US proceeded to apply a 50 per cent tariff on about US$20 billion (S$25.4 billion) in Canadian goods, and Carney announced retaliation that will take effect on Sept 8. The US is pledging to escalate if he proceeds.
The Canadian dollar was quoted as much as 0.5 per cent weaker as currency markets reopened in Asia, underperforming major peers.
The move pared last week’s 0.8 per cent rally that stemmed from a weaker greenback and indications that the two sides were nearing a deal.
“News over the weekend is certainly CAD (Canadian dollar) negative, and I think we will see plenty of volatility in the currency, especially once North America comes in and we get further expected comments from both sides,” said Nick Twidale, chief market analyst at AT Global Markets.
“However, moves won’t be too excessive as we’ve all seen this movie before over the last couple of years, so I’m expecting some sort of a deal or resumption of trade talks to be announced during the week,” he added.
It is not clear whether negotiations will take place between now and then, but Wiseman said the timeline is not about creating an overtime period for talks. “I don’t think it should be viewed that way,” he said.
Talks were bogged down, in particular, by a dispute over tariff treatment of medium and heavy vehicles, on which the US was resisting cutting tariffs.
Wiseman said Canada “needed medium- and heavy-duty vehicles to be included” in tariff relief. The issue affects General Motors and Ford Motor, two US automakers operating in Canada, he said.
“That’s just something we could not accept because we want to protect the existence of an automotive assembly industry in Canada for cars, light trucks, you know, medium trucks and heavy-duty trucks.”
But he added: “This is not why the deal fell apart. That is a very specific example of one of a number of things where, you know, as the interpretation of the details became clear, it became obvious that there wasn’t going to be a meeting of the minds.”
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the deal would have offered Canada tariff reductions on steel, aluminium, automobiles and lumber, but blamed Canada for walking away. Carney said he walked away when the US demands became too great.
Greer told The New York Times on Aug 22 that the deal would have cut the “majority” of Canadian steel exports to a 25 per cent tariff up to a quota, with anything above that remaining at 50 per cent.
The US would have lowered the aluminium tariff to 25 per cent without a quota.
It would also have cut the tariff on passenger vehicles, suspended the since-enacted tariffs and eliminated a lumber tariff.
A1sked to confirm that, Wiseman declined to get into details but called it “broadly accurate”.
“We’re disappointed,” he said. “We worked hard, but at the end of the day, the terms that were put forward on a deadline – that was created by the United States – it didn’t work for us.”
Carney said the US demanded that Canada constrain its ability to do separate trade deals with other nations.
Wiseman declined to fully elaborate, saying that the matter was not with any one country, such as China, but was broader.
The US “has changed its view of economic partnership”, and “in the face of that, Canada, among other things, has said that we will look to diversify”, he said.
“So we have to ensure that any agreement we would come to with the United States does not constrain our ability to create trading relationships, open and free trading relationships with other jurisdictions. But to be clear, this was not an issue about China.”
Language issue
Carney also said the administration was looking to curtail the use of French, one of Canada’s two official languages and a political lightning rod. Wiseman said the dispute pertained to digital services and US-based streaming services and levels of French-language content.
Wiseman cast the matter as a red line.
“It is non-negotiable, in terms of our ability to protect – and to not just protect, but to be able to enhance and grow the French language in Canada, in Quebec and in the rest of Canada,” he said.
“Those that want to do business in Canada, be it digital or anything else, must respect that fundamental reality.”
Carney also said the US administration was not united in its approach, signalling that Canadians were getting different and dizzying messages from Greer, who is US President Donald Trump’s top trade official, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who oversees the so-called Section 232 sectoral tariffs that were a core part of talks.
US-Canada ties have frayed substantially during Trump’s second term, with the President pressuring Canada to become the 51st state and applying tariffs that fly in the face of the trade deal he signed in his first term and related side letters that contained pledges he has since abandoned.
The US leader said in a social media post early on Aug 23 that Canada “wants the benefits of being a state, without being one”, but has otherwise said nothing since the collapse of talks.
One of his Cabinet officials, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, said on Fox News that Canada is “foolish” to think it can win a trade war with the US, but Trump’s former vice-president Mike Pence criticised the measure.
Pence critical
“American businesses and American consumers pay American tariffs,” Pence said on CNN’s State Of The Union. “The last thing we need right now, as our economy is getting back on its feet, is a trade war with Canada.”
Pence, who fell out with Trump after the Jan 6, 2021, riot by the President’s supporters at the US Capitol, said his advice would be: “Drive a hard bargain, but let’s pursue free trade with free nations, most especially our trading partners to the north.”
Wiseman declined to say whether Canada was open to restarting talks, but said communications with the administration continue and that the talks were cordial throughout.
Wiseman was hosting guests at the embassy in Washington on Aug 23 to watch the Freedom 250 Grand Prix race taking place along Pennsylvania Avenue.
“We’re just not willing, at the end of the day, to accept terms that were unfair, uneconomic and actually, you know, called into question the reliability of the deal,” he said.
“Because you know one of the things that you’d hate to see happen is you agree on something and then, after agreeing to it, it gets undermined.” BLOOMBERG

Kyiv • UNN
Starting in September, bicycles will be banned from approximately 30 streets in Como’s historic center. The mayor’s decision has been criticized by residents and activists.
The mayor of the Italian city of Como, Alessandro Rapinese, banned bicycles from the city’s historic center after he was hit by an electric bicycle in June. The ban will take effect in September and will cover around 30 streets, The Guardian reports, according to UNN.
Details
Under the new rules, cyclists, including electric bicycle users, will have to dismount and walk through designated areas. Rapinese explained the decision as necessary to improve safety in the historic center, which is regularly overcrowded with tourists.
The ban has drawn criticism from residents, politicians and cycling activists. Opponents of the decision believe that the mayor introduced it because of his personal experience, while activists are already collecting signatures to repeal the restrictions and are planning a protest ride through the streets where cycling will be banned in September.
I was accused of adopting this measure because I was hit by an electric bicycle — of course, that is true. People act based on their own experiences, and I know what it is like to be hit by one of these things
The ban will affect couriers and shops
Critics emphasize that some of the streets affected by the restrictions are among the widest in central Como and provide convenient access to the lake. In their view, the ban will also limit the use of an inexpensive and environmentally friendly form of transport.
This could particularly affect couriers and shop owners who use bicycles to deliver goods. Representatives of local civic organizations are calling for action against the dangerous behavior of individual cyclists rather than restrictions applying to everyone.
Como deserves a mobility system that guarantees pedestrian safety without punishing residents, workers and those who choose this form of transport
Rapinese has no intention of lifting the ban and says the decision was made after information was gathered about the safety situation in the city center.

Many poor in queue, can't allow 'luxury litigation' by rich: SC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
21:06:40 UTC
06:06:40 KST

NEW DELHI: At a time when poor litigants have to wait in line for years to get their plea heard, Supreme Court Friday disapproved the practice of influential people indulging in "luxury litigation", resulting in hearing of genuine cases getting delayed. It imposed a cost of Rs 5 lakh each on warring litigants for not approaching the court with "clean hands".A bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta rejected the plea of actress Rehana Khan and her lawyer Rizwan Siddique who have been fighting legal battles for past 11 years before different forums, including Bar Council of India, Bombay HC and SC."Each of these parties has come to us complaining of a wrong, and each has been the author of a good part of it. Between them, they have occupied the time of the Bar Council, an HC and this court for 11 years. That time belonged to other litigants, waiting for relief they genuinely needed. We record our strong disapproval of the conduct of both. In view of the conduct of each party, we find it fit to impose costs," the bench said.The bench noted that the two litigants approached the court in the confident expectation of vindication.
"Every fact of consequence has had to be prised out of a record in which suppression, embellishment and afterthought are the common currency of both sides. The machinery of justice is not a facility placed at the disposal of parties to settle scores, to salvage reputations they have themselves imperilled, or to extract advantage from a controversy of their own making.
We say at the outset, and give our reasons in what follows, that neither the appellant nor the respondent leaves this court with credit," it said."Record in these matters makes for compelling reading. Litigation of this kind holds a certain fascination, and we do not pretend otherwise. But a court is not an auditorium, and the drama of a case is no measure of its merit. Stripped of its theatre, what these proceedings disclose is a controversy which two litigants have between them manufactured, prolonged and brought to the highest court in the country, each in the hope that we would be sufficiently diverted by the spectacle to overlook their own part in creating it. We have not been," it said.

Syria, Israel hold high-level US-mediated de-escalation talks in Jordan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
20:58:59 UTC
05:58:59 KST

Rania Abushamala
23 August 2026•Update: 24 August 2026
High-level Syrian and Israeli delegations met in Jordan under US mediation on Sunday to achieve “de-escalation” following recent Israeli strikes on Syrian territory, a diplomatic source told the Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA).
The Syrian delegation was led by Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani and included the heads of the General Intelligence Directorate and Military Intelligence, the Foreign Ministry source said.
The meeting was held following “recent Israeli bombardment of Syrian territory and rising tensions in southern Syria” and efforts to “support stability in Syria and the region,” the source said.
The discussions focused on establishing “practical mechanisms to halt Israeli attacks, arrests and targeting operations” and reviving negotiations aimed at reaching a security agreement that could form the basis for “a more comprehensive future agreement.”
The Syrian delegation stressed that Syria is “a sovereign state” with “the full right to rebuild and develop its national army and determine its alliances and partnerships in accordance with its national interests.”
Damascus “will not accept any arrangements or mechanisms that would restrict these sovereign rights,” the source added.
Syria also reiterated its position that “the occupied Golan is Syrian territory,” noting that discussion of its final status and the process leading to it remains “premature at the current stage.”
“The immediate priority is the withdrawal of Israeli forces to the lines held before Dec. 8, 2024, and the reactivation and full implementation of the 1974 Disengagement Agreement,” the source said.
The talks also addressed the importance of “supporting Syria’s stability and preserving regional security,” including efforts to “bring the positions of Türkiye and Israel closer together and ensure that tensions between the two countries do not spill over into Syrian territory.”
The meeting focused on taking “practical steps toward de-escalation” while discussing ways to resume negotiations, the source said. Syria stressed that “any security arrangements must respect its sovereignty, territorial integrity and sovereign rights.”

Chemist Warehouse co-founder says it's all about culture

Asked by JBWere chief investment officer Alexandra Campbell about how he (and his brother) got here, he says something interesting about culture.
The model previously for chemist visits were "80% prescriptions and 20% 'front of shop'". He sought to - and did - flip that.
Gance was able to make it work by lowering rent (by getting bigger spaces per square metre) and lower staff costs because not all of them need to be highly qualified pharmacists.

The biggest thing is how you treat people and how you work at it.
"Culture's really important.

Key Event
Oil slips ahead of US announcement, as supplies shrink and diesel shortages build
Global oil prices have continued to slide ahead of the announcement of what the US has described as "the greatest financial offensive ever marshalled" with economic sanctions set to target Iran's trade partners.
Iran in turn vowed to shut down all oil exports from the Gulf "if the economic war continues."
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent will hold a press conference this evening (11 pm AEST) detailing the new sanctions package.
"At dawn begins an economic D-Day — the single greatest financial offensive ever marshalled against an adversary," Mr Bessent wrote in an opinion piece published in the Financial Times.
The warring nations have not conducted military strikes against each other for weeks, but they also have not engaged in meaningful talks to end the six-month-old conflict.
Oil traders appear to be embracing a degree of hope in the latest US plan to break the deadlock with the global Brent crude futures down 1.3% today to $US93.14/barrel.
CBA commodities analyst Vivek Dhar says prices are quick to fall on any talk of a US-Iran deal, or the hint of good news, as only 50 60% of pre-war oil flows are required to transit through the Strait of Hormuz to reassert oversupply expectations in oil markets from the start of this year.
"The reason that the Strait of Hormuz does not need to see pre-war levels of flow is because of the pipeline bypasses to the Strait of Hormuz, structurally lower Chinese oil imports and rising oil supply outside the Middle East," Mr Dhar said.
Certainly, on official data, shipping through the Strait is being throttled again with fewer than 20 commodity vessels transited the Strait over at the weekend.
Four vessels crossed the strait on Sunday, data from ship tracker Kpler reported.
The figures could change as some ships had switched off transponders on their way through.
That compared with Friday's figure of 16 transits, with two empty very large crude carriers (VLCCs) entering the Gulf with the tracking devices switched off, one heading to Iraq and the other to Bahrain.
Overall traffic volumes remained suppressed last week, as vessels aborted transit plans or switched routes through the strait's north after attacks, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said in a report.
Mr Dhar noted that while prices have bounced around, Singapore gasoil spot prices, which is the main benchmark for Australian diesel prices, has seen price volatility skew more to the upside.
"Diesel prices have been supported by disruptions to diesel exports from the Persian Gulf and Russia.
"Persian Gulf diesel exports have yet to recover in the same way as crude oil compared to pre-war levels due to the longer restart time for refineries in the region, damage to refining capacity.
"Bloomberg New Energy Finance estimates around 40% of the region's refining capacity has been impacted by drone and missile strikes) and as the pipeline bypasses are transporting crude oil only," Mr Dhar said.
ANZ commodity analyst Daniels Hynes says conditions remain exceptionally tight in the oil market, despite signs that some Persian Gulf exports are continuing to find their way to market.
"The seven-day average of inbound transits fell to just 0.1 vessels per day, while outbound movements remained weak at 0.4," Mr Hynes said.
"Should these official transit numbers persist, the modest recovery in exports may prove temporary, raising the risk of renewed declines in Persian Gulf crude and product shipments in coming weeks."
He agrees that the diesel market is the oil industry's key pressure point.
"With around 60% of Persian Gulf exports comprising medium and heavy crude grades that are particularly suited to diesel production, ongoing disruptions are having an outsized impact on distillate supply.
"As a result, diesel crack spreads continue to outperform crude oil and gasoline, refinery margins are rising and product prices continue to strengthen, increasing the risk of persistent inflationary pressure and elevated energy costs across the global economy," Mr Hynes said
With Reuters

The effects of climate change are getting more intense and there are predictions that an "El Nino" event on the horizon could make Australia's summer one of the hottest, driest and most dangerous on record — yet another one of those one-in-a-hundred-year scorchers that seem to roll around every few years these days.

"AI is the fourth industrial revolution": NAB boss
As noted, the CEO of NAB, Andrew Irvine, has been speaking at a function for customers in Melbourne this morning.
His big push is on AI.
From speaking to him at a previous event he discusses the immense differences between the pace and complexity of AI implementation between here and the US.
Here's what he's said today:
"Be under no illusion, AI is the fourth industrial revolution and it will be as consequential to how we live and work as the steam engine, electricity and the computer was to humanity.
"Just as steam powered rail and shipping connected people and markets over the world, and as electricity and the computer gave us back time, AI will remove friction from how we learn, how we create and how we solve problems.
"At its best, AI will expand human capability bycompressing complexity and scaling outcomes at unimaginable speed.
He moves onto a particularly strong point that will resonate with people who've used the most complex AI tools: they're only tools.
"But AI will not be a silver bullet. It's an amplifier.
"In strong organisations with good cultures, processes and governance, it will accelerate productivity, trust and innovation. It will be a source of competitive advantage.
"In weaker organisations, it will expose flaws, magnify problems and deepen distrust between workers and management."
Fortunes to be made... and lost..
"Over the coming years, business models and profit pools will shift at much greater speed and fortunes will be made and lost as businesses jostle to compete. Organisations that do not adapt quickly to AI will fall behind"
And yes, impact on jobs. But a useful link to the past:
"Just like with previous industrial revolutions, some roles will go. Some roles will change. And new roles will be created.
"For example, at the turn of the 20th century, 25% of Australians worked in agriculture. Today that figure is less than 2%. Agriculture remains a key contributor to Australia’s economy but the majority of those last century jobs have been mechanised and replaced by jobs supporting new industries and new innovations.
"Decades ago, NAB employed thousands of bank tellers, thousands of administrative clerks and we had large typing pools. Today, we employ more colleagues than we did then.
"The point is, our workforce is always changing. What is important is that we help Australians run to AI not from it, learn how to use it to be better at their work and teach them the skills they need to be future fit.
"History shows that economies that lean into technology change and new industries see much better outcomes than economies that seek to protect legacy industries and slow the march of progress."
Don't worry, there's still some good news for the humans.
"Lastly, and I believe very importantly, AI will not replace the human skills that matter in business and in life."
NAB boss: don't be afraid of AI
The CEO of Big Four bank NAB, Andrew Irvine, has been speaking at a function for customers in Melbourne this morning. A lot of the speech is about how Australia can boost productivity.
After discussing the economy (mainly, 'Woah, when we got together last year we thought things were wild') he's moved on to the Big P.
Here are some of the key lines:
"Longer term, Australia should be optimistic.
"We have the resources the world needs, abundant energy, strong institutions, world-class businesses and talented people. And we have enormous opportunities to drive growth in energy, agriculture, infrastructure, technology and housing.
"The ingredients are there. The foundations are strong. But the facts are that we're not making the most of them.
"I spoke earlier this year about the risk that we were at Peak Australia. That economic conditions were as good as it gets.
"We were growing but without real reform we would soon hit the limits of what the economy could deliver.
"You see, when demand outpaces supply, inflation goes up and the RBA needs to raise rates to put a handbrake on demand and reduce growth.
"That is largely what has happened.
"The risk now is not that we are at the peak of the mountain – it’s that we slide down the other side, stuck in a low-productivity, low-growth trap that’s been slowly strangling Australia for decades.
"Without urgent action, we’ll be locked in a slow lane – sitting in the rear-view mirror of other advanced economies surging past us.
"Consider the facts. Australian labour productivity growth averaged 2 ¼ % annually over the decade to 2005 and slowed to around 1 ½ % over the decade to 2015.
At 1.1%, the decade to 2020 was the slowest productivity decade in 60 years. If anything, this slide has continued to worsen since then. Today, labour productivity growth in the US is twice that of Australia. In Singapore, it’s more than three times higher.
"These countries combine high capital intensity, business friendly regulatory regimes, strong digital adoption and deep integration into global value chains.
"So my question today is: ‘is Australia prepared to do what it takes to realise our nation's ambition?’
"Australia will only achieve future prosperity if we deliver broader reform that encourages capital investment, that encourages risk taking and that encourages entrepreneurship."
Irvine goes on to cite reduction of building regulation in WA (the state has taken planning approvals from local councils for large developments) as an example of this.
"Lifting productivity must be the number one priority for government at all levels. It must also be the number one priority for businesses including NAB, regulators and unions. Ultimately, we all have the same goal – raising living standards for all Australians.
"Without a collective national effort across all jurisdictions, we will not make the progress we need, and future generations of Australians will suffer the consequences of our inaction."
But his big point is about AI, which I'll explore shortly.

Owner of Swiss bar in deadly blaze held for domestic abuse, report says
GENEVA - The owner of the Swiss bar ravaged by a deadly New Year fire is in pre-trial detention, accused of domestic abuse against his wife and co-owner of the establishment, media reported on Aug 23.
French couple Jacques and Jessica Moretti have been the focus of intense scrutiny since the fire ripped though their bar Le Constellation, in the Crans-Montana ski resort in the early hours of Jan 1.
The blaze killed 41 people, most of them teenagers, injuring 115 other people.
The Morettis are among 16 people facing criminal investigation in the case. They face charges including manslaughter by negligence and arson by negligence over the fire.
Jacques Moretti has now been arrested and detained following alleged violence against his wife earlier in August, local Geneva broadcaster Leman Bleu reported.
The incident reportedly happened on the night of Aug 11 at the couple’s home in Switzerland’s south-western Wallis canton, and was so serious that Jessica Moretti had to be hospitalised.
Neither the public prosecutor’s office nor the couple’s lawyers responded immediately to requests for comment.
However, the Moretti’s lawyers released a statement the evening of Aug 23 referring to the report, stressing that the alleged events were being investigated in a separate case pertaining “exclusively to their private life”.
“They should not be confused with the Constellation tragedy,” the lawyers said in the statement.
They added though that the reported events “nevertheless fall within a context that cannot be ignored: that of a particularly intense ordeal that the Morettis have been trying to face together since January 1”. AFP

Hungary plans to restore the full capacity of its only nuclear power plant within a week after the drought
Kyiv • UNN
Two of the three halted reactors at the Paks nuclear power plant have resumed operation. The plant is planned to reach 2,000 MW by Wednesday following the drop in the Danube's water level.
Hungary plans to bring its only nuclear power plant, "Paks," back to full capacity by midweek after drought and low water levels in the Danube threatened its operation. Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar said this, Bloomberg reports, writes UNN.
Details
Two of the three reactors that had been shut down over the past month resumed operations over the weekend. This made it possible to increase electricity generation from approximately 10% at its lowest level to more than half of the plant's capacity.
According to Magyar, "Paks" is expected to reach its full capacity of 2,000 MW by Wednesday. The nuclear power plant provides about 40% of Hungary's electricity.
World War II mines found in Slovakia due to the Danube’s low water level18.08.26, 00:56 • 4146 views
Hot weather and drought this summer lowered water levels in European rivers, particularly the Danube, making it more difficult to cool nuclear power plant reactors. Because of production problems, Hungary was forced to increase electricity imports and urge households and businesses to voluntarily reduce consumption.
Hungary is seeking a long-term solution
To prevent a complete shutdown of "Paks," the authorities resorted to emergency measures. In particular, two barges were sunk near the plant and an underwater barrier was built to raise the water level in the Danube.
At the same time, the Hungarian authorities are considering long-term measures because of the risk of recurring droughts. Magyar said that water resource management needed to be modernized and announced that the government was planning comprehensive climate legislation.

Kirkwood gives the Freedom 250 an American winner on the streets of downtown Washington
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
20:53:02 UTC
05:53:02 KST

Kirkwood gives the Freedom 250 an American winner on the streets of downtown Washington
WASHINGTON (AP) — On the streets of downtown Washington, an American led almost the whole way.
Kyle Kirkwood raced to his second victory of the IndyCar season Sunday, dominating the Freedom 250 in his No. 27 Honda. Kirkwood crossed the finish line in front of the U.S. Capitol 3.09 seconds ahead of Christian Lundgaard, after leading for 128 of a possible 147 laps.
“This likely is the most satisfying win that I’ve had, just the magnitude of it. This one and my first are pretty similar,” said Kirkwood, who now has seven career IndyCar victories. “When you think about the magnitude, what this means, having this race here in D.C., being the Freedom 250, as an American, it might top the first win for me.”
The race was set up as part of the country’s 250th birthday celebration. President Donald Trump gave drivers the green flag at the start and District of Columbia Mayor Muriel Bowser served as grand marshal.
Organizers could hardly have asked for better weather, with plenty of sun but not so much heat that fans would stay away. The area was awash in red, white and blue. Even the Canadian flags on that country’s embassy — located along the track’s Pennsylvania Avenue straightaway — featured two of those three colors.
“This was not a race. It was an event,” race chair Bud Denker said.
Will Power and Marcus Ericsson, Kirkwood’s teammates with Andretti Global, finished third and fourth. Pole winner Alex Palou, who had a chance to clinch the series title, finished 20th in his second-worst showing of the year.
After several prerace flyovers and Trump’s green flag, the field quickly went under caution because of debris on the track. The first big wreck came when David Malukas went into the wall and Sting Ray Robb could do little to avoid crashing into him coming around a turn. Just like that, two of the race’s eight American drivers were out.
Several cars went onto pit road, and that’s when the day started to fall apart for Palou. He appeared to hit a tire in someone else’s area while exiting, and he was assessed a drive-through penalty.
On a subsequent pit stop, one of Palou’s tires was loose when he started driving. That caused another delay, and he ended up off the lead lap. Palou later spun coming through a turn. His lead in the standings dropped from 133 points over second-place Kirkwood to 91 with three races to go.
“Things happen. I’m at least kind of happy that everything happened at the same day instead of spreading out throughout different races,” Palou said. “We had some issues in pit lane — one my fault, one out of my control.”
Kirkwood had a commanding lead before Palou’s spin caused a caution. On a restart with 19 laps remaining, Scott McLaughlin tried to pass Kirkwood and went into a tire barrier.
“Quite honestly, I thought he was going to make it stick initially,” Kirkwood said. “Once he got alongside me, there’s no way he’s stopping.”
After another caution, Kirkwood pulled off a strong restart with 13 laps to go and Lundgaard didn’t mount much of a threat as the 250-mile race wound down. Nicknamed the “King of the Streets” because of his success on tracks like this, Kirkwood looked right at home on the 1.7-mile circuit that was being used this weekend for the first time.
Misplaced blame?
Marcus Armstrong was penalized for avoidable contact when he sent Christian Rasmussen into a spin. Rinus VeeKay went into the wall during that incident but appeared unaware of Armstrong’s culpability when he went on TV for an interview.
“If Rasmussen’s around, you know you’re going to crash. Either he does or you do,” VeeKay said. “It sucks. It’s stupid. It’s a long race, and some people seemingly don’t know that.”
The race’s future
Denker had plenty of impressive stats ready for his postrace news conference: over 215,000 people attending over the last two days, and over $969,000 in merchandise sold Saturday.
As for whether the race will continue in the future, Denker said he’ll discuss it with series owner Roger Penske.
“Mr. Trump hit me 15 times today about having to have this,” Denker said. “‘Let’s do it for five years,’ is what he’s saying, ‘because that guarantees you’re going to be here through my term, then two more years for whoever is in office next.’”

deliberately uncomfortable stainless steel chair turns sitting into social commentary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
20:43:31 UTC
05:43:31 KST

Armenian designer Shushana Khachatrian, founder and design director of STUDIO SHOO, deliberately removes comfort from an object normally defined by it with The Woman’s Chair. Conceived as a reflection on the relationship between women and contemporary social structures, the piece uses posture, instability and restricted movement to explore ideas of cultural expectation, visibility and control. At first glance, its polished stainless-steel body appears precise and minimal; sitting down reveals a rather less accommodating agenda.
The chair rests on three stainless-steel legs, introducing a subtle instability, while its angled backrest prevents the sitter from reclining comfortably. Instead, the body is held in an upright position that Khachatrian uses as a metaphor for expectations around composure and restraint. ‘The piece is about boundaries — how women are often expected to hold themselves in a certain way, to occupy space with restraint,’the designer explains. Here, discomfort is not an unfortunate ergonomic oversight but the project’s central design device.
Integrated into the backrest is a mirror that complicates the relationship between sitter and object further. Rather than returning a stable portrait, the reflective surface offers a partial image that shifts or disappears as the body moves. Khachatrian connects this fleeting reflection to changing perceptions of identity and visibility, examining how the image of oneself can become dependent on position, perspective and external expectations.
Material contrasts reinforce the idea. The chair’s hard, reflective stainless steel is paired with an optional satin cushion edged with delicate frills, introducing softness and ornament into an otherwise severe structure. Handmade by Armenian fashion designer Hrachuhi Martirosyan, the textile element establishes an intentional tension between strength and vulnerability, rigidity and decoration — though the addition of satin does not suddenly turn the chair into somewhere to spend a lazy afternoon.
polished stainless steel shapes the deliberately uncomfortable seat
SITTING BECOMES SOCIAL COMMENTARY
The stainless-steel structure was produced by Armenian furniture manufacturer Canate, translating Khachatrian’s unconventional geometry into a functioning object. Chosen for its durability, strength and corrosion resistance, the material also gives the chair an uncompromising visual character: reflective enough to implicate its surroundings, but physically hard enough to keep the sitter constantly aware of the object beneath them.
Operating somewhere between furniture and sculpture, The Woman’s Chair uses the familiar typology of seating to ask less familiar questions about who is permitted to feel comfortable, how bodies are expected to behave and how much space they are encouraged to occupy. Rather than illustrating those pressures directly, Khachatrian embeds them into the mechanics of the chair itself. It can be sat on, technically. Whether it wants you to relax is another matter entirely.

U.S.-Canada trade negotiations failed over minor differences in the details of the agreement
Kyiv • UNN
The U.S. and Canada failed to reach a trade agreement due to disagreements over tariffs, digital services, and trade partnerships. Washington imposed a 50% tariff, and Ottawa is preparing a response.
Trade negotiations between the United States and Canada ended without a deal after the parties discovered significant discrepancies between the agreements and the wording in the draft document. Canada's ambassador to the United States, Mark Wiseman, said this, Bloomberg reports, according to UNN.
Details
Wiseman said the talks did not break down because of one specific issue. According to him, during a detailed analysis, the Canadian side discovered that its understanding of the agreements reached differed substantially from what was written in the documents.
During a more detailed analysis, we discovered that our understanding of what had been agreed upon differed quite significantly from what was stated in the documents
According to him, one of the key issues was tariffs on medium- and heavy-duty vehicles. Canada insisted on including these categories in the tariff exemptions because this is important for preserving the country's automotive manufacturing.
The United States and Canada are preparing new tariff measures
After the talks failed, the United States imposed a 50% tariff on Canadian goods worth approximately $20 billion. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced retaliatory measures that are to take effect on September 8.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the proposed deal provided for lower tariffs on Canadian steel, aluminum, automobiles, and lumber. According to him, Canada rejected the proposed terms.
Wiseman also said that the United States demanded limits on Canada's ability to conclude trade agreements with other countries. According to him, this was not about a specific state, but rather a broader demand that could have limited Canada's economic diversification.
Requirements concerning French-language content and digital services became a separate problem. Wiseman called this issue a "red line" for Ottawa, stressing that Canada was not prepared to limit its ability to protect and develop the French language in the country.
Ultimately, we are simply not prepared to agree to terms that were unfair, uneconomic and, in fact, called the reliability of the deal into question

Canada rejected US trade deal over 'unfair' and 'uneconomic' demands: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
20:09:52 UTC
05:09:52 KST

Yasin Güngör
23 August 2026•Update: 23 August 2026
Canada rejected a proposed US trade agreement following a series of "last-minute" demands from Washington that officials characterized as fundamentally lopsided, according to a report by Canadian newspaper The Globe and Mail.
 
“Last-minute changes in the US proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic and called into question the reliability of any deal,” Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said after he said suspended trade talks with Washington.
 
He emphasized that the proposed framework failed to protect national interests, prompting a vow to implement dollar-for-dollar retaliatory tariffs beginning Sept. 8.
 
The Globe and Mail, citing unnamed sources, detailed significant friction over sectoral barriers, with the US seeking a 4-million-tonne quota on Canadian steel exports coupled with a 25% tariff that would double for excess volume.
 
On automotive trade, US negotiators are said to have sought to exempt only American-made content from duties, while demanding Canada scrap all retaliatory measures against US steel and vehicles.
 
The US insisted that Canadian provincial governments "end retaliatory bans on American alcohol."
 
US negotiators also did not want the forestry sector covered by the deal, despite Canadian insistence that it was a necessary component.
 
Agricultural, provincial friction
 
Washington also targeted internal Canadian policies, demanding an overhaul of the dairy supply-management licensing system and an end to provincial “Buy Canadian” procurement practices.
 
In Quebec, Premier Christine Frechette said US officials pushed for concessions on French-language cultural laws and appliance instruction manuals.
 
The failed deal attempted to integrate trade with national security, including Canada’s F-35 fighter jet purchase and the "Golden Dome" missile defense system. US negotiators also sought tighter regulations on oil exports and coordination on critical minerals.
 
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer accused Ottawa of upending the balance through "walk backs."
Patterns of misinterpretation
 
Mark Wiseman, Canada’s ambassador to the US, told Bloomberg that the collapse was not caused by a single issue but a consistent pattern of discrepancies. “As we drilled down, what we discovered was that what our understanding of what had been agreed to was quite different from what was showing up in the documents,” Wiseman said.
 
He noted that when every interpretation is "the most negative interpretation," it reaches a point where negotiators must walk away.
 
Earlier, Carney accused the US of using new tariffs to "hurt and divide" Canada, calling the measures "a miscalculation."
 
US President Donald Trump on Sunday said on his social media platform Truth Social that Canada "wants the benefits of being a State, without being one.”

Parents of kids with disability more likely to be burnt out, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
20:05:04 UTC
05:05:04 KST

Parents of children with disability more likely to experience psychological distress, survey finds
A major Australian study has found parents caring for young children with disability are twice as likely to experience psychological distress and nearly twice as likely to say they are not in good health.
The results also show they are 50 per cent more likely to feel parenting is demanding, compared to carers without children with disability.
The figures were revealed in the Parenting Today study, a survey of more than 10,000 carers conducted by the Parenting Research Centre.
"This has significant consequences, not only for the parents and their mental health, but for the safety and wellbeing of the children," said Skye Kakoschke-Moore, chief executive of Children and Young People with Disability Australia (CYDA).
In her work with CYDA, Ms Kakoschke-Moore said she heard regularly from exhausted parents who were at breaking point.
She said if support was not available, they may have to make difficult decisions.
"They may be left with no other choice but to relinquish their child into care," she said.
The survey asked more than 120 questions across seven topics including emotional and physical wellbeing, the types of support people were accessing and family structures.
The results compared the experience of nearly 5,000 respondents who said they were caring for a child under nine years old.
Of those surveyed, 600 were parents of kids with a disability.
It comes as the government prepares to divert some families from the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) onto the new Thriving Kids program, which begins in October, and will be jointly delivered by the federal, state and territory governments.
The reforms are intended to move some children with lower support needs into mainstream and community-based supports, while the NDIS focuses on those requiring more intensive assistance.
In its first phase, the $4 billion program will provide general supports, including online information and parenting courses.
Later stages, which are scheduled to be completely rolled out by January 2028, will offer more targeted supports such as access to therapies in places like preschools.
But for some families, the changes have created uncertainty about whether the new system will provide the support their children need.
Parents feeling loneliness, frustration and guilt
The latest research found 48 per cent of parents caring for children with disability experienced loneliness, compared to 31 per cent of parents whose children did not have disability.
It also showed many often felt frustration, guilt or that they were not meeting their own expectations of parenting.
"The risk there is, that when we're feeling frustrated as parents, we're more likely to escalate into more irritable, hostile, aggressive reactions to our children,"
"There's something going on for parents right now that's putting [them] under stress, that's making parents feel that they're not doing a good enough job," she said.
She pointed to multiple factors adding to the strain, including cost-of-living pressures and confusion about where supports would come from.
"[It's] a lack of assurance about what the future holds for them and for their child," she said.
'In survival mode every day'
Sarah Galea is one of those parents feeling burnt out.
The Sydney mum adores her three young sons who all live with disabilities, but she also admits managing their complex needs can be hard.
"You just feel numb," she said.
"I live in survival mode every day."
As well as supporting the boys to navigate their emotions and at-times complex behaviours, Ms Galea also assists them with tasks neurotypical children of the same age would likely do independently, like feeding and personal care.
Ms Galea had to change careers to be available to support her boys at short notice, if school or daycare called.
"The phone will ring now, and my palms get clammy and sweaty, and the heart rate increases," she said.
"You know you're managing the next major meltdown."
While Ms Galea has seen her sons progress thanks to feeding and speech therapy funded by the NDIS, she does worry what will happen to those supports if they are moved onto Thriving Kids.
"We just now have constant fear of the unknown because we don't know what's happening to our boys' plans,"
Medical professionals have suggested she seek help for burnout but she said she was struggling to find the time.
In a statement, a government spokesperson said the proposed model for Thriving Kids was designed by an advisory group consisting of experts from a range of sectors including paediatrics, disability, early education and health care.
"Members also consulted through their networks and the national model proposed by the advisory group was tested with groups of families with lived experience," the statement said.
"The advisory group recommends that Thriving Kids will be the best way to help parents and families build their own skills and networks and better connect with targeted services that support Australian children."
Parents reach out to support programs
Despite high levels of burnout, the parents in the surveyed group were actively seeking information or advice online and were more likely to participate in parenting or peer support programs.
The My Time program is one such peer group providing support to parents of children with disability through fortnightly sessions, usually led by a facilitator.
The program, which began two decades ago, operates 180 groups across Australia both in person and online.
"It's a bit of a lifesaver," senior program manager Jenny Boadle said.
"They feel more connected, they have a sense of belonging and hope for the future."
Each session is directed by the needs of the parents and focuses on the day-to-day challenges they might be experiencing, such as navigating sleep or continence issues.
Ms Boadle acknowledged that time pressures and a lack of childcare options made it difficult for some parents to attend.
But she said there were always people on hand at the sessions to mind preschool-aged children so their parents could take part.
"Parents that come tell us that once they realise, taking a little bit of time out for themselves and connecting with their peers is just so valuable," she said.
"They can go back and feel more confident in caring for their children."
Ms Kakoschke-Moore said parenting courses simply would not help everyone.
"[They] can be really valuable, particularly when families are first embarking on their journey of caring for a child with disability," she said.
"But parenting programs are no substitute for one-to-one support or respite and to prevent families from entering burnout."
For Ms Galea, who already runs on an average of five hours of broken sleep a night, the idea of finding time to attend a peer support group or parenting course is laughable.
"You need 24 hours in my shoes and then you won't offer me that course,"
Ms Kakoschke-Moore said that it went without saying that not all parents of children with disability were in distress or that these parents loved their children any less.
"What it pointed to was that parents in this cohort needed to know support would be there for them when they did reach out," she said.

Hapoel Tel Aviv and Atalanta played to a goalless draw in the first leg of UEFA Conference League Playoff Round action.

Both sides continued to play cautiously as neither wanted to make a mistake. The Reds made a double substitution in order to try and open the match up a bit with Xander Silva and Mor Buskila coming on. Tentative play again littered the pitch, but Atalanta had a pair of brilliant chances in second-half injury time when Ederson’s back-to-back shots were saved by Assaf Tzur as the time ran out to send the tie to the decisive second leg at Hapoel’s home-away-from-home in Miskolc.

The two warned against the accelerated preparations for the International Stabilization Force's (ISF) entry into the Gaza Strip.

The ministers also noted that the camp, where training continues at an intensive pace, will eventually accommodate about 5,000 soldiers.

Smotrich, Strock claim preperations underway for a larger-than-expected ISF
Smotrich and Strock claimed the preparations underway are for a force much larger than what was presented to the cabinet, and that its aim also appears fundamentally different from what was presented to the ministers.
According to them, this is happening at a time when Hamas is not showing any willingness to disarm and demilitarize.
In their letter to the Prime Minister, the ministers warned: "We must not reach a situation where the ISF, of such a huge scale, will be ready and willing to enter the Gaza Strip, and enormous pressure will be exerted on Israel to allow its entry, even though the demilitarization has not yet been carried out."
In light of this, Smotrich and Strock demanded that the cabinet adopt an affirmative resolution tomorrow, which will prevent the entry of the ISF and any other multinational force into the Gaza Strip before Hamas is fully disarmed and Gaza is fully demilitarized.

New evacuation orders were also in effect for the Somersett community, including areas north of Somersett Parkway to Robb Drive, as well as neighborhoods north of W. 7th Street to N. McCarran Boulevard, the sheriff’s office said.
Three civilians and three first responders were injured, said Shane Akerson, a unified incident commander with the Truckee Meadows Fire Protection District. About 5,000 people were also without power, he added
The sheriff said the fire was human-caused and urged about 90,000 people to evacuate.
