Notes from Central Taiwan: The violent Taiwan we forgot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
16:38:15 UTC
01:38:15 KST

When we recall the 1990s, we usually identify them as the time of great transitions, from authoritarianism to democracy, and the public’s shift to acknowledging a Taiwanese identity. But another transition occurred, one that we take for granted and hardly notice anymore.
The 1980s opened with the massacre of members of the family of democracy activist Lin I-hsiung (林義雄). While Lin was in detention, on Feb. 28, 1980, persons still unknown broke into the Lin family home despite round-the-clock police surveillance. Lin’s mother and two of his three daughters were slain. His eldest daughter survived multiple stab wounds. The following year saw the murder of Carnegie Mellon professor and democracy activist Chen Wen-chen (陳文成) after being detained by the state security apparatus.
BLACK GOLD POLITICS
Photo: Sun Yi-fong, Taipei Times
Those crimes were part of a long pattern of violent crime by the state, its opponents, organized crime and individual criminals stretching back to the advent of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) era in Taiwan, and continuing through the 1990s when climactic, horrific crimes riveted the public, yet left it aghast at what appeared to be a spectacle of decline.
In 1983 someone bombed the Central Daily News and United Daily News. The government identified the perpetrators as Taiwan independence movement activists. A UPI piece at the time gave it another context: “the explosions came in the midst of a Taipei newspaper campaign led by the Central Daily News against sex publications and organized crime. Many newspapers have received threatening letters from purported gangsters.”
Nostalgia for the era of president Chiang Ching-kuo (蔣經國) revolves around the public forgetting the general lawlessness during his time, how business, government and organized crime intertwined incestuously. Many of us, remembering that lawlessness privately, transmute it into a feeling of freedom, that in those days you could do what you wanted.
Photo: Liao Jui-hsiang, Taipei Times
The case that typified the lawlessness of the 1980s was the collapse of Tsai Wan-lin (蔡萬霖) family’s Cathay-affiliated business empire in 1985, which was responsible for a measurable chunk of GDP. Its Tenth Credit Cooperative collapsed in February of 1985, the worst financial collapse in the nation’s history to that point. The shenanigans leading to its collapse were intricate and extensive. Regulators had periodically fined the group and knew what was happening, as the ramifications of the case reached the highest levels.
“Three senior government auditors were dismissed for providing Tenth Credit with advance warning of official financial examinations, and a dozen other officials have been reprimanded,” the Christian Science Monitor reported.
The group had also made “loans” to the tune of US$35 million to five legislators, apparently to get the banking laws changed.
Photo courtesy of the Pingtung County Government
Three crimes defined the 1990s, all horrific murders. The first was the Nov. 21, 1996 murder of Taoyuan County magistrate Liu Pang-yu (劉邦友), along with seven others. The brutality of the crime, in which the assassins blindfolded the victims, forced them to kneel and then shot them in the head, shocked the nation. Liu had faced investigations and allegations involving corruption and land deals. The enormous sums of money he was alleged to have taken were a dark signal of the rampant corruption in local governments.
The Liu murder was followed immediately by one of the cruelest murders in the nation’s history, that of Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Woman’s Affairs Department director Peng Wan-ru (彭婉如). She disappeared on Nov. 30, 1996. Three days later she was found raped and murdered, with over 30 stab wounds on her body. She was last seen getting into a taxi, a vehicle, as anthropologist Nick Pazderic put it: “that serves as a sign — despite the professional demeanor of most drivers — of reckless individualism, lawless social relations, aggressive male domination and unrestricted urban migration.”
The climactic crime of the 1990s was the April 1997 kidnapping and murder of 16 year old Pai Hsiao-yen (白曉燕), the daughter of popular entertainer Pai Bing-bing (白冰冰). The case immediately turned into 24-7 media nightmare.
“When Bing-bing set out to deliver the ransom days later, tailed by undercover detectives, they were pursued by not just a motorcade of reporters but even a news chopper,” Ryan Ho Kilpatrick recounts in a piece chronicling the changes in the media as a result of the case. “The hostage exchange, unsurprisingly, did not go through.” Her naked and abused corpse was found at the end of the month.
Her kidnappers killed another four people in the following months as they ran from the police. The spree ended with the last suspect still at large breaking into the home of the South African Military attache and holding his family hostage. The media conducted live interviews with the hostage taker even as the police were attempting to negotiate.
MEDIA CIRCUS
The media circus around the killings and the manhunt, including printing photos of the naked corpse of Pai Hsiao-yen and bodies of her killers, sparked nationwide revulsion. A massive protest march was held in Taipei. Many worried that Taiwan was becoming a “little Sicily.” As Pazderic put it, for the emerging middle class, the deaths demonstrated “that the social conditions from which they sprang, including the long-time alliance of government and organized crime and the actions of uncontrolled capitalists required continued and aggressive cleansing and re-ordering.”
To anyone in Taiwan in the late 1990s and early 2000s, where the Legislature’s Justice Committee co-chairman, Lo Fu-chu (羅福助), was a widely known gangster whose election to the Legislature also afforded him the considerable legal protections then enjoyed by lawmakers, where high ranking officials attended the funerals of a prominent gangsters, it seemed like a Wild West of instability. Yet, as a friend of mine put it in a private message, that now-forgotten era “melted into a kind of stability.” What happened?
The KMT government in 1990 launched Operation Thunderbolt (掃黑行動) — the premier named Lo Fu-chu one of the targets — and rounded up many gangsters. President Lee Teng-hui (李登輝) in August 1992 shut down the Taiwan Garrison Command, the secret police and public security bureau, apportioning its functions among various other agencies. Policing began to improve. Democratization brought an end to systematic authoritarian political repression and increasingly gave citizens peaceful means to express their expectations for society.
(Incidentally, an earlier crackdown in 1984 known as Operation Clean Sweep (一清專案), rounded up more than 2,000 alleged gangsters — including Lo — and contributed to the creation of the Celestial Alliance when imprisoned gang figures formed alliances on Green Island, where they were incarcerated.)
During the 1990s numerous factory owners packed up their businesses and moved them to the People’s Republic of China (PRC). Many gangsters did the same, expanding their operations in the PRC as it opened up. With factories gone the service industries they sustained, dominated by gangsters, shrunk.
The government also changed as public expectations changed. Government programs changed the way local government offices behaved. Today one enters the local household registration office and there is a helpful information officer and orderly lines served by friendly officials, a far cry from the Taiwan I knew of the late 1980s. Surveillance cameras on the streets and in residential areas were hurriedly introduced in 1998, partly in response to the 1996-97 crimes. In 2009 the government expanded the program to put cameras everywhere.
The effects of all these changes all came together in roughly a decade after 1998. Looking back, it is shocking how quickly it all came together.
And how quickly we became used to it, and forgot.
Notes from Central Taiwan is a column written by long-term resident Michael Turton, who provides incisive commentary informed by three decades of living in and writing about his adoptive country. The views expressed here are his own.
An interesting essay in the spring issue this year of International Security by Kerby Davis and Eugene Gholz explores the possibilities and outcomes of simulated missile attacks by the People’s Republic of China (PRC) on Taiwan’s ports to carry out a blockade. “Substantively,” they conclude in Blockade by Fire: China’s Potential to Blockade Taiwan Using Missile Attacks on Ports, “our article raises serious concern about Taiwan’s vulnerability to Chinese military coercion. Even if Taiwan and the United States take steps to better prepare for a Chinese blockade, they face a greater threat from China than analysts previously believed.” The authors
“She is gone, but she used to be mine,” go the words of Sara Bareilles’ poignant and powerful anthem from Waitress, the quintessential Broadway 11 o’clock number. For musical theater fans, the mere sound of those opening chords is enough to send tear ducts into overdrive. So when at the beginning of Don’t Say Good Luck, high schooler Sophie Birenbaum gets the lead role of Jenna in “Waitress,” we immediately know what’s eventually coming: a tear-jerking scene where She Used to Be Mine takes center stage. Everything that comes before? Just the appetizer. Don’t Say Good Luck, directed by Julia Hart, is

Their stories are therefore all the more urgent to preserve, offering an invaluable glimpse into what Taiwanese went through during a period of great change. Torrential rain caused by the combined effects of southwesterly winds and a low-pressure belt battered southern Taiwan yesterday, causing widespread flooding across Tainan, Kaohsiung and Pingtung County.
More than 2,300 people were evacuated as authorities warned of continued heavy rain through tomorrow.
Tainan, Kaohsiung and Pingtung County yesterday announced that work and classes would remain suspended today for the second consecutive day amid heavy rain and flooding.
Photo: Liu Wan-lin, Taipei Times
Chiayi, Hualien and Taitung counties later last night also announced that work and classes would be canceled today.
The Kaohsiung City Government said it expected cumulative rainfall over the five-day period of the low-pressure system to exceed 1.3m, nearly half what the city typically expects in an entire year.
Taiwan Railway said there would be disruptions on the main east coast line and trains to and from Kaohsiung and Taitung with express services canceled and local trains dependent on weather conditions.
Photo courtesy of a member of the public
"If you've got nothing on, for goodness sake don't go out," Taitung County Commissioner April Yao (饒慶鈴) wrote on Facebook.
In Kaohsiung, 2,203 people were evacuated from across multiple districts, while 34 rivers in Liouguei (六龜) and Maolin (茂林) districts were under red debris-flow alerts. Another 115 people were evacuated across Pingtung County as heavy rain triggered flooding and other disruptions.
Several motorists were caught in floodwaters. In Kaohsiung’s Niaosong District (鳥松), a car traveling along a flooded road was nearly submerged, but the three people inside escaped and were rescued without injury.
Kaohsiung’s light rail service was briefly disrupted yesterday morning after a train traveling between Heart of Love River (C24) and Longhua Elementary School (C23) stations made light contact with a fallen tree.
Fallen trees and mud blocked roads in Renwu District (仁武), while trails around the Heart of Love River (愛河之心) in Sanmin District (三民) were inundated, with water reaching waist height in some areas.
Flooding was reported in numerous parts of Kaohsiung, including Gushan (鼓山), Nanzih (楠梓), Zuoying (左營), Renwu, Yongan (永安), Gangshan (岡山), Daliao (大寮) and Yancheng (鹽埕) districts.
The Kaohsiung City Government upgraded its disaster response center from Level 2 to Level 1 yesterday as the rain intensified.
In Tainan, rain fell almost continuously from late Saturday night through yesterday morning, causing flooding in Yongkang District (永康).
Although the rain eased at about noon and floodwater began to recede, another round of heavy rain struck between 2pm and 3pm, causing renewed flooding in Yongkang. Police were again deployed to control traffic.
The Tainan City Government had prepared 511 mobile water pumps and 68 pumping stations, while five additional pumps were requested from the central government to accelerate drainage.
Pingtung County had reported flooding at 36 locations as of 4pm yesterday, including areas in Jiadong (佳冬), Neipu (內埔) and Shihzih (獅子) townships and Pingtung City. Eight fallen trees were also reported, and several roads were closed, including sections of Provincial Highway No. 1 and the northbound entrance ramp of the Linbian Interchange on National Freeway No. 3.
Provincial Highway No. 24 between kilometer markers 27.4 and 37.3 was also closed as a precaution because about 400mm of rainfall was forecast over 24 hours in the mountainous area.
Extremely heavy rain or more severe rainfall was expected to continue in southern and eastern Taiwan through tomorrow, Central Weather Administration forecaster Yeh Chih-chun (葉致均) said.
Weather conditions are forecast to become relatively stable on Wednesday, before rainfall in northern Taiwan increases from Thursday, depending on Typhoon Saudel’s movements, he said.
As of 3pm yesterday, accumulated rainfall in Kaohsiung exceeded 300mm, while Tainan and Pingtung recorded about 270mm to 290mm. Taitung had also received nearly 200mm.

The Ministry of National Defense (MND) is implementing 14 measures to boost military recruitment as the number of new recruits declined for the second consecutive year.
The armed forces recruited 18,900 people in 2023, 17,971 in 2024 and 17,113 last year, while the overall fill rate was 80 percent, 78 percent and 80 percent respectively, the ministry said.
According to an estimate by the Ministry of the Interior’s Department of Conscription Administration, the number of men eligible for regular military service is expected to fall below 80,000 next year.
Photo: Taipei Times
To address recruitment challenges and reduce personnel attrition, the MND has introduced 14 measures, including recruitment cooperation agreements with 116 universities and more than 400 senior-high and vocational schools, higher recruitment bonuses and salary increases for volunteer military personnel.
Other measures include improving recruitment organization, increasing media promotion, setting clear targets and responsibilities for recruiters, expanding recruitment outreach during new-recruit training, increasing the number of recruiters, improving leadership and management, upgrading service conditions, creating clearer career prospects for service members, providing proactive guidance to new recruits, adjusting assignments so personnel can serve where their families are registered and strengthening internal management, the MND said.
The measures are aimed at increasing young people’s willingness to join the armed forces, it said.
The military uses recruitment centers in northern, central and southern Taiwan, along with dedicated personnel teams, to coordinate resources from military operational areas, it said.
Through school outreach, students interested in military service are invited to visit military academies and take part in hands-on activities, while media campaigns raise public awareness of military recruitment, it added.
Recruitment efforts are also incorporated into special, regional and regular activities, as well as community outreach, to encourage students interested in military careers to join the armed forces, the MND said.
Recruiters are also given targets based on individual units and recruitment cohorts, with performance evaluations conducted monthly, quarterly and semiannually, it said, adding that recruiters who fail to produce results during a quarter would undergo review, while those who meet their targets would be eligible for rewards.
The armed forces have also adopted an “everyone is a recruiter” approach, rewarding personnel who refer friends and relatives to apply for military service, and recruitment bonuses and other incentives have been increased to encourage such referrals, it said.
In addition, the ministry has adjusted assignments based on the characteristics and needs of individual units, allowing personnel to serve where their families are registered and matching personnel with appropriate positions on a case-by-case basis, the MND said.
As part of the Hsing-an Project, the armed forces have improved living and accommodation conditions in barracks, it said.
The military is also improving its promotion system to encourage personnel to pursue advancement opportunities, such as academic degrees, professional certifications and specialized training through part-time or full-time study, it said.
The military would coordinate its education initiatives with the Executive Yuan’s plan to build a learning-oriented government and the Ministry of Labor’s national certification policy, it added.
Unit commanders are authorized to allow volunteer officers, non-commissioned officers and enlisted personnel to pursue further education, provided that doing so does not affect training or operational duties, the MND said.

China showcases robots at Beijing games
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
16:38:14 UTC
01:38:14 KST

China’s humanoid robots have shown they can run quicker than the fastest humans.
Now comes the real test: Can they also handle packaging and warehouse operations while reliably performing precision tasks like connecting cables designed to evaluate their ability to work like humans in less flashy jobs?
The five-day World Humanoid Robot Games, which began in Beijing on Saturday, combines events modeled on human sports with those designed to test the robots in simulated factories, restaurants, offices and in emergency situations.
Photo: Reuters
Heavily promoted in Chinese state media, the games, held at Beijing’s National Speed Skating Oval and which run through Wednesday, feature 51 events, including 30 sports competitions and 21 scenario-based contests. More than 40 percent require robots to operate fully autonomously, according to Huawei Technologies Co, a tech partner of the games.
On Saturday, two robots ran faster than Usain Bolt’s 9.58-second world record in the 100m. That was a sharp improvement from last year, when the winning robot’s time was more than 20 seconds. Braking was an issue, as the machines slammed into a thick mat that organizers placed several meters after the finish line.
Another humanoid, the same model as the 100-meter champion, ran 400m in 39.7 seconds, faster than South African Wayde van Niekerk’s world record of 43.03 seconds.
Photo: EPA
“The intensity is higher than last year, which places significant demands on the robot’s battery management and thermal dissipation capabilities,” spectator and robotics investor Xu Qiaosheng said.
“It holds huge significance for the development of China’s industrial sector,” Xu said.
Robots are to compete in tug-of-war and weightlifting, while taichi and pitch-pot — in which contestants throw arrow-like sticks into a narrow-necked vase — would give traditional Chinese sports a futuristic twist.
Photo: AFP
Beyond the spectacle, the more revealing tests could come when robots encounter the small imperfections of the physical world: a cable at the wrong angle, an object just out of reach, a shifting package or a missed step.
That tests whether robots can identify objects, accurately position their hands and bodies, apply controlled force and recover from errors without human intervention.
Lumos Robotics CEO Yu Chao (喻超) said the games could help improve hardware and provide a showcase for the industry, but the longer-term value would depend on real-world problem-solving.
“Only when it can work in those end scenarios does it have real value,” Yu said. “Simply running and jumping does not improve efficiency.”
In addition to more familiar events drawn from human sports, robots would compete in electric-vehicle charging, restaurant work, emergency incident handling and hand-dexterity contests. There are also industrial assembly and material loading events. A cable connection challenge is a test of vision, mechanical alignment and force control.
Beijing-based robotics startup Galbot said it would stage an autonomous humanoid tennis match, with robots attempting singles and doubles play, including ball tracking, serving and returning shots.
For Hua Rong (花蓉), chief marketing officer at robotics firm Zeroth, the real test would come after the demonstrations end.
“The competition will be whether, after the product is sold, it can really solve users’ problems,” she said.

Argentina court overturns acquittal in sex abuse case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
16:38:14 UTC
01:38:14 KST

An Argentinian court has overturned the acquittal of a former nun in a notorious sex abuse case involving deaf children, authorizing a lower court to determine her punishment, a ruling showed.
Kumiko Kosaka, a Japanese national, had been acquitted in 2023 of abusing students at the Provolo Institute of Mendoza, a free boarding school for underprivileged children with hearing and speech difficulties.
The 51-year-old former nun could face up to 50 years in prison following the reversal by the Mendoza Province Supreme Court of Justice, the plaintiff’s attorney, Sergio Salinas, said of the ruling issued on Friday.
Photo: Reuters
The court decision was “historic,” he said. “It means the children told the truth and the court acted very arbitrarily when it acquitted her.”
A sentencing date has not yet been set.
The case, with allegations first surfacing in 2016, had sent shock waves through the Catholic Church in the homeland of former pope Francis.
Two priests at the institute in the city of Lujan de Cuyo were jailed for more than 40 years each in 2019 for sexual abuse, including rape, of 20 minors.
A school gardener and an altar boy were also convicted of sex crimes and sentenced to prison.
The crimes in question were committed between 2004 and 2016 and involved victims who were between the ages of four and 17.
Kosaka had been charged with aggravated sexual abuse and covering up crimes.
Eight other female employees of the school, including another nun, had faced criminal charges and all were acquitted at their 2023 trial.
The Mendoza court on Friday upheld the acquittals of the eight other women in its decision, which spanned more than 200 pages.

Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Legislator Weng Hsiao-ling (翁曉玲) has gained much attention in the past month, as she aggressively proposed to cut large portions of the government budget, becoming the focus of discussions across social media and drawing negative attention to herself and her party.
On Aug. 14, the opposition-controlled Legislative Yuan, after nearly a full-year delay, finally passed this fiscal year’s central government general budget, with several deep cuts proposed by Weng. It included cutting the culture ministry’s entire publicity fund and a NT$10 million (US$313,991) cut from the Preisdental Office’s discretionary state affairs fund with an additional NT$20 million freeze — the entirety of the fund — sparking much public comment.
A Presidential Office official said that a part of the state affairs fund is usually used for purchasing mooncakes and gift boxes made by shelter workshops for the Mid-Autumn Festival next month, but Weng insisted on cutting and freezing the entire fund, despite Legislative Speaker Han Kuo-yu’s (韓國瑜) attempts to mediate.
Presidential Office Secretary-General Pan Men-an (潘孟安) on Aug. 20 invited members of the shelter workshops to explain the situation and urged the public to purchase mooncakes made by the workshops to support them during the upcoming holiday — the peak sales season during which the government has traditionally purchased a large amount of their wares. The Presidential Office cannot do so anymore. The office released a list of 62 workshops and social welfare groups, encouraging the public to help people with disabilities by purchasing holiday gift boxes from them.
As many people have accused Weng of a lack of empathy in gutting the fund that was used to help vulnerable groups, she was seen in a video allegedly cutting in line to enter a movie theater on Aug. 15 (which she denied) and posting a picture alleged to show a movie screen on Facebook (later deleting it), sparking more discussions about her questionable behavior.
Weng added fuel to the fire by saying that she objects to using taxpayers’ money for charity, adding President William Lai’s (賴清德) was “guilt tripping” the opposition lawmakers and that he should use his own salary for charity work, drawing more criticism, as many see her actions as political retaliation and using the income of vulnerable people for political gain.
Weng has criticized the Presidential Office’s call to help shelter workshops and Lai’s NT$200,000 out-of-pocket purchase, saying “‘doing good without others knowing’ is a core value shared by Chinese people,” while she said in an interview that she is a “proud and upright Chinese” who is “living in Taiwan,” drawing immediate praise from Chinese state-owned media, but causing a public backlash in Taiwan.
While most members of the public do not pay close daily attention to bill debates or budget reviews at the legislature, and politicians can easily manipulate public perception on complicated issues by crafting simplified and emotional messages that benefit their own interests, many important public issues that need rational and substantial discussions are drowned out by constant partisan conflict “noise” and overlooked as the public grows more indifferent to politics.
However, the incidents involving Weng, her “merciless” budget cuts, and controversial actions and remarks, as well as the Presidential Office’s decision to invite shelter workshops to promote their holiday gift boxes publicly, have helped people see who are being hurt by their actions and put a “face” to the opposition legislators making those decisions.
Many people are realizing that the so-called “rational oversight” of government budget and “compromises” made by the KMT and Taiwan People’s Party lawmakers are not what they claimed, highlighted by Weng’s callous attitude, backed by votes from their lawmakers. A Web site that analyzed YouTube view counts linked Weng to negative comments and keywords such as “cruel,” “shelter workshops” and “buy it yourself.”
Weng does not seem to worry about the criticism. When Democratic Progressive Party lawmakers told the public that the culture and public media budget would not have passed without the support from “59 Wengs in the legislature,” including several who are running for local government heads this year, she replied by saying she aims for “113 Wengs in the legislature.”
With the nine-in-one local elections coming in less than 100 days, Weng may prove to be a major liability for the KMT, as more voters are associating her arrogant attitude, her heavy-handed use of unchecked legislative power and her questionable national identity — as some polls have shown that 2.5 percent of the people in Taiwan identify themselves as “Chinese only” — with her party.

Beware bingeing on snacks during Ghost Month: specialist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
16:38:12 UTC
01:38:12 KST

A weight-loss specialist on Saturday warned that bingeing on stockpiles of high-calorie snacks left over from the Ghost Festival’s pudu (普度) ceremonies can affect liver fat and metabolism before weight gain appears.
Pudu, held to honor ancestors, is a common ritual during the seventh lunar month — traditionally regarded as Ghost Month in Taiwanese folk belief.
Liu Yao-tseing (劉曜增), obesity medicine specialist at the Genesis Clinic’s Kahosiung branch, said that after the pudu ceremonies, offices often suddenly end up with large amounts of snacks.
Photo: Lee Ching-hui, Taipei Times
If they are all placed on desks, near water dispensers, or beside coffee machines, they are easy to grab, making increased consumption more likely, he said.
To avoid eating too many snacks, changing one’s environment can also be effective, he said.
Liu cited a study published in the journal Appetite that found there is a positive correlation between a food item’s proximity and the chances that it would be consumed by an office worker.
The research, which observed Google employees in the company’s New York City office, found that 23 percent of men and 17 percent of women took snacks placed near the water cooler area, he said.
When snacks were placed farther from the water cooler, only 12 percent of men and 13 percent of women consumed the items, Liu said.
Nutritional studies in the US also found that 25 percent of an American’s caloric intake comes from snacks, he said.
From this perspective, the Taiwanese custom of laying snacks on tables during Ghost Month creates a risk of sudden weight gain, Liu said.
More importantly, bingeing on large quantities of snacks often has an adverse effect on metabolism long before increases in body weight can be observed, he said.
Medical literature suggests that healthy men who consumed extra high-calorie snacks for five consecutive days took in about 1,200 additional calories a day on average, he said.
Although their weight did not increase significantly, liver fat rose from 1.55 percent to 2.54 percent, while some areas of the brain also showed changes in their response to insulin, he said.
People should consider leaving snacks in less accessible cupboards and ration Ghost Festival leftovers to avoid causing harm to their health, Liu said.
He recommended eating a proper meal and making sure to get enough protein and fiber before having snacks, which can make it easier to curb cravings and keep blood sugar levels stable.
Liu said snacking occasionally is not necessarily a problem, adding that the real concern is the impact of long-term eating habits.
If weight gain, an expanding waistline, fatty liver or abnormal health checkup results have already emerged, people should look more closely at their diet, body composition and metabolic health to identify the underlying causes, rather than simply resorting to restrictive dieting to lose weight, he said.

====================================================================================================

Doctor warns of poor contact lens care
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
16:38:12 UTC
01:38:12 KST

Contact lens wearers with 3D nail art are warned to take extra care when removing their lenses, as decorative nail embellishments can cause damage to the cornea, a Kaohsiung-based ophthalmologist said.
Hung Chi-ting (洪啟庭) said an office worker who regularly wears contact lenses visited his eye clinic after fragments of a lens became stuck in her eye. The woman attempted to remove the fragments with her fingernail, severe pain.
Her cornea had numerous irregular, tiny and scattered areas of epithelial damage, Hung said, adding that an examination found more than 100 scratches on her cornea resembling claw marks, which Hung said he believed were caused by 3D decorations on her nails.
Photo courtesy of Hung Chi-ting
She also had a large blister and conjunctival swelling, he added.
Doctors eventually retrieved the fragments of the lens, which had become lodged deep in the conjunctival fornix, Hung said.
The woman recovered after treatment, with the corneal injuries and conjunctival swelling resolving, and her corrected vision recovering, he added.
Hung said contact lenses can become brittle after prolonged use. Dry eyes, forceful blinking, rubbing the eyes, improperly sized lenses and activities such as surfing, skateboarding, swimming and diving can also cause lenses to fall out, shift or become folded and difficult to locate.
He said cases of broken contact lenses becoming trapped in the eye have become more common in the past few years. He recommended wearing contact lenses for no more than 10 hours a day and replacing them regularly.
Wearers should also take care when removing lenses to avoid injuring their eyes with nail decorations. If a lens disappears in the eye or cannot be removed, people should seek immediate treatment from an ophthalmologist, he said.
Citing another case, he said one university student forgot to bring his glasses while on a camping trip and wore the same contact lenses continuously for a week. When the trip ended, he developed eye discomfort, but could not remove the lenses.
Doctors found corneal epithelial erosion in both eyes. His vision in the right eye had fallen to just 0.05, leaving him nearly blind in that eye.
Hung said most commonly used contact lenses are soft lenses, primarily hydrogel and silicone hydrogel types. They include daily, biweekly and monthly lenses.
Soft lenses are comfortable and cause less of a foreign-body sensation. Hydrogel lenses have high water content and provide good oxygen permeability, but prolonged use can cause dry eyes. Their hydrophobic areas, static properties and relatively large mesh structure can also make them prone to accumulating debris.
Silicone hydrogel lenses have better oxygen permeability and are suitable for people with dry eyes, but they are more lipophilic, and can accumulate oils and proteins, Hung said.
He said another patient wore contact lenses continuously for four days and nights before developing blurred vision and a stinging sensation on the fifth day. Doctors found a thick layer of white deposits on the inside of the contact lens in his left eye, consisting mainly of proteins, lipids and calcium from tears, as well as airborne debris.
Fortunately, the corneal damage was minor, and the blurred vision and stinging improved within several days, he said.
Hung added that wearing contact lenses is a medical procedure and that improper cleaning or wearing lenses for too long can cause irritation from protein deposits, leading to red eyes and conjunctivitis. In severe cases, it can cause corneal ulcers and inflammation and even impair vision.
He urged contact lens users not to neglect proper care, particularly removing their lenses before going to sleep to reduce the risk of eye damage.

Brahma Chellaney On Taiwan: Taiwan is becoming a harder target for China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
16:38:09 UTC
01:38:09 KST

The Iran and Ukraine wars are rewriting modern military strategy. These conflicts are demonstrating that a less conventionally powerful state, by leveraging asymmetric capabilities, can impose major costs on an aggressor and fundamentally reshape the outcome of conflict. Taiwan is not only drawing lessons from those conflicts, but also translating them into practice.
Far from seeking to match China ship for ship, missile for missile or aircraft for aircraft, Taiwan needs to make Chinese aggression so costly, problematic and uncertain that Beijing is deterred from launching an attack. Taiwan cannot become a bigger wolf than China, but it can ensure that no predator seeks to swallow it without getting badly wounded.
That is the logic driving Taiwan’s long-overdue pivot toward asymmetric capabilities — aerial drones, autonomous attack boats, land-based anti-ship missiles, mobile air defenses and other relatively inexpensive, distributed weapons.
The shift has been accelerated by developments in two very different wars: Ukraine’s growing capability to target energy and other strategic sites deep inside Russia and Iran’s refusal to bend to American coercion, leaving US President Donald Trump struggling for a face-saving way to exit the war he initiated. Both conflicts have shown that, despite sophisticated and expensive weapons remaining important, large numbers of cheap, mobile and expendable systems can impose disproportionate costs on a stronger opponent.
Ukraine has been the more important model for Taipei, given how Kyiv has stalled Russia’s advances on the battlefield by taking the war to the enemy’s heartland. Ukraine has shown that drones can transform the battlefield by providing surveillance, targeting and strike capabilities at a fraction of the cost of conventional aircraft. Taiwan’s defense planners are also studying Iran’s use of drones and missiles to impose regional costs on the US by striking American bases and facilities in the Middle East.
Nothing matters more for Taipei than deterring Chinese aggression.
For Beijing, invading Taiwan would be an exceptionally difficult amphibious operation for several reasons: the Taiwan Strait is about 130 kilometers wide at the narrowest point; weather is favorable for a major crossing only during a few windows each year; Taiwan has relatively few beaches suitable for large-scale amphibious landings; and many of those beach approaches lead into mountainous or urban terrain. Above all, China would have to move enormous quantities of troops, equipment, ammunition and supplies across the Strait while under attack.
That is exactly where Taiwan’s asymmetric strategy can impose significant costs on its foe. To turn the Strait and the approaches to Taiwan’s coastline into a killing zone, land-based anti-ship missiles can attack Chinese vessels while autonomous attack boats can swarm larger naval ships and landing craft. Drones, for their part, can provide constant surveillance and strike targets without putting Taiwanese pilots at risk. Mobile air defenses can frustrate China’s effort to establish air superiority.
In such a scenario, the objective will not be to win a traditional naval battle, but to prevent Beijing from achieving the quick victory on which its invasion strategy would depend.
Taiwan, learning the right lessons from conflicts elsewhere, is already making substantial progress. It is on track to produce more than 1,000 Hsiung Feng II and III anti-ship missiles by this year-end. Its heavy investment in layered air defenses combines expensive Patriot interceptors with much cheaper and more widely distributable Stinger missiles.
What stands out, however, is the scale of Taiwan’s drone-manufacturing goal, which is aimed at creating deterrence against China while also building export leverage abroad. It plans to produce 100,000 drones a month within four and a half years, with roughly half intended for export, while its military is likely to acquire more than 210,000 aerial and sea-based drones.
To plug a potential vulnerability, Taiwan has formed a new “Littoral Combat Command” to help integrate drones, mobile missiles and artillery so that these separate systems become components of a unified coastal-defense architecture. This is a wise step.
Reducing its traditional reliance on imported big-ticket platforms in favor of relatively cheap, distributed asymmetric systems is making Taiwan a harder target for China.
Taiwan, of course, still needs fighter aircraft, submarines, sophisticated air defenses and other high-end capabilities. But big-ticket systems should form the upper layer of a broader defense architecture rather than constitute its foundation. The foundation should be survivability, dispersion and punitive response.
That is especially important because China may choose to begin a war not with an amphibious invasion, but by seeking to isolate and slowly strangle Taiwan.
A blockade or quarantine could be used to disrupt shipping, intimidate commercial traffic, restrict energy supplies and even sever Taiwan’s communications with the outside world. Taiwan’s dependence on subsea cables makes this a particularly acute vulnerability. Without a single Chinese soldier setting foot on Taiwan, a communications blackout could create confusion and panic, disrupting financial markets, government operations, emergency services, logistics, military command-and-control, and the flow of information to the outside world.
Seen in this light, Taiwan’s recent exercise simulating an internet disruption was more than just a civil-defense drill. By deliberately throttling mobile data across parts of the island, Taiwan tested how citizens, businesses and institutions would function if communications were degraded during a crisis.
Such preparations are pivotal to an asymmetric strategy. Overwhelming an invading force with asymmetric capabilities depends on resilient networks so that drones and unmanned attack boats can detect targets, sensors can transmit information, missile batteries can receive targeting data, military commanders can communicate with dispersed units, and civilian authorities can coordinate emergency responses. If China were to sever Taiwan’s communications before the Taiwanese military could respond to an invasion, even an impressive arsenal of drones, missiles, artillery and autonomous attack boats would not be able to repulse aggression.
If resilience is to define national defense, Taiwan needs to invest not only in redundant communications and alternative satellite links, but also in hardened command networks, distributed data centers, backup power, and communications systems that can function when conventional internet access is cut. Taiwanese society should be able to operate under degraded communications conditions for weeks. And even when portions of the communications network are destroyed or jammed, Taiwan’s drones, missiles, sensors and command centers must remain operational.
Taiwan is rightly seeking to leverage its extraordinary technological and manufacturing base to build a defense-industrial ecosystem capable of mass-producing drones, autonomous systems, sensors, communications equipment and other expendable technologies. In fact, Taiwan has already begun to emerge as a significant drone exporter.
The ultimate purpose of the pivot from prestige weapons to asymmetric capabilities is not to prepare Taiwan to fight a war indefinitely. Rather, it is to make Beijing realize that starting a war would be a disastrous gamble.
Making Taiwan too hard to blind, too hard to blockade, too hard to invade and ultimately too painful to conquer would establish enduring deterrence.
Brahma Chellaney, professor emeritus of strategic studies at the independent Center for Policy Research in New Delhi, is the author of nine books, including the award-winning Water: Asia’s New Battleground (Georgetown University Press).

Industrial PC maker Neousys Technology Inc (宸曜科技) expects strong growth in its edge artificial intelligence (AI) business from this year, driven by rising demand across manufacturing, transportation, semiconductors, defense and healthcare.
Edge AI computers account for about 40 percent of its product mix, said Neousys, whose edge AI portfolio includes fanless industrial computers, graphics processing unit (GPU)-enabled AI systems and mission computers designed for harsh environments.
The company expects edge AI-related revenue to grow 10 to 20 percent year-on-year this year, Neousys vice president Bryan Lan (藍林忠) said in an interview with the Taipei Times on Thursday.
Photo: Meryl Kao, Taipei Times
“This year, we’ve seen growing demand for computers with AI computing or expansion capabilities, even for applications that previously required only data collection or human-machine interaction,” he said.
High-performance AI systems are used mainly in autonomous driving and defense applications, but customers are increasingly demanding basic AI inference capabilities even in smaller industrial computers, Lan said.
In view of growing demand for edge AI, Neousys is preparing products based on Intel Corp’s next-generation Nova Lake platform, with a launch possible as early as the first quarter of next year, he said.
The platform’s integrated neural processing unit would allow smaller, task-specific AI models to run at the edge without significantly increasing system costs, he added.
The company’s edge AI products are largely deployed in factory safety control, traffic enforcement and semiconductor optical inspection, Lan said.
At the Taiwan Automation Intelligence and Robot Show in Taipei last week, Neousys and its partners demonstrated its latest factory safety-monitoring system based on Nvidia Corp’s Jetson platform that can detect workers who have entered hazardous areas and issue real-time alerts.
The company is seeing growing demand from the semiconductor sector, with products used in wafer fabrication equipment accounting for about 10 percent of its total revenue, Lan said.
Neoysys counts the world’s two largest foundries among its customers, he added.
“AI data center expansion is also creating new opportunities,” Lan said. “For example, our POC-700 series compact industrial computers are being used by server makers as controllers for coolant distribution units, monitoring temperature, water pressure, and flow in in-rack and in-row systems.”
The company is also expanding into smart manufacturing by tapping into autonomous mobile robot and automated guided vehicle projects, he said.
In Asia, Neousys has participated in outdoor delivery projects using automated guided vehicles and other autonomous vehicles, Lan said.
As markets such as South Korea establish regulations for autonomous delivery vehicles, demand is expected to grow, he said, adding that Neousys is involved in autonomous vehicle applications for law enforcement, suspect tracking and agriculture.
Neousys expects the defense-related business to be a key growth driver over the next two years, as products for the sector carry higher margins, Lan said.
The company supplies products to drone makers and system integrators for uncrewed ground military vehicles, he said.
The defense-related business accounts for about 20 percent of its total revenue and is expected to rise to 25 percent by the end of this year, he added.
Neousys plans to expand into healthcare next year, targeting AI medical imaging, patient monitoring and care applications amid healthcare labor shortages, Lan said.
“We plan to enter the market through image processing, AI computing and rugged edge computing technologies, as healthcare tends to have longer product cycles and is less sensitive to economic fluctuations,” he said.
Neousys reported revenue of NT$1.14 billion (US$35.80 million) in the first half of this year, up 36 percent year-on-year.
The company expects revenue this year to grow 40 percent from NT$1.64 billion last year, and is targeting double-digit revenue growth next year, driven by edge AI, defense, smart manufacturing and demand in the US market, Lan said.

Choking Iran’s economy is the least bad way to end the war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
16:38:05 UTC
01:38:05 KST

Over the years, I’ve witnessed at first-hand countries going literally broke under US economic pressure: Iraq, Venezuela and Cuba. The scenes I saw in Baghdad, Caracas and Havana were all very similar. The national currency became worthless, inflation skyrocketed and unemployment spiraled higher. And yet, US economic sanctions alone failed to force political change.
US President Donald Trump is betting he can break Iran economically and, in the process, achieve the political concessions he wants — all in record time — but historical precedent suggests he is wrong. The Islamic Republic has demonstrated many times before its deep capacity to endure financial suffering, and its pain threshold is likely even higher now that the threat is existential. With Trump and his brother-in-arms, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, running short of options to end the war they started without much of a plan, the route of economic asphyxiation is probably the least bad plan. Needless to say, “least bad” is far from “good.”
What is the alternative? Trump could admit defeat and accept Iran’s terms; he can opt for more bombing, hoping for a miraculously different outcome; or he can put boots on the ground, embarking on the sort of forever Middle Eastern war he promised to avoid.
Put yourself in the shoes of anyone inside the White House, then look dispassionately at the gameboard, and it feels like choking Iran financially is worth a try. Sure, it would have been better if the war had not started, or at least had been planned better, but we are where we are.
Would a financial stranglehold succeed? Maybe. The amount of economic pressure on Iran is, certainly, unprecedented. Yes, Washington has imposed sanctions on Tehran since the Islamic Revolution of 1979, but it had never stopped the country selling its oil completely, as it is doing now, and has never bombed the country so heavily as it did from late February until early April. And Trump does not need the regime to collapse; he just needs sufficient leverage at the negotiating table, hurting Iran enough for Tehran to soften its demands for ending the conflict.
However, to work, Trump needs to outlast Iran economically — and oil is the key. If the White House can keep crude below US$100 a barrel or thereabouts, it has a chance. Right now, West Texas Intermediate, the US oil benchmark, is changing hands at about US$85 a barrel. For that to continue, enough barrels need to keep flowing via the Strait of Hormuz. China needs to help too, by keeping its oil imports well below prewar levels. So far in August, both elements are working in Trump’s favor; however, there is no guarantee, that the situation would persist.
Iran is, undeniably, hurt, but is it “broke” as Trump claims? It surely feels like it. Its economy is on track to see the biggest annual contraction since the nadir of the Iran-Iraq War in the mid-1980s. Inflation is running well above 50 percent, the highest annual rate since records started nearly 70 years ago. Worse, the cost of food and other necessities has already doubled from a year ago. Its currency, the rial, is worthless. In the black market, the exchange rate has collapsed to a record low of about 1.85 million rials to one US dollar; five years ago, about 50,000 rials were enough to buy a greenback.
“This level of economic change must be taken very seriously,” Masoud Nili, a former Iranian government economic adviser, wrote earlier this month in the Donya-e-Eqtesad liberal newspaper.
The US blockade is exacerbating the penury as Iranian oil exports have fallen to virtually zero, leaving the government with little income to pay salaries. Instead, Tehran is printing money, fueling the inflation crisis.
However, the encirclement is not the wall of steel Trump talks about. Geography is a powerful ally of the Islamic Republic. More than 5,500km long and neighboring seven countries — Pakistan, Afghanistan, Turkmenistan, Azerbaijan, Armenia, Turkey and Iraq — the Iranian border significantly exceeds the distance from New York Ciry to Los Angeles, and is too extensive and too porous to be closed completely. Rail links are burgeoning. Via the Caspian Sea, Iran shares a maritime border with Russia and Kazakhstan, too. Moscow has already helped Tehran stay afloat via that route.
Washington plans to apply yet more economic pressure; the United Arab Emirates has already severed its economic and financial links, depriving Iran of a key route to launder its oil proceeds, and Iraq is likely to follow suit.
On Wednesday night, Trump announced on social media what he described as “the MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN AGAINST ANY COUNTRY,” threatening any country that helped Iran with “oil smuggling, swap lines, cash transfers, exchange houses, ship registries, front companies.” Trump appears to be hoping that his threats would be enough to persuade other nations to halt business dealings with Iran, rather than any specific measure.
Tehran knows this war of economic attrition would only get worse.
Earlier this week, Iranian Islamic Consultative Assembly Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the country’s top negotiator, on social media said that while the White House thinks that “squeezing Iran harder” would force concessions, US Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent lacks the competence to succeed.
“Stop waiting for the clown crew to pull a rabbit out of their hat,” he said.
Bravado aside, the regime seems worried — and it should. When Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian met face-to-face with Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei for the first time earlier this month, the encounter focused on people’s livelihoods and employment, as well as “the problems caused by sanctions.”
Iran is a huge country, with about 90 million people who have endured decades of hardship. On a per-capita basis, it is poorer than it was 40 years ago. Unsurprisingly, the population has revolted against its leaders multiple times over the years. The best hope for Trump is that the economic pressure creates fear in Tehran that domestic social unrest is approaching the melting point once again. Hope, though, rarely works as a strategy.

The call for a Ukrainian election is compelling and wrong
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
16:37:57 UTC
01:37:57 KST

Former Ukrainian minister of defense Mykhailo Fedorov is perhaps the standout political figure to have been forged in Ukraine by Russia’s invasion. He is smart, young, so far untouched by any corruption scandal and the force behind two transformations that have proved critical to his nation’s survival: drone warfare and digital government. Even so, his demand this week for wartime presidential elections was reckless and wrong.
Fedorov, whose July 15 sacking as defense minister prompted street protests, dropped a video address on Tuesday night that delivered as powerful an expression of what Ukrainians are fighting for as you could hope to see. It is worth watching what amounts to Fedorov’s nine-minute presidential campaign launch, because he distils what has driven so many Ukrainians to risk all in resisting not just Russian occupation, but also their own kleptocratic leaders when these have threatened the country’s democratic future.
Taken alone, almost every argument Fedorov makes is self-evidently true. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy was elected president in 2019, so his five-year term expired two years ago, and democracy would be served by submitting him to the judgement of voters sooner rather than later. And although the constitution forbids holding a vote under martial law, Fedorov is right that the conflict with Russia could go on for years more, creating unavoidable issues of political accountability.
Illustration: Yusha
Other arguments are just as convincing. For example, that Russia should not be allowed to dictate when Ukraine holds elections, or that Ukrainians are fighting, because they want theirs to remain a free European state. Likewise, that “democracy is not a peacetime luxury,” and that in time of war, corruption and the hiring and firing of critical personnel for reasons of loyalty, rather than merit, are unaffordable.
All of this is true and Zelenskiy has questions to answer on every count. That fact was underscored again on Wednesday morning, when anti-corruption investigators raided the home of his administration’s deputy head, Iryna Mudra. Nevertheless, when Fedorov said the complexities of holding a ballot in wartime could be addressed, or implied that holding elections would defy Moscow, he was misguided and surely knows it.
Perhaps the longstanding logistical hurdles to holding a vote universal and reliable enough to command trust could be overcome. It is possible that with enough preparation, the about 10 million Ukrainians who have been displaced could be given a fail-safe way to vote on the Diia (Action) app that Fedorov developed as minister for digital transformation, a post he held from 2019 until last year. Maybe getting tens of thousands of front-line soldiers to a reliable secret ballot is a problem that could be solved without risking their lives or Ukraine’s defense, too. Maybe.
However, without extensive cooperation from Moscow, it is inconceivable that a safe and meaningful election could be held in areas that are within glide-bomb distance of the front. And now that Russia is firing near-daily barrages across the entirety of Ukraine and Kyiv has run out of interceptors to stop the most powerful ballistic missiles, just the thought of civilians gathering outside polling stations should be enough to end all discussion.
Moreover, holding a wartime vote would not defy Russian President Vladimir Putin. It would answer his prayers. Russia’s leader has been calling for Ukrainian elections for years. His goal is to sow doubts about Zelenskiy’s legitimacy as a negotiating partner, and to divide and destabilize the target of his invasion through the inevitable political polarization that such a vote would bring.
Ukraine cannot afford these distractions. It is about to face the most brutal winter of the war as a result of its lack of missile defenses. Preparing for that challenge must now be the focus of the nation and most Ukrainians understand this. There is no clamor for elections within Ukraine, only in the Kremlin, and among the populist politicians and influencers of the West who like to parrot its propaganda. Moreover, while Fedorov ranks high among Ukrainian politicians in terms of trust, he was added to regular voting-intention polls only last month and still has a distance to go before he could beat Zelenskiy.
All of this could change quickly with peace, after which the popularity of Ukraine’s wartime president is likely to plummet.
That might explain why Zelenskiy has said that, as soon as a ceasefire is in place, he would call a presidential vote to run alongside a referendum on the settlement. This is a self-serving proposal, but abiding by the Ukrainian constitution and waiting for the bombs to stop before attempting a nationwide election is the only sane choice.
Zelenskiy made a mistake when he fired Fedorov. The younger man’s brief six-month tenure at defense was marked by improved battlefield performance, combined with high levels of friction over strategy with top Ukrainian commanders. He was offered a return to government with a vague new portfolio, but the damage was done.
The same wartime imperative that makes Fedorov’s call for elections so wrong also argues for Zelenskiy find a way to bring him back into government, even at defense, putting his own political interests aside despite his rival’s now public presidential ambitions. As long as the country is at war, it would be inexcusable not to.
Fedorov has proved effective, innovative, untainted by scandal and trusted by the public. That combination is rare in Ukraine or, for that matter, anywhere else.
Marc Champion is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Europe, Russia and the Middle East. He was previously Istanbul bureau chief for the Wall Street Journal. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

Nvidia announces AI-related price hikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
16:37:56 UTC
01:37:56 KST

Some of Nvidia Corp’s biggest customers have been told that the prices of servers containing its artificial intelligence (AI) chips are going up more than 15 percent in many cases with memory costs soaring.
The price hikes would go into effect on systems shipped early next year and impact systems including those with the flagship Vera Rubin and Grace Blackwell chips, people familiar with the process said on condition of anonymity.
The increases would depend on the generation of Nvidia chips and the memory configurations, they said.
Photo: Ritchie B. Tongo, EPA
Companies who build the servers under contract for large data center operators such as Microsoft Corp, Alphabet Inc’s Google and Oracle Corp have notified their customers of the forthcoming increases, the people said.
The inability of the industry’s most dominant company to hold the line on prices or absorb rising costs shows how much leverage makers of memory chips — Samsung Electronics Co, SK Hynix Inc and Micron Technology Inc — have amid a surge in demand for AI infrastructure.
Major technology companies including Apple Inc and Qualcomm Inc have said they have been forced to charge more for their products because of chip shortages.
Nvidia’s accelerator processors are the heart of computers that create and run AI software. Their effectiveness depends on how much DRAM they are paired with. The two South Korean companies and Micron account for most of the world’s production of that type of chip. While they have been increasing output, they still have not caught up with surging demand.
Nvidia is one of the most profitable companies in semiconductors. It is able to charge tens of thousands of dollars per chip because supply — from contract manufacturer Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (台積電) — still cannot meet runaway demand.
Nvidia has also raised prices for its gaming-oriented PC graphics cards, Tom’s Hardware reported earlier this month.
How Nvidia’s customers react to the move and whether it would create an opening for its competitors would likely depend on whether they are able to secure enough memory themselves.
Major customers such as Amazon, Microsoft, Google and Meta are all pursuing their own in-house chip programs, but are still dependent on purchases from Nvidia for their data center build-outs. Their ability to push forward with greater independence would also depend on their access to supply from Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron.
The price increases are also likely to add complexity to the industry’s massive AI data center build-out ambitions. Project delays, labor shortages, tightening capital markets and community resistance to developments have already complicated many plans.

Syria 'arrests 70% of Assad-era pilots' involved in bombing
Syrian authorities have arrested around 70 percent of the pilots who took part in bombing civilian areas of the country under the former Assad regime, a transitional justice official has said.
Radif Mustafa, director of the Accountability and Oversight Department at Syria's National Commission for Transitional Justice, said efforts were continuing to pursue those implicated in violations and crimes committed during Assad's rule.
Speaking to Syria's official Al-Ikhbariya television channel, Mustafa said uncovering the truth about crimes involving the use of chemical weapons was a right owed to victims and a responsibility of the National Commission for Transitional Justice.
He said accountability for such crimes represented "a national obligation borne by state institutions".
Mustafa added that reparations and compensation for victims were primarily the responsibility of the government, while stressing the need to build an inclusive national narrative around crimes and violations committed by the former regime that preserves victims' rights.
He said Syria's transitional justice process remained at an early stage and required greater efforts and resources to achieve its goals of uncovering facts, ensuring accountability and providing reparations.
Mustafa's comments came as Syrian Interior Minister Anas Khattab said authorities were continuing to pursue those involved in the chemical weapons massacre in Eastern Ghouta 13 years ago.
Khattab said a number of people who participated in the attack had already been arrested.
In a post on X on Friday, the minister said images of the victims and the suffering of their families remained present in Syrians' memories, stressing that their right to justice remained intact.
He said authorities would continue pursuing the remaining suspects, adding that "no criminal will escape punishment, no matter how much time passes".
Syrian authorities have announced several arrests in recent months linked to the former regime's chemical weapons programme.
On 29 April, the Interior Ministry announced the arrest of Major General Adnan Abboud Halwa, whom Khattab described at the time as one of the most prominent officers accused of involvement in the Eastern Ghouta chemical weapons massacre.
In May, Syria's mission to the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons announced the arrest of 18 people, including former officers and experts from the Scientific Studies and Research Centre, as part of investigations into the former regime's chemical weapons programme.
The Interior Ministry also announced on 15 July the arrest of Colonel Ahmed Habib Ali, saying he was a chemical weapons specialist who had supervised the manufacture of bombs loaded with sarin gas while working for the former regime.

Tunisia says recovered 12 migrants' bodies

Breadcrumb
Tunisia says recovered 12 migrants' bodies
The Tunisian national guard said Sunday it recovered 12 bodies from the sea after a boat carrying irregular migrants capsized off the country's southeastern coast, with six people still missing.
The boat was carrying 15 people, only one of whom was rescued after it sank some 14 nautical miles off the shore of Zarzis on Friday night.
"Search operations resulted in the recovery of three bodies yesterday and nine bodies today, bringing the total to 12," the national guard said in a statement.
Searches for the remaining missing passengers were still ongoing, it added.
On Saturday night, residents in Ben Guerdane - the city bordering Libya where 14 of the migrants were from - staged protests, blocking roads and setting tires on fire.
Tunisia, whose coast is some 145 kilometres (90 miles) from the Italian island of Lampedusa, is a key departure point for migrants seeking to make the perilous journey across the Mediterranean in search of better lives in Europe.
The central Mediterranean crossing is the deadliest migration route in the world, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).
The IOM said earlier this month that the number of migrant deaths on the central Mediterranean route had more than doubled in the first four months of 2026 compared to the same period last year.
At least 914 migrants have died or gone missing along the route this year, according to the IOM.
In 2023, Tunisia signed a 255-million-euro ($290 million) deal with the European Union, nearly half of which was earmarked for tackling irregular migration.
The deal, strongly supported by Italy's hard-right government, aimed to bolster Tunisia's capacity to prevent boats leaving its shore.
(AFP)

====================================================================================================

US envoy Tom Barrack’s Israel criticism tests his credibility as a mediator - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
16:10:55 UTC
01:10:55 KST

A statement Defense Minister Israel Katz put out via X/Twitter was unusual on two counts.
First, it was posted on Shabbat afternoon – something generally done only in emergency or especially unusual situations. Second, it included a frontal critique of an influential US administration figure: Washington’s ambassador to Turkey and special envoy to Syria and Iraq, Tom Barrack.
On Friday, Barrack was hosted on Mario Nawfal’s podcast and, while discussing last Tuesday’s IDF bombing of the Abu al-Duhur airbase in northern Syria, made several remarks that – and this is an understatement – raised eyebrows in Jerusalem.
First, he contradicted US policy and said that Israel was occupying the Golan Heights in contravention of UN resolutions and the “international order.” In 2019, US President Donald Trump issued a presidential proclamation recognizing Israeli sovereignty over the Golan.
Second, he said that Israel’s attack may have been an attempt to “bait” the Turks before the October 27 election, something he said would play well with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s base.
Third, he said that the US checked into intelligence Israel provided showing that Turkey was planning to move troops and equipment into the site and found that it was incorrect.
And, fourth, he said that Turkey, including its president, Recep Tayyip Erdogan, was not interested in “attacking” or in any kind of “adversarial” relationship with Israel. Ironically, this statement came just as Turkey called for Interpol to issue a request to law enforcement agencies worldwide to arrest Netanyahu and a number of other Israeli officials on various charges, including genocide.
Barrack’s version of what happened last Tuesday is pretty significant. It goes beyond the boilerplate complaint that Israel often hears from Washington after carrying out a strike: that it was done without sufficient coordination with the US. Here you have a senior US official publicly disputing Israel’s threat assessment and floating an electoral motive for the attack.
Katz responds to Barrack’s comments
Apparently, Katz thought Barrack’s comments serious enough to warrant a swift response – even on Shabbat.
He wrote that Israel had clear intelligence indicating that Turkey planned to take actions at the site that would endanger Israeli security, and that the IAF attack was taken only after Israel delivered a direct warning to the Syrian regime and provided the necessary intel to the relevant US authorities.
“When the Syrian regime did not heed the warning, the strike was authorized and successfully carried out,” Katz wrote. “Erdogan was caught with his hand in the cookie jar and was forced to back down.”
Katz said that Barrack’s comments were “full of inaccuracies” and that his position on the Golan contradicts Trump’s own policy. He also said that efforts by opposition leaders and some in the media to paint the operation in Syria in “political colors” stem from “a combination of ignorance, a lack of understanding of Israel’s security interests, and a constant desire to attack the government – and it is deserving of every condemnation.”
Though he prefaced that comment by directly addressing it to opposition politicians and media figures, it is difficult to believe – since Barrack made the same speculation – that he was not also included in this group.
The brickbats come at a particularly sensitive time, as Barrack is trying to reduce the temperature between Israel and Turkey. The problem is that with comments such as these – clearly siding with Turkey’s explanation and interpretation of the events, perhaps as a result of his job as ambassador to Turkey – Barrack is harming his ability to play a constructive role.
Barack may have undermined his credibility as a mediator between Syria, Israel
Barrack’s dual role as ambassador to Turkey and special envoy to Syria matters. As ambassador to Turkey, he is responsible for reassuring Ankara; as Syria envoy, he is supposed to mediate a potential Israel-Syria security arrangement. By publicly appearing to credit the Turkish-Syrian account over Israel’s, he may have undermined his standing in Jerusalem as a trusted intermediary.
Barrack, in other words, is now becoming part of the dispute he is meant to manage – hardly the ideal position for a mediator.
By publicly questioning Israel’s intelligence, suggesting an electoral motive behind the strike, whitewashing Erdogan’s antipathy toward Israel, and contradicting Trump on the Golan Heights, Barrack may have reassured Ankara – where he temporarily lives and works – but at the cost of losing Israeli confidence in his ability to play the role of mediator.
Doubts about Barrack’s objectivity predate this particular incident.
Differences between Barrack and Israel surfaced over Lebanon earlier this year, with disagreements about how to deal with Hezbollah and its Iranian patron.
Following the June 26 trilateral Framework Agreement brokered in Washington, Israel expected a policy aimed at isolating Hezbollah, restoring Lebanese sovereignty and keeping Iran out of Lebanon’s political and military future. From Jerusalem’s perspective, all that was essential to secure the northern border.
Barrack, however, argued that no lasting settlement can be reached without involving Hezbollah and Iran. Because Lebanon is caught up in the wider conflict between Israel and Iran, he said, both must be part of any serious effort to resolve it. “How is it going to go away if you don’t have Hezbollah and Iran involved?” he asked, describing Lebanon as a “very complicated Rubik’s cube where removing one piece moves three others.”
Jerusalem viewed that approach as legitimizing Hezbollah and giving Iran a continuing say over Lebanon’s future.
Trusted mediator must understand both parties’ concerns
This does not mean that Barrack must accept Israel’s position on every issue. A mediator is not an advocate for either side. But to be effective, he must convince both sides that he understands their concerns, takes their intelligence seriously, and is not publicly embracing the other side’s version of events.
That is what makes Katz’s unusual Shabbat statement significant. It was more than a rebuttal of a few inaccurate comments. It was a public warning that Israel’s confidence in the man Washington has chosen to manage some of the region’s most delicate disputes is beginning to erode.
Barrack wants to lower the temperature between Israel and Turkey. To do that, however, he will first have to restore a measure of trust with Jerusalem. A mediator whom one side increasingly sees as speaking for the other will have a difficult time mediating anything.

Israel says backchannels to Turkey remain after Syria strike
Unknown

2026-08-23
16:04:53 UTC

Breadcrumb
Israel says 'secret channels' to Turkey remain after Syria strike
An Israeli security official has said Israel has "no intention of turning Turkey into an enemy" despite striking a Syrian airbase over alleged plans by Ankara to deploy radar and air defence systems there.
The official told Israel's Kan Reshet Bet radio on Sunday that "secret channels" remained open between Israel and Turkey to exchange messages and prevent direct conflict, amid heightened tensions following the Israeli attack on Abu al-Duhur military airport in northern Syria.
However, the official warned that "when messages do not work, Israel is forced to act".
According to Kan, Israel has drawn "red lines" around any Turkish military reinforcement in Syria, particularly the deployment of air defence systems, drones or missiles that could restrict the Israeli air force's ability to operate over the country.
Israeli aircraft struck buildings and runways at Abu al-Duhur airport in eastern Idlib province last week "before the Turkish military equipment reached its destination", Kan reported.
The broadcaster said Israel had sought to send a message to Damascus that it "will not allow a new threat to be established near its borders", while stressing that Israel does not oppose the rebuilding of the Syrian army itself.
Turkey denied that it had any military presence at the airbase at the time of the attack.
"There was no Turkish military mission at the Syrian air force base before or during the Israeli attacks," Ankara said in a statement following the strike.
Kan reported on Saturday that Israeli security officials had informed the US that Turkey was preparing to install radar equipment at Abu al-Duhur, with plans for Turkish-operated air defence systems to follow.
Israeli officials claimed such a deployment could alter the regional balance of power by limiting Israel's ability to carry out air operations over Syria.
Abu al-Duhur lies around 70 kilometres from the Turkish border.
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said on Saturday that the military had repeatedly recommended striking the base after receiving what he described as "clear intelligence" about Turkey's plans.
"The army recommended several times carrying out the strike at Abu al-Duhur airport, in light of clear intelligence obtained regarding Turkey's intention to undertake activities there that would endanger the security of the State of Israel," Katz said.
Katz said Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and senior security officials had agreed to warn Damascus before authorising the attack.
"It was agreed that before approval was granted, a direct warning would be sent to the Syrian regime at the highest levels, in an attempt to prevent this move, and that is indeed what happened," he said.
He added that the intelligence had also been shared with Washington.
According to Katz, Damascus failed to act on the warning, prompting Israel to approve the strike.
"Erdogan was caught with his hand in the cookie jar and was forced to back down," Katz said, referring to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
Israeli officials quoted by Ynet said Ankara had been preparing to install radar at the base before deploying air defence systems and a Turkish commando unit to operate them.
The officials said Israel believes Turkey could attempt a similar deployment elsewhere in Syria in the future.
They also claimed that Turkish-operated air defences in Syria could make any future Israeli strike on Iran more difficult by restricting Israeli aircraft operating in Syrian airspace.
Under international law, Israel has no general right to strike Syrian territory or dictate Damascus's foreign and security relationships. Syria's decision to establish military or political ties with Turkey is a matter of its sovereignty and self-determination, subject to its own international obligations.
The attack comes amid renewed tensions between Israel and Syria despite recent efforts to reach a security arrangement between the two countries.
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa said last month that Damascus wanted an agreement with Israel that could "pave the way for a comprehensive peace", while insisting Syria would not abandon its claim to the occupied Golan Heights, which is considered illegally occupied and annexed under international law.
Israel also carried out another strike in Syria on Saturday, targeting a vehicle in the town of Beit Jinn in the Damascus countryside.
The Israeli military said it had fired on a person who posed "an immediate threat" to its forces and threatened further attacks against perceived threats.
Reserve Israeli officer Eyal Dror told Ynet that recent developments suggested relations with Syria were moving away from stability.
"In the absence of an attempt to reach some kind of arrangement or settlement, we may see these events with greater frequency," Dror said.
