Feature: When a Chinese mythic world travels without translation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
19:01:53 CST
20:01:53 KST

Chen Aijun works in an optical shop in Chengdu, southwest China's Sichuan Province, Aug. 14, 2026. (Xinhua/Lu Youyi)
CHENGDU, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- The video came with almost no instructions.
There was no narration explaining the mythology behind palaces rising above an ocean of clouds in the video, nor subtitles identifying the heavenly gates, cranes or tiny figures moving beneath them.
Yet viewers outside China quickly began naming the world for themselves.
Some called it "paradise." Others saw a "Celestial Palace" or an "Immortal Realm" familiar from Chinese fantasy games and television dramas. One user wrote, "Waiting on Wukong to show up," invoking the Monkey King from the Chinese literary classic "Journey to the West," or the hit game "Black Myth: Wukong."
The interpretations differed, but viewers did not seem to need the same cultural knowledge to enter the conversation.
Earlier this month, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning shared the 33-second AI-generated video on social media with a question: "What does the Chinese heaven look like?"
It opened up a hermeneutic discussion, with responses overseas suggesting a cultural image does not necessarily need to elicit exactly the same interpretation for everyone in order for it to be viewed meaningfully.
"The right to interpret ultimately lies with the audience," said Zhang Zheng, deputy dean of Tsinghua University's School of Journalism and Communication.
People encountering unfamiliar cultures inevitably draw on what they already know, Zhang said. Rather than fully grasping every cultural reference, what matters is whether audiences can encounter the work, understand it and respond to it emotionally.
Before strangers abroad could interpret this particular world, however, it first had to get out of one man's head.
Chen Aijun, 34, is an optometrist in Chengdu, capital of southwest China's Sichuan Province.
By day, Chen leads a quiet, down-to-earth life in a neighborhood optical shop. Inside, he worked among eyeglass frames and optometry equipment. On his computer was another landscape entirely: cloud seas, immense palaces, flying cranes and figures in ancient robes.
Chen's heaven did not come from any single ancient text.
Growing up in the 1990s, he watched "Journey to the West" and later encountered "The Investiture of the Gods," xianxia (immortal heroes) novels and fantasy games. Those stories mixed over time with images of Chinese architecture and landscapes he saw online.
He has never visited nearby Mount Emei, and most of what he knows of Mount Huangshan's famous sea of clouds comes from videos.
What appeared on his screen was therefore not a reconstruction of one fixed mythological scene, but a world shaped by traditional stories already filtered through television, novels, games, the internet and his own memory.
For years, Chen had no way to make that world visible.
He never studied painting, design, photography or 3D modeling. After high school, he joined his parents' optical business and eventually took over the shop.
Generative AI changed the gap between imagining an image and possessing the technical skills to show it to someone else.
More than a year ago, Chen began teaching himself through free online tutorials. In September 2025, he started regularly posting AI videos, and a month later began experimenting with palaces floating above clouds. He has since published more than 200 videos.
The process, however, involves far more than entering a few prompts. The technology lowered the technical threshold, but it did not make the choices for him.
When creating Nantianmen, the mythical heavenly gate, Chen first defines the spatial rhythm and tonal hierarchy, pairing towering architecture and cloud seas with deliberately miniature figures to amplify the celestial realm's grand scale.
If the result does not match the picture in his mind, he tries again. He often generates over 1,000 images a day, revising a single scene repeatedly before moving on to animation, editing, color grading and music.
The machine can generate a thousand possible heavens. Chen still has to decide which one is his.
"AI-produced images can be soulless, and it takes human inspiration and aesthetic sensibility to endow works with warmth and vitality," he said.
Zhang believes Chen's experience reflects a broader shift brought about by generative AI. He said AI is giving people without conventional artistic training access to forms of expression that once required specialized skills. But what they create still depends on what they bring to the tool.
"A person's existing knowledge inevitably shapes how they use AI," Zhang said.
Chen brought his memories to the machine. Viewers abroad, in turn, brought theirs to the image.
"Everyone brings their own associations to these scenes," he said.
If his imagined world had to be reduced to three elements, he would keep clouds, architecture and people. The first two should feel immense, he said, while the last should remain small.
The details are culturally specific, but the visual effect is more immediate: tiny human figures dwarfed by vast clouds and monumental architecture. The responses suggest that viewers did not need to understand every cultural reference to find a way into the image.
Chen has no overseas social media accounts and learned that the video was attracting attention abroad only when friends sent him screenshots.
His life at the optical shop has changed little. He still checks eyesight and fits glasses when customers come in, then returns to his computer when the shop grows quiet.
He now hopes to make longer AI videos with fuller stories. He also wants to visit Mount Emei and, one day, Mount Huangshan.
For years, images of distant mountains and clouds reached Chen through screens. His imagined landscapes later traveled through screens to people he had never met.
Now he wants to see the real mountains and clouds for himself. ■
Chen Aijun makes AI videos in an optical shop in Chengdu, southwest China's Sichuan Province, Aug. 14, 2026. (Xinhua/Lu Youyi)

Divorcing devices: how digital detox helps Hongkongers ‘carve out moments’

He has also switched his phone to greyscale to make it less appealing and checks his emails in batches rather than as they arrive. He stops checking them at 8.30pm each day.

Explainer: Why the latest round of Canada-U.S. trade talks collapsed?
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
19:01:22 CST
20:01:22 KST

OTTAWA, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- Canada will impose "dollar-for-dollar" tariffs on about 20 billion U.S. dollars' worth of American goods from Sept. 8 in retaliation for Washington's latest duties, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Saturday.
The 50-percent U.S. tariffs, covering an equivalent value of Canadian goods, took effect just after midnight Saturday following the collapse of trade talks on Friday, further straining relations between the longtime allies.
LAST-MINUTE BREAKDOWN
Carney said he suspended the talks because Washington introduced last-minute changes that were "unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal," even though the two sides had appeared close to a mutually beneficial agreement earlier in the week.
U.S. President Donald Trump signed three proclamations on July 20 to impose additional 50-percent tariffs on certain goods from Canada, citing Ottawa's "discriminatory treatment of American products."
On Tuesday, Trump announced a three-day pause of the tariffs, which were scheduled to take effect on Wednesday, saying the two sides had reached a deal pending the finalization of formal documents.
Carney said on Saturday that Canada had been prepared to remove its remaining retaliatory tariffs on U.S. steel, aluminum and automobiles if Washington substantially reduced its corresponding duties, and was also willing to encourage Canadian provinces to return U.S. alcoholic beverages to store shelves.
"They asked too much and offered too little," he said.
According to Carney, the U.S. proposals restricted Canada's ability to pursue trade arrangements with other countries, and undermined its protections for the French language, culture and national sovereignty. He did not disclose the details of those demands.
Washington, however, blamed the breakdown largely on late demands from Canada, with U.S. tariff rates on heavy-duty trucks emerging as a key sticking point, Politico reported, citing people familiar with the talks.
"They've always had the best deal, and they still would have an even better deal, but they didn't want that," U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told Fox News, adding that no further trade talks are scheduled with Canada.
A UNITED RESPONSE
In his televised address, Carney announced retaliatory tariffs targeting U.S. steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics, and promised to release the details in the coming days.
"You're at war when you're attacked, and we got attacked," Carney said when asked whether Canada was in a trade war with the United States.
Carney's tough position has drawn broad support across party and provincial lines.
Pierre Poilievre, leader of the main opposition Conservative Party, called on Canadians to stay united against "unfair attacks."
"Canada cannot accept one-sided tariffs that will deindustrialize our country. Nor can we accept a bad deal," he said.
Several provincial premiers also backed Carney's decision.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford said the prime minister had his "full support" for a strong response "tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar," urging provincial leaders to remain united as "Team Canada."
British Columbia Premier David Eby noted that U.S. demands that Canada cut or reduce its trade with other countries would turn it into "the economic equivalent of the 51st state," which he described as "never acceptable" to Canadians.
Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said in a statement that while the U.S. tariffs will hurt, Carney made the right decision to reject an "unfair and unreliable" deal.
A recent Leger poll found that 56 percent of Canadians wanted the government to take a hard line and make no further concessions in talks with the United States, and more than 70 percent supported stronger retaliatory trade measures.
A BROADER SHIFT IN ECONOMIC TIES
In his address, Carney argued that the decades-long expansion of economic integration between Canada and the United States was over.
He accused Washington of using economic integration as a weapon.
"We have recognized from the beginning that America has changed, and that we will not return to our old relationship," Carney said.
He also criticized the shifting U.S. justifications for tariffs, ranging from fentanyl and a television advertisement quoting former U.S. President Ronald Reagan to bridge tolls and wildfire smoke, as lacking seriousness and severely damaging foundational trust.
Since taking office in 2025, Carney's government has accelerated efforts to reduce Canada's economic dependence on the United States and diversify its trade relationships.
Ottawa has sought to expand trade with markets in Europe and Asia, develop ports and energy corridors, remove internal trade barriers and double Canadian exports to non-U.S. markets over the next decade, Carney said in his address.
The collapse of talks has also added uncertainty to the future of the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement. The pact remains in force, but the latest U.S. tariffs apply even to Canadian goods that comply with its rules, unlike many earlier U.S. duties.
The scope for a rapid shift, however, remains limited. The United States still accounts for roughly three-quarters of Canada's merchandise exports, while cross-border supply chains in sectors such as automobiles and energy remain deeply integrated.
Meanwhile, Carney underscored the importance of Canadian energy to the United States, noting that Canada supplies 99 percent of U.S. natural gas imports, 85 percent of its electricity imports and 60 percent of its crude oil imports.
"I don't think they want us to stop sending it," he said. ■

Israel’s war on Gaza forces Palestinians to rely on ‘Stone Age’ toilets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
11:00:18 UTC
20:00:18 KST

Israel’s war on Gaza forces Palestinians to rely on ‘Stone Age’ toilets
Deir Al-Balah, Gaza – Eman Mahmoud Shamia has been uprooted several times since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023, before finally settling into a new home – a tent in a camp.
It provides rudimentary shelter for 33-year-old Eman, her husband, Yahya Shamia, 50, and their five children, all under 11, but it lacks many of the basic amenities her old home provided.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Israeli army and settlers injure several Palestinians across West Bank
- list 2 of 4Israeli forces kill Palestinian boy in West Bank as EU condemns E1 plan
- list 3 of 4Where water conflicts pose the biggest threat in 2026
- list 4 of 4Israel kills 3 in Gaza as Netanyahu threatens attacks over kite launches
With the help of a worker who specialised in digging soakaway underground drainage pits, the community in the camp built a “municipal toilet”. It provides relief but Shamia said it reminds her of the Stone Age.
There is little in the way of privacy, particularly for women and children, and for some it is difficult to use or access, particularly for her husband, who suffers from an advanced stage of lung cancer.
“I am deprived of my basic right to have a proper toilet seat in my tent. This is exhausting for me as a woman and a mother of five children and my husband is sick and unable to use the makeshift toilet. What is happening to us is madness,” Shamia told Al Jazeera.
“I cannot believe this is our situation. Sometimes I feel like I am going crazy. How did the toilet become like this and how did the door become just a piece of cloth?”
While hundreds of thousands have lost their homes in Gaza, often overlooked are the daily struggles the displaced face in maintaining some level of dignity in their tent towns. The primitive communal toilets they often rely on are an example.
The ongoing Israeli siege has seen the price of sanitation supplies shoot up with a used toilet seat now costing between 1,500 ($503) and 2,000 shekels ($671).
Due to unaffordable prices, Palestinians are making their own primitive toilets by cutting holes into plastic chairs with a layer of sand underneath.
Mohammad Al-Hanouti, 30, from Al-Bureij refugee camp, has an unstable income from his small streetside stall and lives in an unfinished apartment without proper plumbing. What little he earns, he puts towards a toilet.
“I will live without tiles, without a kitchen and without a proper toilet… I have been saving to buy a toilet seat because it is the most important thing in the apartment. Honestly, I am in trouble – getting the basic necessities will cost me around $2,000,” he told Al Jazeera.
“The crisis over toilet seats needs to be addressed urgently. I am not the only one suffering from this; I have friends in the tents who are also struggling.”
He said proper toilet access is a “most basic right” and called on international organisations to import toilets and distribute them in Gaza to those in need for free.
Economist Omar Salouha said the toilet crisis is the result of a “severe supply shock” caused by restrictions on importing toilets, sanitation supplies and plumbing materials.
With more than nine in ten Palestinians in Gaza displaced and over 90 percent of homes damaged or destroyed during the war, there has been a massive increase in demand for toilet products.
“The huge imbalance between supply and demand has caused the prices of used toilets to increase several times over and created a market suffering from scarcity and distortion,” Salouha says.
Some Palestinians are using the rubble of their destroyed homes to make toilets, but Omar says that is not a low-cost option, with seats becoming “a monopoly commodity”.
This means that communal toilets are the only option for most in Gaza, with a single toilet being used by 20 or 25 people.
“There are usually no separate facilities for men and women… [making toilet access in Gaza] a daily necessity linked to health, privacy and dignity”, said Omar.
These facilities often lack proper sinks and taps, so residents use water hoses or barrels of water. Hand sanitiser and toilet paper have become “luxuries”, he added.
In some areas of Gaza, water is only available once a week and many of the camps lack integrated sewage networks, forcing residents to dig pits next to communal toilets to dispose of wastewater.
Hossam Al-Huwaity, spokesperson for the Chamber of Commerce, said it is encouraging traders to submit formal import requests to bring in essential sanitation supplies to help cope with the crisis.
The chamber has also called on UNICEF, the World Food Programme, OCHA, the European Union and Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) organisations to help. But, the main obstacle remains the Israeli blockade on Gaza, he said.
“Most commercial requests and appeals remain stuck due to unjustified restrictions and delays at the crossings,” Al-Huwaity added.
A WASH assessment by the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) found that only half of people surveyed in Gaza had access to basic sanitation. Around 60% were exposed to wastewater or human waste within 10 metres of where they lived, contributing to the spread of diseases.
Dr Ahmed Al-Jedi, an emergency department physician at Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital in Deir al-Balah, said large numbers of children, women and older people are arriving at the emergency department with recurring cases of diarrhoea, skin diseases or gastrointestinal problems.
“Many of these cases are linked to the difficult living conditions inside the tents, where there are not enough facilities for bathing and personal hygiene, and some families may only be able to bathe once a week,” he said.
“Children spend long hours outside the tents because of the heat, playing in the sand, while the same limited space is used for eating, drinking and sleeping, and in some cases toilets are located very close to living areas.”

Unpredictable work schedules increase the risk of romantic breakups, new study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
11:00:17 UTC
20:00:17 KST

Unpredictable and erratic work schedules may take a heavy toll on romantic relationships, according to new research published in the Journal of Marriage and Family. The findings suggest that hourly service workers who deal with unstable work hours are at a higher risk of going through a separation or divorce. The study highlights how the stressful demands of modern low-wage jobs can spill over into personal lives and disrupt family stability.
Past research exploring the link between economic hardship and relationship stability has largely focused on wages and employment status. Financial milestones are often seen as a prerequisite for marriage, and job loss is a well-known stressor that strains family dynamics. Earning a steady income tends to provide a foundation for harmonious domestic life.
Less attention has been given to the actual day-to-day scheduling conditions of a person’s job. Job attributes like schedule control and shift predictability have profound effects on the rhythm of daily life. When a person cannot predict their work hours, they may find it difficult to coordinate childcare, manage household duties, or simply spend quality time with a partner.
Unpredictable schedules can lead to negative work-to-family spillover, where the time and energy demanded by a job interfere with family responsibilities. Psychological stress from work can cross over to a partner, potentially reducing positive social behaviors and emotional support within the relationship. The authors of the current study wanted to test whether this specific type of precarious work is associated with an increased risk of relationship dissolution.
“The topic of my recent article, Predictably Unstable, weaves together two of my longstanding interests,” said Kristen Harknett, a professor of sociology at the University of California, Berkeley. “Lately, my research with The Shift Project has focused on the many ways that unpredictable and unstable work schedules affect workers and their families. In my earlier research, I was interested in how economic conditions affect family structure. This paper unites these two interests by asking whether routine instability in work schedules disrupts marital and cohabiting relationships.”
To explore this dynamic, the scientists analyzed longitudinal survey data from 6,918 hourly service-sector workers in the United States. The data were collected between 2019 and 2024 as part of The Shift Project. The sample included employees at large retail and food service companies who were either married or living with a romantic partner at the time of their first survey.
The researchers followed up with these workers an average of nine months later to record if their relationships were still intact. The main predictor in the study was a measure of schedule instability based on five specific conditions in the month prior to the survey. These conditions included being placed on-call, having shifts canceled, experiencing last-minute timing changes, and receiving less than two weeks of advance notice for a work schedule.
The fifth condition was working “clopening” shifts. A clopening shift happens when an employee works a closing shift late at night and then returns for an opening shift early the next morning. The authors counted how many of these five unstable scheduling practices each worker experienced, creating a score ranging from zero to five.
The researchers then compared this schedule instability score to the likelihood of the worker separating from their partner by the follow-up survey. The statistical models controlled for various demographic and economic factors. These controls included the worker’s age, parental status, race, education level, hourly wage, and whether their partner was employed.
The findings indicate a consistent link between erratic schedules and relationship breakdowns. Among married workers with completely stable schedules, 94 percent of their marriages were still intact at the follow-up survey. In contrast, for married workers who experienced four or five types of schedule instability, the rate of intact marriages dropped to 82 percent. This represents an absolute decrease of 12 percentage points in marital stability associated with severe schedule unpredictability.
A similar pattern emerged for couples who were cohabiting, meaning they were living together but not married. For these workers, 87 percent of relationships remained intact when schedules were completely stable. When workers faced four or five types of schedule instability, the rate of intact cohabiting relationships fell to 75 percent.
Harknett summarized the core finding simply. “When work schedules are assigned and changed on short notice, married and cohabiting couples are more likely to break up,” she told PsyPost.
The study also provides evidence that cohabiting relationships might be more sensitive to moderate levels of schedule unpredictability than marriages. Married couples mostly saw an increased risk of divorce only when they faced the highest levels of schedule instability. Cohabiting relationships began to show a heightened risk of separation even at moderate levels of instability, such as experiencing just three types of unpredictable schedule conditions.
To account for the possibility that certain personal traits cause both unstable schedules and unstable relationships, the researchers created a predicted schedule instability measure. This measure estimated the typical schedule unpredictability a worker should expect based purely on their employer, job tenure, age, and education. This predicted measure also correlated with marital dissolution, suggesting that the job conditions themselves, rather than unmeasured personal traits, are driving the relationship stress.
The scientists also looked at whether the association between work schedules and relationship dissolution varied by gender. For cohabiting couples, the association was roughly the same for both men and women. For married couples, men’s schedule instability was tied to a higher risk of divorce than women’s schedule instability.
Specifically, men with the most unstable work schedules were 12 percentage points less likely to still be married at the follow-up compared to men with stable schedules. Women with the most unstable schedules were only 4 percentage points less likely to remain married compared to women with stable schedules. Unpredictable work conditions for men might violate traditional breadwinner expectations, creating unique friction in marriages.
The study relies on survey data from only one partner in each relationship. Lacking information on the work schedule of the second partner leaves an incomplete picture of the household’s overall economic and scheduling stress. The dynamic interplay between two partners’ daily schedules remains unmeasured, meaning the study cannot account for how couples might navigate overlapping erratic shifts.
The research design did not capture the total length of the couples’ relationships at the start of the study. A very new relationship might react to schedule instability differently than a marriage that has lasted for many years. Without baseline relationship duration data, the findings cannot determine if established couples are more resilient to scheduling stress than newly formed couples.
The sample consisted of workers recruited through social media advertisements rather than a randomized national sample. This recruitment method might underrepresent certain demographics, such as individuals without internet access or undocumented workers.
“The study focuses on workers paid by the hour in the retail and food service sector in the United States,” Harknett noted. “These workers have little input into their schedules and limited financial resources.”
Future research could aim to recruit a broader representative sample to see if these associations hold true across a wider variety of employment contracts and industries. “My hope is that this study will inspire others to pursue a research agenda revealing how erratic work schedules affect relationships and family life,” Harknett said.
The study, “Predictably Unstable?: Precarious Work and Precarious Relationships in the U.S.,” was authored by Kristen Harknett, Kevin Bruey, and Elizabeth Kuhlman.

Transistors Changed Everything. Here’s How They Work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Last week I revealed the sneaky physics behind the “joule thief,” an electrical circuit that lets you squeeze more energy out of seemingly dead batteries. The key, it turned out, was a clever pairing of a transformer and a transistor. But the transistor deserves its own headline, because it's maybe only the most important invention of the 20th century.
Life would be completely different without transistors. For starters, there would be no personal computers or cell phones, so no Amazon, no video games, no dating apps, no messaging, no streaming, no social media, no Apple Pay or Google Maps, and no AI (hmm). Cars contain billions of transistors. They're really everywhere. So what is a transistor?
The best way to understand this pivotal technology is to follow the evolutionary trail, all the way back to the electric relays used in telegraphs in the 1800s.
Electric Relays
Telegraph lines were basically long electrical circuits. And you probably never thought about it before, but they ran on batteries—primitive, low-voltage batteries that filled an entire closet at the telegraph station—because there was no electrical grid back then.
The electric relay, invented in 1835, was a key component in these systems. Basically, it was a switch that turned an electrical current on and off—sort of like the wall switch that you use to turn a light on. But lacking fingers, the relay used a second electric current to flip the switch. Why would you use a current to turn on a current? That's a good question.
Suppose you wanted to turn on a light in another town 50 miles away. Well, you’d string real long wires on utility poles. Then you could toggle the light on and off, and even use a code with dots and dashes to send text messages. But there was a problem: The longer the wire, the more resistance it had, so not enough current would get through to deliver an intelligible signal.
The solution? Split the circuit into two 25-mile lengths and connect them with a relay. When you closed the switch on the first circuit, it operated the relay, sending the same pattern of current from a second battery through the next circuit and turning on the light. Here's a diagram:
Of course, the telegraph used a buzzer instead of a light, but same idea. Anyway, relays are still widely used today, and the idea of using a current to turn on another current opened up all kinds of possibilities. In cars, for example, it lets you use low-power dashboard controls to switch on high-power circuits that operate things like starters, headlights, or air conditioners.
How does the relay work? Basically, it's just an electromagnet. Here's a simple diagram, along with a real-life example:
Inside there’s a coil of wire wrapped around an iron core. When a current flows through this control wire, it creates a magnetic field. This pulls down the metal switch on top, which contacts the output wire. You've heard relays. When your oven’s thermostat turns the heating element on and off, it’s what makes that audible click.
Although relays are cool and useful, they are basic on/off switches. We have something else that’s sort of like a variable relay—the vacuum tube, invented around 1905, which made possible old-time radios.
Vacuum Tube
You can think of a vacuum tube as a modified light bulb. An incandescent light is just a thin wire that gets super hot when current runs through it, so that it glows. That filament is put inside a glass container, and the air is pumped out so the filament doesn't burn. (That's the whole purpose of the bulb—to keep out oxygen.)
But there's something else that happens, which you can't see: When the filament gets super hot, electrons are ejected from it. Since a flow of electrons is an electric current, you can use these thermal electrons in a way that's similar to a relay. Here's a diagram of a rudimentary vacuum tube:
Electrons travel across the bulb to a collector plate, which creates the output current. Now, it might seem like a silly way to do that. But if we add another wire (a grid) between the filament and the collector, we can control this output current. A negative voltage on the control will push the electrons back away from the collector to reduce the output current. Putting a positive voltage on the grid increases the flow of output current.
So this is again a current switch, and just like the relay, it's controlled by a different wire. But there are two big differences: First, there's no mechanical contact, which means the output current can change much faster. Second, the output current is not just on or off; it can vary with the strength of the control voltage.
This is what made the first audio amplifiers possible. If you had a weak signal from a distant radio station, it would not produce enough current to drive a speaker so that you could hear anything. But if you fed that signal into the control voltage in a vacuum tube, you could get an output that's much stronger yet maintains the same pattern (like music) as the original signal.
But wait! There's something else you could do with vacuum tubes—you could build a computer. Yes, early computers were just a bunch of vacuum tubes controlled by other vacuum tubes, creating logic gates. You used an input signal that is either 1 volt or 0 volts. An AND gate had two signal inputs and one output. If both inputs are 1 volt, it output 1 volt. Otherwise it gave 0 volts. An OR gate would output 1 volt if either of the inputs was 1 volt.
Actually, you could have built a computer with electric relays. But relays are much slower than vacuum tubes, and all that clicking and clacking would have been maddening. Vacuum tubes were silent, purely electronic components, with no moving parts, and that was a game changer.
Transistor
Still, there were three problems with vacuum tubes. They used a lot of power, so early computers ran hot, required massive cooling systems, and were insanely expensive to operate. Second, the tubes were fragile and easily burned out, so the computers required constant maintenance. (Literally, like full-time crews that spent their days locating and replacing dead tubes.) Finally, the tubes were just big. Those early computers, like ENIAC in 1945, filled entire rooms.
The transistor, invented at Bell Labs in 1947, fixed all that by using semiconductors. That's a word you hear all the time, but what is a semiconductor? Well, you know how some materials (like copper) conduct electricity, while others (like rubber) are insulators? Well, a semiconductor (like silicon) can switch between being one or the other.
There are two types of semiconductor: If you add extra electrons to silicon, you get an n-type semiconductor; take away electrons and you get a p-type. Electrons, of course, have negative charges, so the missing electrons act like positive charges, and we call those “electron holes.”
A transistor is created by combining different types of semiconductors. Here’s an example called an NPN transistor:
The two n-type semiconductors are separated by a p-type. This prevents electrons from moving from the input region (the “source”) to the output region (the “drain”). However, if a voltage is applied to the control, or gate, then electrons can move to the output. Yes, once again, it's basically a switch, where one current turns on a second current—but now with much finer control.
Best of all, they could be miniaturized—and boy oh boy oh boy, were they ever. Floor-standing radio consoles were replaced by “transistor radios,” carried everywhere by teens in the 1950s and ’60s. They contained six to 10 transistors. Today, the iPhone 17 Pro contains up to 30 billion transistors. That is crazy, but it's what makes our computer-based world run.

In a filing ahead of Friday’s decision, the state asked the court to exempt funding needed for the rabbinical courts, warning that the freeze would begin affecting their computer and support systems starting Sunday.
Religious Services Ministry director-general Yehuda Avidan then told the court that the problem extended beyond the rabbinical courts. He said the frozen transfer was also needed for salaries, supplier payments, security and cleaning at holy sites, insurance, rent, and outsourced computer services.
Avidan warned that without the money, the ministry would have to begin closing 125 holy sites, including Mount Meron, Rachel’s Tomb, and the Cave of the Patriarchs, and would struggle to pay suppliers and maintain computer systems.
He also said the ministry could not meaningfully separate the urgent components of the transfer because it had already shifted funds internally in recent months while waiting for the additional budget.
The court ultimately exempted the entire Religious Services Ministry transfer rather than only the funding connected to the rabbinical courts, although the petitioners maintain that the legality of the broader transfer still needs to be examined.
The decision followed a dispute over whether some of the frozen funds should be released before the court rules on the petition itself.
At a hearing on Tuesday, the High Court instructed the Finance Ministry to identify sufficiently urgent funding that could be released in the interim.
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich opposed dividing the transfers according to urgency. In the state’s subsequent filing, the ministry said that it considered all of the August 4 transfers important for implementing government decisions and providing public services and argued that the court should instead decide the petition as quickly as possible.
The ministry also warned that if the freeze remained in place after September 1, it could begin affecting the work of some bodies intended to receive the funds.
On Sunday, the petitioners themselves asked the court to narrow the freeze further, seeking the release of several other transfers they said were urgent while keeping disputed coalition funding blocked.
Their request included funding connected to rehabilitation and security needs in northern and southern communities, as well as some Education Ministry payments to local authorities. They asked the court to leave the freeze in place on other education and National Missions Ministry funding that they argue is political or coalition spending.
The Knesset and Finance Ministry were asked to file their responses on Monday.
The dispute began after the Finance Committee met on August 4 during the Knesset election recess. Lazimi and Hiddush argue that another committee session required approval from the coalition-opposition Agreements Committee, which they say was not given.
Justice Alex Stein initially declined to stop the meeting before it took place. After the committee approved the transfers, however, he issued a temporary order on August 5 blocking their implementation, except for civil emergency expenditures.
The Knesset disputes the petitioners’ interpretation. It has argued that Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana had authority under parliamentary rules to approve the meeting and that similar approvals have been given during previous election recesses.
The Finance Ministry has separately argued that the budget requests stemmed from government decisions adopted before the election recess and that advancing the coalition funding they contained did not violate the rules requiring government restraint during an election period.
The High Court has not yet either accepted or rejected those arguments. For now, the Religious Services Ministry can use the additional funding, while the substantially larger dispute over the remaining transfers awaits a ruling.

Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Pakistan invited Iran to join newly-established Mecca defense pact - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
10:56:37 UTC
19:56:37 KST

Iran has been invited to join the Mecca Agreement for Mutual Defense, the new security alliance established by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan earlier this month, Al Mayadeen reported on Saturday, citing a senior Iranian official.
The invitation has not yet been officially confirmed by Iran's Foreign Ministry or by any of the three countries that are parties to the agreement.
Mehdi Rahimi, head of the Iranian parliament's Khaneh Mellat news agency, told the channel that "Iran has received an invitation to join the Mecca Agreement, and the matter is under review."
Rahimi added that countries in the region "are moving toward seeking a regional security umbrella," and claimed that this represented "a victory for Iran, because it has been calling for this for a long time."
The Mecca Agreement was signed on August 7 by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.
The agreement establishes a principle of mutual defense under which an attack on any one of the three countries would be considered an attack on all of them. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan compared the mechanism to Article 5 of the NATO treaty, but stressed that the agreement was not directed against Iran or any specific country.
The member states have already begun developing mechanisms for diplomatic and military coordination, including meetings among foreign and defense ministers and military commanders, joint exercises, and cooperation between their defense industries.
Alliance could expand to include more countries
Turkey has said the alliance could expand to include additional countries. Egypt has been publicly mentioned as a possible candidate for membership.
Iran has so far responded to the agreement with cautious approval. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said on August 10 that Tehran had "no reason for concern" over the establishment of the alliance.
According to Baghaei, the move reflects growing recognition among countries in the region of the need to build regional security mechanisms.
If the claim that Iran was invited is officially confirmed, Iranian membership would significantly alter the character of the alliance, which was established by three countries with close security ties to the West, and would turn it into a substantially broader regional framework.

Syria’s foreign minister says door open for diplomacy with Israel
Asaad al-Shaibani urges Israel to seize ‘historic opportunity’ for diplomacy.
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani says the door for diplomacy with Israel is open, urging it to seize a “historic opportunity”.
In an interview with the Reuters news agency, published on Sunday, al-Shaibani said he expects the talks over a security deal that would lead to Israel’s withdrawal from Syrian territory to resume soon.
Recommended Stories

He said negotiations over the security agreement were frozen at the start of the US-Israel war on Iran and that no date has been set for a resumption of talks.
Al-Shaibani also stressed that Damascus’s priority is to halt Israeli attacks, saying confidence-building steps were needed in this direction.
The United States has been trying to broker a security deal between Israel and the government of Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, a new US ally in the Middle East, for more than a year. But an agreement has proven elusive as Israel has sent troops into Syrian territory and attacked government assets, citing threats to its security.
“We believe there should be contact, especially with a party that constantly threatens the security of Syria. But if this contact doesn’t bring results, then we don’t need it,” al-Shaibani said. “We do not trust Israel currently.”
The Israeli prime minister’s office did not respond to a request for comment.
Al-Sharaa has said Syria poses no threat to other countries and that it is instead focused on rebuilding after 14 years of civil war.
Israeli officials have talked about a range of potential dangers in Syria, with several last year criticising the new government, even as al-Sharaa worked to strengthen ties with Washington.
In the days after the ouster of President Bashar al-Assad in 2024, Israel seized territory in southwest Syria, citing the need to safeguard its citizens against attack, and bombed dozens of Syrian military sites.
“Israel has tried to maintain its security through brute force, and it hasn’t succeeded” anywhere, al-Shaibani said. “I believe negotiations will resume soon.”
He said the US is pressuring Israel to return to the dialogue table.
Asked how optimistic he was that talks would resume, al-Shaibani said: “It’s very hard to bet on Israel.” But Syria had “very great hope” of building stable relationships with its neighbours.
“Syria is extending its hand for understandings, for peace, for diplomacy” and regional stability.
Israeli attacks cast doubt on will to make deal
Tensions over Syria were brought into focus last week when Israel bombed the Abu al-Duhur airbase, saying Damascus was about to allow Turkish forces to deploy there. Syria and Turkiye denied the claim.
Al-Shaibani said Syria respected Israel’s security concerns but that it must also respect those of Damascus, instead of violating its airspace and conducting raids and arrests in the south of the country.
He said earlier this year, the two sides had “agreed on paper to almost everything” regarding a security deal that would require Israel to stop attacking Syria and was tied to its withdrawal from territory seized after al-Assad fell.
That deal would include several security zones in Syrian territory near the Israeli border, including a buffer zone where only the United Nations would be present, and others where Syrian forces would deploy in varying degrees of force.
However, he said, Israel had sought to evade implementation, adding: “We did not see they had the real will to reach an agreement.”
Golan Heights a sticking point
Syria and Israel have technically been in a state of war since 1948. Israel seized the Golan Heights from Syria in the Six-Day War of 1967.
Al-Shaibani said the priority now is to “stop Israeli aggression even before reaching a security agreement”, and then “perhaps we can open the topics of peace and the Golan”.
Israeli officials have indicated they are not willing to return the Golan Heights to the al-Sharaa government.
US special envoy for Syria, Tom Barrack, said last week that Washington was working to establish a mechanism to prevent conflict among Israel, Turkiye and Syria.
Al-Shaibani said there was no agreement yet on the mechanism, which he said must stop attacks and pave the way for the security deal rather than “entrenching … Israeli occupation”.
The US Department of State did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Al-Shaibani said Israel had bombed Abu al-Duhur even after Syria conveyed a message that it would not be a Turkish base.
Syria draws on Turkish support in military training and cooperation, he said, noting that this was also the case with Jordan, Saudi Arabia and others.
Damascus was thankful for Turkiye’s support in rebuilding its military, “and we won’t forgo support”, he said.

US comedy star trapped in Hermès toilet for 80 minutes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
10:29:58 UTC
19:29:58 KST

What started as a brief visit to a Hermès store ended badly for US comedian Zarna Garg: she was stuck for 80 minutes in the Berlin shop's toilet and now blames the retailer.
Indian-American comedian Zarna Garg, who has made a name for herself with her humorous take on the lives of Indian immigrants, has circulated a story about her experience in a luxury shop on Berlin’s Kurfürstendamm.
Garg, who is currently in Berlin as part of her comedy tour, posted footage of the incident on Instagram (source in German).
Shortly after using the toilet at the Hermès store, the comedian tried to open the sliding door, but it jammed.
At first, Garg saw the funny side and, together with her team, started filming the wait to be rescued. She even made little origami figures out of paper towels. But as more and more time passed, the situation stopped being amusing.
According to Garg, staff initially tried to force the door open on their own.
Crowbar and store alarm
The staff asked her to push against the door from the inside while they used a crowbar. To make matters worse, the alarm went off during the attempt. Garg said she was afraid the crowbar might injure her, while her daughter and her team stayed outside and watched the increasingly tense rescue attempt.
Garg said her team pressed staff to call the fire brigade, but they hesitated, according to Garg, because they were worried the door might be damaged.
After 80 minutes, she was finally freed by Berlin’s fire brigade.
After the incident, Garg said she was relieved that a fire had not broken out on top of everything else. She had been worried about being locked behind a door which, in her view, was cheap and flimsy and might not have met the required fire safety standards.
Garg turns down offer of champagne
For Garg, the ordeal did not end there. After she was freed, no one apologised to her, explained what had happened, or even tried to speak to her, despite the fact that she had been shut in for more than an hour.
Instead, a member of staff approached her with a bottle of champagne – apparently as a gesture of compensation. Garg and her team turned the offer down.
Her family had to watch everything unfold
What particularly upset Garg was that her children and her team had to witness the dramatic rescue operation from outside. They watched helplessly as staff tried to open the door. Afterwards, she says, nobody looked after them or tried to reassure them.
In the end, the comedian responded with the humour that has become her trademark: she drew a pointed comparison with Hermès bags, joking that they are famously often difficult to open and close – just like the bathroom door that had trapped her.
Her final verdict was far less light-hearted: she described the incident as a story of a "useless bag, a useless door and useless people".
Her post has sparked a wave of reactions on social media.
Many users argued that a simple apology and an acknowledgement of the incident would have been more appropriate than a "gift".
Hermès has not issued a statement. Garg said she understood that the luxury brand might be holding back due to potential legal consequences and pointed to her own legal background.
Before her career as a comedian, Garg worked in New York as a civil litigation lawyer – specifically in personal injury law and compensation claims.
Euronews has contacted Hermès for comment.

The ruling Adilet Party led with 71.17 percent of the vote, followed by the Auyl Party with 6.26 percent, the commission said.
Kazakhstan's new Constitution, which took effect on July 1, provides for a 145-member unicameral parliament, with deputies serving five-year terms. The country previously had a bicameral parliament.
Kazakhstan held its first Kurultai election on Sunday, with 545 candidates from seven political parties contesting the vote. Final results are expected to be announced within 10 days after voting ends. ■

Thailand's labor market expands 5.1 pct in Q2
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
18:32:18 CST
19:32:18 KST

BANGKOK, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Thailand's labor market continued to grow in the second quarter of 2026 due to increases in both agricultural and non-farm employment, led by the construction sector, official data showed on Monday.
The number of employed persons in the Southeast Asian country rose 5.1 percent year-on-year to 41.5 million in the April-June period, accelerating from a 4.6 percent gain in the previous quarter, according to the National Economic and Social Development Council (NESDC).
Agricultural employment increased 6.5 percent from a year earlier, supported by higher farm output and agricultural prices, even as delayed rainfall pushed up the seasonally inactive labor force, the state planning agency said in a statement.
Meanwhile, the non-farm sector expanded 4.5 percent, benefiting from an 8.3 percent pickup in construction jobs in line with stronger private investment and a 5.8 percent increase in hotel and restaurant employment fueled by growing domestic tourism, particularly during long-holiday periods.
However, the nation's overall unemployment rate stood at 0.95 percent in the second quarter, representing around 400,000 unemployed individuals, edging up from 0.91 percent in the same period last year, said NESDC secretary-general Danucha Pichayanan.
The number of quasi-unemployed individuals working fewer than 24 hours per week climbed 8 percent year-on-year, driven by elevated underemployment, especially in the non-agricultural sector, Danucha told a news conference.
Looking ahead, he identified employment risks in the farm sector owing to the El Nino weather pattern, which is expected to intensify toward the year's end as lower rainfall and longer dry spells have already caused drought conditions in several areas, putting more pressure on agricultural production and rural labor. ■

Why Vijay scrapped Chennai’s second airport plan at Parandur
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
10:22:19 UTC
19:22:19 KST

Why Vijay scrapped Chennai’s second airport plan at Parandur
Edited by: Ayush Pandey / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 24, 2026, 15:56 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay
NEW DELHI: Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay on Monday announced that his government would abandon the proposed greenfield airport project at Parandur, saying the project would affect agricultural land and disrupt the livelihoods of farmers and residents.The announcement was made in the assembly as Vijay said Chennai still needed a new airport to meet rising passenger demand, industrial growth and increasing cargo movement. However, he said the new airport should be located at a site where agricultural and residential areas would face minimal disruption."To fulfill the promise I made to the people that day... the steps taken to establish a new airport in Parandur will be abandoned by this government," Vijay said.The government is now considering alternative locations and plans to conduct technical feasibility studies before finalising a new site.
Why Vijay rejected Parandur
Vijay said he had visited Eganapuram and other villages on January 20, 2025, and heard the grievances of residents protesting against the proposed airport in Parandur and 12 surrounding villages."I stand firmly with the people protesting against the airport to be established in Chennai's Parandur and 12 surrounding villages," he said.
The chief minister said farmers were the backbone of the country and backed those protesting to protect their agricultural land.Vijay said he had also opposed the Parandur project at a public meeting in Vikravandi in October 2024, while making clear that he supported industrial development and the role of airports in it."However, this project should not be located in Parandur. The government must reconsider this project," he said.He added that an alternative site should be identified where the impact on agricultural land and people's livelihoods would be minimal.
Chennai airport to be expanded
While dropping Parandur, the government said Chennai's existing airport would be expanded.Vijay said the Meenambakkam airport, operated by the Airports Authority of India, currently has the capacity to handle around 30 million passengers annually. With the under-construction Terminal 3 becoming operational, capacity is expected to rise to 34 million passengers a year.The government plans to expand the airport on its north-western side by constructing a fifth terminal, which is expected to handle another 20 million passengers annually.The government is also considering alternative sites for a new airport, with technical feasibility studies to be conducted by expert teams.
Why Parandur was chosen
The Parandur project had received in-principle approval from the Civil Aviation Ministry in April 2025 for an International Greenfield Airport in Kancheepuram district.The proposed project had faced opposition from residents of villages that were expected to be affected by land acquisition and construction.However, the DMK has criticised the decision to abandon the project, arguing that it could hurt Tamil Nadu's industrial growth and investment prospects.Former chief minister and DMK president MK Stalin said dropping the project would set the state's development back by several years."The announcement made today by the Hon'ble Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu to drop the Parandur International Airport project will set the state's development back by several years. Tamil Nadu's interests cannot be mortgaged for petty political considerations," Stalin said.He also called the decision a setback to employment opportunities for Tamil Nadu's youth.
DMK warns of economic fallout
Former Tamil Nadu minister and DMK MLA Thangam Thennarasu also criticised the decision, saying the Parandur site was selected after studying options for establishing two runways."Possibilities for setting up two runways were all studied and only then Parandur was selected," he said.Thennarasu argued that scrapping the project for political reasons could hurt the state's economy and push industries towards neighbouring Andhra Pradesh."It would be best to have the airport at Parandur. Dropping the Parandur Airport project for political reasons will cause economic damage," he said."Many industries will move towards Andhra Pradesh. We have already lost the Hosur Airport," he added.Thennarasu also said compensation had already been provided to people whose land was acquired for the project and cited the Land Acquisition Act while arguing that the acquired land should be used for its intended purpose.
The announcement triggered an immediate confrontation in the Tamil Nadu Assembly, with DMK MLAs staging a walkout after Speaker JCD Prabhakar denied DMK leader KN Nehru permission to respond to the statement, citing Assembly rules.The opposition accused the government of making a policy U-turn that could affect Tamil Nadu's industrial momentum and prospects of attracting investment.Vijay, however, maintained that the government supports airport-led industrial development but believes the proposed airport should not come at the cost of agricultural land and people's livelihoods.

His reporting focuses on elections, national security, and institutional affairs, tracking the decisions and conflicts that shape public life.
He specialises in sharp explainers and in-depth feature stories that go beyond headlines to decode political shifts, defence strategy, geopolitical flashpoints, and changing public sentiment. His work combines speed, clarity, and depth for a fast-moving digital audience.

DMK chief MK Stalin moves Madras High Court challenging TVK candidate VS Babu's victory in Kolathur
NEW DELHI: Former Tamil Nadu chief minister and DMK president MK Stalin on Monday moved the Madras high court challenging the victory of TVK candidate VS Babu from Kolathur in the assembly elections.In his petition, Stalin alleged malfunctions in voting machines and irregularities involving VVPAT machines, and sought an order for a recount of votes in the Kolathur constituency.Stalin also sought a declaration that Babu's election be declared void and that he himself be declared the winner.In the Tamil Nadu Assembly polls, Babu defeated Stalin by a margin of 8,795 votes.Following the results, VS Babu attributed his victory to party chief Vijay and his local connection. Touching upon the anti-incumbency factor, Babu said that his win came against the backdrop of people's desire for change in Tamil Nadu."I have won only with our leader. Our leader's face is the face of Tamil Nadu. People wanted a change, and they have changed this. I was born and brought up in that area. We know the pulse of people. It's we who made him (MK Stalin) enter Kolathur," Babu had told news agency ANI after his victory.
"He doesn't know anyone in Kolathur. Whether he is CM or MLA, he should mingle with the local people first. People are watching it," he had added.
Stalin was a three-time MLA from Kolathur but could not retain the seat for a fourth consecutive term. Despite the setback, Stalin thanked voters, noting that the DMK alliance secured over 1.54 crore votes, with a narrow 3.52 percent difference from the winning party.
